On March 11, 2026, the French version of this Universal Registration Document was filed with the French 
Financial Markets Authority (Autorité des marchés financiers, AMF), the competent authority pursuant to (EU) 
Regulation No. 2017/1129, without prior approval, in accordance with Article 9 of said regulation.
The French version of this Universal Registration Document may be used for the purposes of a public offer of 
securities or the admission of securities to trading on a regulated market if it is supplemented with a securities 
note and, if required, a summary note, as well as all updates made to the Universal Registration Document. The 
whole is then approved by the AMF in accordance with (EU) Regulation No. 2017/1129.
This Universal Registration Document is a reproduction in PDF format, translated in English, of the official 
version of the universal registration document established in ESEF (European Single Electronic Format), which 
was filed with the AMF on March 11, 2026 and available on the AMF website: https://www.amf-france.org/en
.
This reproduction is available on our website www.saint-gobain.com.
It is not a binding document. In the event of a conflict of interpretation, reference should be made to the 
French version which is the original text. The auditors’ report applies to the French version of the Management 
Report and the financial statements.

Editorial
n a global environment undergoing 
profound transformation, Saint-Gobain 
once again demonstrated its robust 
operational performance in 2025, 
attesting to the relevance of its 
strategy as worldwide leader in light 
and sustainable construction. With a legacy 
spanning 360 years, Saint-Gobain’s long-term 
vision is fully aligned with its purpose: “Making 
the World a Better Home”.
The current context is very challenging. Economic 
tensions, geopolitical shocks, rising uncertainties 
and de-globalization are rapidly reshaping 
global balances. However, in this fragmented and 
unsettled world, Saint-Gobain has a solid 
governance structure, with a country-based, 
decentralized operating model in place in all our 
regions. This is a fundamental asset because it 
ensures we have a close relationship with our 
customers in local construction markets 
and allows us to adapt with agility to different 
opportunities and situations. Our annual financial 
results, which are both very solid and resilient, 
confirm the relevance of our strategic 
and organizational choices.
Moreover, Saint-Gobain’s medium- and long-term 
growth prospects are very promising because the 
Group provides essential solutions to the major 
challenges of our time: rapid urbanization and 
population growth, the housing crisis, energy 
efficiency and the green transition of buildings 
and infrastructure, adaptation to climate events 
and protection of natural resources via the circular 
economy. Saint-Gobain is ideally positioned 
to meet these challenges as a leader in all major 
regions and its solutions-based approach offers 
performance and sustainability in construction, 
combining a wide range of products and systems 
with recognized expertise.
The “Grow & Impact” plan covering 2021 to 2025 
was a success. We achieved all our financial, 
non-financial and strategic objectives 
by profoundly modernizing Saint-Gobain. 
We renewed and rebalanced our geographical 
presence, with Europe, North America, Asia 
and emerging markets now contributing equally 
to our results. And we invested boldly to create a 
leading global platform in construction chemicals.
2026 sees the launch of the “Lead & Grow” plan, 
which will open a new chapter of profitable 
growth. Between now and 2030, we will continue 
to enhance and extend our solutions and will 
expand and accelerate their roll-out in the 
non-residential buildings and infrastructure 
markets, which already account for nearly a third 
of our sales. Saint-Gobain will pursue its 
development in high-growth geographical areas, 
while continuing to strengthen its positions 
in construction chemicals, a critical element 
of differentiation and value creation 
in sustainable construction. 
I would like to thank all the women and men 
at Saint-Gobain around the world for their 
exceptional commitment in their daily work, 
which is critical for the implementation 
of our strategy. Nearly 70,000 of our employees 
are shareholders, demonstrating their confidence 
in the Group’s future. 
Our experienced and dedicated Board 
of Directors provides Saint-Gobain with solid 
governance, reflecting the Group’s international 
development. 
More than ever, Saint-Gobain is facing the future 
with confidence, clarity and ambition. History 
has taught us that sustainable performance 
requires innovation, responsibility, solidarity 
and the mobilization of everyone around shared 
values. Based on these convictions, we are 
building tomorrow’s growth and success 
every day.

Our solutions-based approach WHAT WE DO
WE COMBINE OUR EXPERTISE THROUGH 
A SOLUTIONS-BASED APPROACH
A solution is much more than just a product. It is a complete, high-performance offering. It brings our materials 
together with high-value-added services – consulting, logistics, digital tools – and can include a combination 
of multiple products or a recommended suite of products and systems. Each solution is designed to precisely meet 
the needs of our customers. By delivering performance to our customers and supporting them in all aspects of a 
project, from design to delivery of complete, integrated solutions, we stand out from the competition and position 
ourselves as the worldwide leader in light and sustainable construction.

OUR SOLUTIONS-BASED APPROACH
SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 7
How Saint-Gobain transforms its customers’ 
expectations into concrete solutions
WHAT IS THE SOLUTIONS-BASED 
APPROACH?
It’s very simple: at Saint-Gobain, everything starts 
with a discussion. A project is first and foremost 
an intention: improve comfort, reduce the 
carbon footprint, renovate an old building, 
or build faster. We start with this intention then 
build the response by combining materials, 
systems, and services. Lastly, a solution is the 
intelligent assembly of everything that will make 
the project a success. This approach works for 
all our markets. A solution can be as much about 
providing a craftsman with a product accompanied 
by a service as it is about supporting a construction 
or renovation megaproject, right from the 
specification phase.
AND ON A CONSTRUCTION SITE? 
WHAT DIFFERENCE DOES IT MAKE?
On the ground, it changes everything. Take the 
example of more efficient façades with the 
EnveoVent range, which combines insulation, 
acoustics, and fire resistance in a single wall system, 
while reducing CO₂ emissions compared with 
conventional methods. This solution was created 
by combining several areas of expertise 
(insulation, structure, glazing, etc.) to address 
concrete performance and sustainability 
challenges. Another example: Cool-Lite Xtreme 
Oraé glazing solutions demonstrate that it is possible 
to combine highly effective solar control, particularly 
for summer comfort, and a significant reduction 
in the carbon intensity of the material.
Superior quality and maximum 
comfort characterize the 
Varso complex, located 
in Poland’s capital. 
All three buildings have 
earned the BREEAM 
“Excellent” certification 
(environmental assessment 
standard) and the WELL 
Building Standard 
certification 
(corporate well-being).
On this project, Saint-Gobain 
provided solutions for 
partitions, ceilings, floors, 
glazing, insulation, and 
construction chemicals.
HOW TO CREATE THE CONDITIONS 
FOR PROXIMITY TO OUR CUSTOMERS?
Our multi-local organization is based on a strong, 
decentralized presence in the field. Our teams know 
the craftsmen, architects, construction methods, 
regulatory requirements, voluntary initiatives (labels 
and certifications), and specific climatic conditions 
of their region. This allows worldwide solutions to 
be adapted to very local needs – since construction 
methods vary greatly from one region to another – 
always with the same design quality. Today, these 
solutions are deployed in residential, non-
residential, and infrastructure projects, reducing 
lead times while ensuring performance and 
sustainability.
HOW DOES THIS ALIGN WITH THE ENERGY 
AND DECARBONIZATION CHALLENGES 
AND CIRCULARITY OBJECTIVES?
We place sustainability at the heart of our approach, 
not only by working to continually reduce 
the environmental footprint of our industrial 
operations, but also by bringing to the market 
solutions that optimize energy efficiency, 
contribute to preserving resources, and help
our customers reduce their own carbon 
footprint. For example, solutions combining thermal 
insulation and CO₂ reduction have reduced the 
carbon footprint of residential buildings in Germany 
by up to 23% and harnessed the full potential of light 
construction by lightening the walls by up to 80% 
for the Wits Museum in Johannesburg 
(South Africa), while maintaining the same 
performance. We also do our utmost – for example –
to collect construction waste to reintroduce 
it into our products, such as Placo® Infinaé 50 
and 100 boards (respectively for 50% and 100% 
of materials derived from recycled 
end-of-life plaster).
“A solution is the story of a 
project designed together”

Markets and activities
WHAT WE DO
WE PROVIDE COMPLETE SOLUTIONS 
FOR ALL CONSTRUCTION MARKETS
Through its wide range of activities, from insulation to roofing and façade products, as well 
as plaster, ceilings, construction chemicals, glazing, materials trading and services, technical textiles, 
and solutions for industry and mobility, Saint-Gobain demonstrates its worldwide leadership in 
light and sustainable construction. The Group is also committed to improving quality of life while 
respecting the environment. Saint-Gobain’s ability to combine all its expertise makes the Group, 
on a global scale, the only provider of complete solutions for new construction and renovation 
in the residential, non-residential, and infrastructure markets.

WE SPECIFY 
INTEGRATED SUITES OF SOLUTIONS
On the construction site of the university hospital center in Nantes, one of the 
largest in Europe, Saint-Gobain was involved through about fifteen of its brands. 
The Group is one of the worldwide leaders in the non-residential market, where 
demand is substantial: schools, hospitals, hotels, and public buildings. We are fully 
implementing our strategy by offering integrated responses to all our customers’ 
expectations, from insulation to acoustics, energy savings, and the circular 
economy. This approach fully showcases innovation, the eco-design of our 
products, and the quality of our services. Among our most innovative solutions 
are EnveoVent Duo, a lightweight low-carbon façade system, as well as interior 
and insulation solutions from Placo®, Isover, and Ecophon, which incorporate 
recycled raw materials and combine high thermal and acoustic performance, 
essential in hospital environments. By engaging very early in large, complex 
projects, Saint-Gobain is able to offer the project owner, the project manager, 
and all partners solutions that are innovative, low-carbon, and economical.

C H A L L E N G E S  A N D  O P P O R T U N I T I E S
Saint-Gobain is the worldwide leader in light 
and sustainable construction. We are a 
leader in Europe, North America, Australia, 
the Middle East, Latin America, and India. 
We offer our customers an unrivaled range 
of solutions tailored to their needs in the 
residential, non-residential, or infrastructure 
sector. Our solutions cover the interior 
and exterior building envelope as well as 
construction chemicals, and our distribution 
network allows us to design integrated 
solutions for construction sites. We offer 
our customers the ability to build faster 
and more efficiently, while reducing their 
carbon footprint and use of raw materials, 
and we are uniquely positioned to meet their 
needs for complete solutions, particularly 
for the overall performance of a building.
Through our low-carbon solutions, we offer 
an integrated approach to meet the needs 
of buildings with environmental certifications. 
We are uniquely able to coordinate the 
entire value chain, from architects 
to developers, to meet the challenges 
of our world.
In addition, our organization is designed 
to offer us new growth opportunities: 
our country platforms are in charge 
of deploying the Group’s entire solutions 
offering in each region, drawing on an 
in-depth, precise understanding of local 
market dynamics, customers, and 
distribution channels. These country 
platforms give us an advantage in 
identifying our acquisition targets or 
integrating them. They allow us to replicate 
our model from one country to another 
by gradually deploying our entire offering 
across all our countries. And they benefit 
from the expertise of the entire Group 
thanks to the cross-functionality of 
commercial and industrial excellence 
and innovation functions.
It is this unique combination of a vision, 
an unrivaled breadth of offerings, and 
an organization dedicated to growth 
that forms the DNA of Saint-Gobain. 
More than ever, we are ready to deliver 
on the promises of our purpose: 
“Making the world a better home".

Our strategy
OUR STRATEGY
PERFECT ALIGNMENT BETWEEN 
OUR PURPOSE, OUR VISION, 
AND OUR STRATEGIC PLAN
After “Grow & Impact”, we have adopted a new strategic plan: “Lead & Grow". 
We want to accelerate our profitable growth by addressing the challenges of a rapidly changing world: global 
demand for construction (residential, non-residential, and infrastructure), climate change mitigation and adaptation, 
and natural resource protection. 
Lead, because we want to be a leader of opinion, the catalyst for change, and the pioneer of a fast-changing sector 
by being the partner of choice for our customers, mobilizing our teams, and shaping a sustainable growth model 
for the entire construction sector, but also because we are the worldwide leader in light and sustainable construction. 
Grow, because, building on what we have achieved, we want to take our growth to new heights, based on an 
expanded and enriched offering in each country, making us stronger, more resilient, and more profitable.

WHY IS SAINT-GOBAIN 
MORE INTERESTED 
IN THESE MARKETS?
Because these markets are very dynamic. 
Airports, roads, tunnels, bridges, power plants, 
metro and rail networks, data centers, hospitals, 
schools, hotels: demand is soaring, and these 
projects require high-performance, certified, 
reliable solutions. The infrastructure market 
is particularly driven by the need for new 
infrastructure in emerging countries, linked to 
their economic development and demographic 
growth, especially transport and energy 
infrastructure; by the growing need for the 
renovation of infrastructure in developed 
countries; but also by growing expectations 
in terms of electricity supply and energy 
independence, which fuel the need for energy 
production infrastructure.
WHAT DO YOU BRING TO THESE 
PROJECTS IN PRACTICAL TERMS? 
We already have the materials and systems 
suited for these demanding environments, and 
it is a field where our expertise can truly shine. 
The strong presence we have built in the field 
of construction chemistry is, for us, a gateway 
to this market; but infrastructure projects go far 
beyond that, and we are capable, for example, 
of combining all our expertise for an airport 
megaproject, from technical textiles for 
reinforcing taxiways to additives and admixtures 
for concrete, as well as all interior and exterior 
solutions (including glazing) for reception 
and logistics buildings.
WHAT IS THE IMPACT 
ON THE GROUP’S BUSINESS MODEL 
AND PERFORMANCE?
By expanding our presence in infrastructure 
and non-residential sectors, we are balancing 
our exposure and reducing dependency 
on residential cycles. These projects are also 
opportunities to continue to improve our 
offering and demonstrate the added value 
of our solutions-based approach. For the Long 
Thanh airport, Saint-Gobain provided 15 solutions 
from across its entire range, offering a much 
wider range than any of its competitors. On every 
tunnel, every hospital, every bridge, every 
school, every power station, it is about proving 
that we are concretely involved in the 
construction and renovation of infrastructure 
and non-residential buildings and making them 
safer, more sustainable, and more efficient. 
It is this combination of technical challenges 
and tangible contributions that makes 
the infrastructure and non-residential market 
particularly stimulating.
Long Thanh Airport will soon be Vietnam’s largest 
airport. At an estimated cost of $18 billion, it is designed 
to accommodate 100 million passengers and five million 
tonnes of cargo per year. The project will be developed 
in four phases, the first including a terminal and two 
runways (2025). 
Three more terminals and additional runways, covering 
an area of more than 10,000 hectares, are expected 
to be completed by 2035. Saint-Gobain’s expertise is at 
the heart of the project, with multiple solutions ranging 
from construction chemicals to technical textiles and 
stone wool.

of the economy: our ambition 
in the infrastructure and

OUR STRATEGY
BY DEPLOYING OUR COUNTRY-BY-COUNTRY 
SOLUTIONS APPROACH, WE CAPTURE 
GROWTH OPPORTUNITIES
Saint-Gobain systematically expands and enriches its offering to cover all aspects of sustainable construction, 
with a coherent, connected suite of value-added solutions. This is the model that was deployed, for example, in India: 
starting from strong positions in glazing and gypsum a decade ago, we have expanded our offering, mainly through 
organic growth but also through acquisitions. Today, Saint-Gobain provides its customers in this country with unique 
solutions, such as its low-carbon solar-controlled glass and its sealing systems. The Group has become a leading 
reference in India for glass and gypsum as well as for insulation and construction chemicals. In doing so, Saint-Gobain 
has enjoyed robust growth in its sales and margin, with revenue quadrupling and operating margin increasing 
sixfold over nearly 10 years.

OUR COMMITMENTS
WE PLACE OUR COMMITMENT 
TO RESPONSIBILITY AT THE HEART 
OF OUR STRATEGY 
This approach guides all the decisions of the Group, which has a dual commitment: maximize its positive impact 
while reducing its environmental and social footprint. CSR challenges are integrated into the Group’s value-creation 
model (see section 1.2.6, p. 57) and strategy. Saint-Gobain’s corporate purpose (“Making the world a better home”), 
its vision (to be the worldwide leader in light and sustainable construction), and its strategic plan (“Lead & Grow”) 
are perfectly aligned. For each of the challenges, Saint-Gobain defines action plans and objectives that are 
deployed in a decentralized manner at the country level. Thus, thanks to its solutions, Saint-Gobain contributes 
to three long-term ambitions.

1.1.2 MARKETS ON A STRUCTURAL GROWTH PATH
Saint-Gobain’s business is structurally driven by 
underlying trends (see section 1.2.1.A, p. 39) that provide 
the Group with long-term growth drivers, not only in the 
residential market but also in the non-residential and 
infrastructure markets. Saint-Gobain relies on a robust 
organizational model based on country platforms as 
management units, grouped into five major regions: 
Northern Europe, Southern Europe – Middle East – Africa, 
North America, Latin America, and Asia-Pacific (see “Our 
global footprint,” pp.  12 and 13). With an industrial 
presence in 80 countries , the Group benefits from 
growth opportunities in every major region of the world.
A – Western Europe
In Western Europe, a recovery is expected in the 
residential markets, which have seen a contraction in 
recent years due to the inflation surge of 2022-2024 and 
the rise in real estate rates. Building permits and housing 
starts are increasing in countries that  are  important to 
the Group, such as France, the  United Kingdom, 
Germany, and Sweden. As of late November 2025, 
building permits were up 14% year-on-year in France  (1). 
The decline in activity in  recent years has exacerbated 
the housing shortage and the housing crisis in Europe, 
degrading property purchasing power and encouraging 
governments to support housing construction . In the 
United Kingdom, for example, there is a shortfall of 
2.5 million homes, and the current government aims to 
build 1.5  million homes between 2025 and 2029, which 
represents a clear acceleration from the construction 
levels of the last decade. 
The winds are also favorable for building renovation. In 
addition to the ongoing recovery in real estate 
transactions in most European countries, which are an 
important driver of renovation, energy renovation is 
supported by public measures , both at the European 
and national levels. In addition to European regulatory 
mechanisms, such as the Energy Performance of 
Buildings Directive (EPBD), many European countries 
have adopted regulatory arrangements (such as the 
Climate and Resilience Act in France, which prohibits the 
leasing of energy-inefficient residences), subsidies, and 
market mechanisms (such as energy saving certificates 
in Spain). Energy renovation also offers significant 
financial benefits for households, through its ability to 
reduce energy bills on the one hand, and also because of 
the growing influence of energy efficiency on  property 
prices. In many European countries, price differentials 
between the most and least energy-efficient homes 
exceed 15%, even comparing homes with equivalent 
structural characteristics: this is the case in the 
Netherlands, for example, as well as in Germany, France, 
Italy and Spain. Non-residential and infrastructure 
markets are also drivers in Europe. 
The need for reindustrialization, particularly in the 
defense sector, and the development of data centers 
represent sources of growth for new construction, while 
the energy renovation of tertiary buildings, both public 
and private, maintains its growth level. In the 
infrastructure sector, some European governments have 
ambitious development projects planned; this is notably 
the case in Germany, where the new €500  billion 
Infrastructure Fund will significantly increase activity in 
this sector over the next 10 years. The requirements of 
renovating aging infrastructure on the continent, 
including bridges and tunnels, offer complementary 
opportunities. Finally, the increasing effects of climate 
crises on buildings, both residential and non-residential, 
imply significant adaptation needs . The solutions 
offered by Saint-Gobain for renovation are perfectly 
adapted to these new needs. For example, protecting 
buildings against heat waves involves insulating external 
walls or installing solar control glass. Similarly, the 
Group’s construction chemicals solutions meet the need 
for buildings to be watertight, against violent rains or 
floods, for example. 
B – North America 
In North America, the housing shortage  is a very 
important factor in the structural growth  of 
Saint-Gobain’s business in the residential sector. In the 
US, the pace of construction in the decade following the 
2008 global financial crisis did not keep up with 
population growth, and the shortfall is currently 
estimated at 3.7  million homes  (2), which represents 
nearly 3 years’ worth of construction at the current pace. 
In Canada, strong population growth over the past 
decade, fueled by dynamic immigration, has also led to 
severe housing shortages, exacerbating the housing 
affordability crisis: an additional 5  million homes would 
be needed to meet the needs and restore the housing 
purchasing power of Canadian households (3). 
Furthermore, the frequency of hurricanes, fires and 
storms, which is unfortunately accentuated by climate 
change, implies non-discretionary renovation needs , 
which represent a source of sustainable growth for the 
Group’s roofing and cladding business in the region. The 
increase in such climatic events due to the climate 
crisis will generate significant adaptation needs in the 
coming years. 
Finally, the non-residential and infrastructure markets 
also benefit from solid structural fundamentals. The 
reindustrialization policies of successive US 
governments, as well as the trend towards reshoring 
industries on US soil, are driving growth in the industrial 
buildings market and the rise of data centers represents 
a significant source of growth. As in Europe, 
infrastructure needs remain high, particularly in terms 
of renovation.

C – Asia and fast-growing regions
Emerging countries are experiencing strong population 
growth, combined with rapid urbanization. The global 
population will increase from 8.2 billion in 2024 to nearly 
10 billion by 2080 (1), and most of this increase will take 
place in emerging countries. Similarly, the urban 
population is expected to grow by almost 2  billion by 
2050, particularly in Asia and Africa. In addition, around 
1.1 billion people currently live in informal settlements and 
are still waiting for decent housing (2). Based on this data, 
the World Economic Forum estimates that  new 
residential construction needs  worldwide will  reach 
2 billion homes over the next 80 years. 
Emerging countries are also experiencing economic 
development trajectories favoring strong growth of the 
middle classes , whose desire for quality housing 
perfectly matches Saint-Gobain’s offer. In India, the 
number of households entering the middle class will 
increase by an average of 16% per year by 2030. This 
growth has also reached 11% in Indonesia, and 21% in 
Vietnam. Urbanization will also continue in the Middle 
East and Latin America : in Brazil, for example, 
the  middle class is expected to grow by nearly 4% 
annually over the coming years  (3). This demographic 
growth and its associated urbanization imply significant 
needs for the expansion of  cities, with consequential 
tertiary housing and  infrastructure needs, representing 
complementary sources of business for the Group. Some 
countries are  starting to build new cities or ambitious 
urban development projects. In Egypt, 37 new cities are 
under construction, and Saudi Arabia is currently 
building 14 large-scale projects to support its economic 
diversification program.
D – Industrial markets
For its industrial customers , Saint-Gobain provides 
performance solutions and meets market expectations 
through its ability to innovate , its research and 
development potential, its closeness to its customers, 
and its use of digital technology and data analysis. 
Industrial markets are expected to continue to grow 
steadily over the 2025-2030 period, driven by 
reindustrialization and strategic autonomy efforts in 
developed countries, ramped-up military spending, and 
the development of new industrial sectors associated 
with “green” technologies. 
The mobility market, in which Saint-Gobain is present 
through a range of insulation, acoustics, and technical 
glazing solutions, is undergoing expansion fueled by the 
natural turnover of car fleets, the transition to electric 
vehicles, and the relocation of value chains by auto 
manufacturers, trends that will structurally drive the 
Group’s business in the coming years.

1.1.3 A SOLUTIONS-BASED APPROACH, 
ROLLED OUT COUNTRY BY COUNTRY 
Saint-Gobain relies on the support of a robust organization that is well suited to a deglobalized world, as well as 
local construction markets. It is based on country platforms as managerial units, which are grouped into five major 
regions: Northern Europe, Southern Europe – Middle East – Africa, North America, Latin America, and Asia-Pacific. 
Within each of these regions, the country CEOs are responsible for all Saint-Gobain product lines, to provide a 
comprehensive response to the most complex needs of their customers, through a solutions-based approach. 
Country by country, Saint-Gobain is deploying this approach in all its markets – residential as well as non-residential 
and infrastructure.
A – Construction and renovation markets
a. Residential
In all its countries, Saint-Gobain has successfully 
deployed a solutions-based approach, enabling it to 
position itself as a “one-stop shop,” a leading supplier of 
integrated solutions both for renovation  and new 
construction of single-family houses and multi-
family housing.
The Group provides a comprehensive range of solutions 
dedicated to the global renovation of housing,  which 
help improve their energy performance, acoustic and 
visual comfort, as well as air quality. In France, for 
example, a customer looking to undertake a  residential 
renovation project can find an integrated offering from 
Saint-Gobain that covers all their needs. First of all, this 
offering includes comprehensive renovation systems, 
particularly external thermal insulation solutions 
combining insulating materials, plasterboard, profiles, 
mortars, fiberglass reinforcement, and finish coats, as 
well as solar-control insulated glazing units and blow-in 
insulation for attics. When combined, these solutions 
help cut a residence’s energy bill by 70%, and 
significantly improve its energy performance diagnosis 
(EPD), raising it from class G to class C.
Saint-Gobain supplements this offering with digital 
solutions available through its distribution businesses, 
making it easier to conduct assessments and issue price 
quotes for improving building energy performance. The 
Group also provides services intended to improve 
productivity for craftsmen on worksites , such as 
logistics and kitting solutions. Aware of the 
environmental issues, Saint -Gobain also provides 
worksite waste collection and sorting services, relying 
on a network of 810 collection and sorting points in 
France, particularly at Point.P stores. Finally, the Group 
invests heavily in training professionals: each year, over 
100,000 craftsmen are trained and supported in France 
on energy renovation issues. 
In North America, and particularly in Canada in the past 
few years, the Group has expanded its offering 
dedicated to lightweight construction , in order to 
provide a comprehensive solution for the building 
envelope, helping improve the quality of buildings and 
their resilience against climate change.
Saint-Gobain stands out in particular by offering 
complete systems for the customer . For example, the 
Group markets integrated roofing systems under the 
CertainTeed brand combining waterproofing 
membranes, impact-resistant ClimateFlex shingles, and 
their associated accessories. These solutions help 
buildings better withstand storms and guarantee roof 
insurability. The Group also develops siding systems that 
are highly resistant to moisture and impacts, while 
providing its customers with interactive digital tools that 
make it easier to choose and customize solutions. 
CertainTeed’s One Precision Assemblies system is 
another example that helps significantly reduce project 
completion times . Pre-assembled panels featuring 
windows, doors, siding, roofing, insulation, storm-
proofing and vapor barrier membranes are produced in 
one week. Once delivered to a modular home worksite, 
they can be installed in under three weeks, compared 
with five months for a construction using traditional 
methods. 
To replace traditional, heavy-construction methods 
which devour resources, time, and labor, Saint-Gobain 
has developed lightweight façade solutions which are 
both ultra-high performance and easy to install . In 
Brazil, for example, such solutions combine Glasroc X 
board, a moisture-resistant fiberglass-reinforced 
plasterboard (Placo and Adfors), glass wool insulation 
(Isover), fiber cement sheets (Brasilit), as well as 
fiberglass reinforcement mesh and joint tape (Adfors), 
and finish coats (Quartzolit) These systems are 
supplemented by technical consulting and project 
monitoring services.  They make it possible to 
significantly improve productivity on worksites , 
particularly in multi-family housing, respond to labor 
shortage issues, reduce waste, and offer superior 
performance – in terms of quality, energy efficiency, and 
occupant comfort – compared with traditional methods.

c. Infrastructure
Over the past five years, Saint-Gobain has built a place for 
itself as a top global leader in construction chemicals. The 
Group now offers solutions to meet the needs of 
worksites and structures, particularly mortars, concrete 
admixtures, cement additives, waterproofing solutions for 
buildings and infrastructure, flooring, and façades, 
concrete repair solutions, adhesives, joint tape and 
adhesive systems. This offering is based on leading brands 
like Weber, Chryso, Fosroc, and GCP. Construction 
chemicals are essential for the infrastructure market – 
bridges, tunnels, airports, hydroelectric power plants and 
wind farms – a potentially significant growth driver.  
Thanks to a broad range of technical products, the Group 
is able to cover the various critical parts of any type 
of infrastructure.
In this context, Saint-Gobain offers, among others, highly 
technical waterproofing solutions for bridges and 
tunnels, concrete admixtures and cement additives that 
help improve the mechanical performance and durability 
of structures, as well as putties and anchoring systems 
for fastening and connecting concrete structural 
elements. The Group is also developing innovative digital 
solutions, like Verifi and Maturix, which are used 
to monitor concrete properties in real time. 
Additionally, Saint-Gobain offers a comprehensive range 
of ductile cast iron pipes  and accessories for water 
transport and distribution through the PAM brand, and 
with the Adfors brand, it designs fiberglass and technical 
textiles used for the repair and reinforcement of roads 
and airport runways.
Thanks to this integrated, innovative offering, 
Saint-Gobain sustainably supports infrastructure 
development and modernization,  while meeting 
increasing requirements concerning performance, 
reliability, and durability. As an example, on the large 
airport construction sites in high-growth countries like 
Vietnam, Saint-Gobain stands out as the supplier of 
integrated solutions  that address both the building 
aspect – fire-resistant glazing and partitions, acoustic 
ceiling and partition solutions, lightweight ventilated 
façade systems, solar-control glazing, waterproofing 
systems for flat roofs, or technical flooring for heavy-
traffic areas – and the infrastructure aspect – 
fiberglass for reinforcing runways and taxiways, 
concrete admixtures, waterproofing solutions for 
bridges and underground passages, and fireproofing 
for steel structures.

1.1.4 AN INSPIRING PURPOSE
With its corporate purpose, “Making the World a Better Home”, the Group 
took on its ambition to improve everyone’s lives by making the planet a fairer, 
more inclusive, more harmonious, healthier and sustainable living space.
Through its business model, generally, and with its solutions, specifically, 
Saint-Gobain has a tangible impact on the life of every individual and on their 
living, working, healthcare, educational and mobility environments. The 
Group’s corporate purpose is the link between the infinitely small unit of each 
person’s living space and the infinitely large one of our shared home: the 
planet. It is fully aligned with Saint-Gobain’s vision – to be the worldwide 
leader in light and sustainable construction – and with its strategic plan, 
“Lead & Grow” (see p. 16 as well as section 1.2.2, p. 42).
Our corporate purpose sets the course for our shared future. It looks like us. It 
represents a call to action, and is based on the values that guide us, the 
Principles of Conduct and Action (see section 1.2.7.E.a, p.  64). This is the 
profound ambition of our corporate purpose: to act every day to make the 
world a more beautiful and more sustainable place in which to live. 
1.1.5 360 YEARS OF HISTORY
Saint-Gobain was founded in 1665 by Louis XIV, King of 
France, under the name of “Royal Manufacture of 
Mirrors”. 
Compagnie de Saint-Gobain diversified into sectors such 
as chemicals, glass products, and the automotive 
industry, rapidly expanding into international markets, 
establishing itself in the United States in 1829, Germany 
in 1858, Italy in 1888 and Spain in 1905.
The Group, which successfully overcame the major crises 
of the century and invested heavily in research and 
development, withdrew from its chemical activities and 
merged with Pont-à-Mousson, created in 1856 and 
specializing in cast iron pipes.
In 1986, the privatization of Saint-Gobain – which had 
been nationalized in 1982 – was a huge popular success: 
1,500,000 shareholders subscribed to the transaction. 
The acquisition of Norton in 1990, then Carborundum in 
1996, enabled the Group to develop its know-how in 
abrasives, plastics and ceramics. 
The 2005 acquisition of British Plaster Board, the world 
leader in plasterboard, combined with Saint-Gobain’s 
insulation solutions, made the Group the world’s No. 1 in 
interior design solutions.
Saint-Gobain focused its strategy on sustainable 
housing, while continuing to serve numerous industrial 
markets, and pursued its expansion in emerging 
countries.
In late 2018, the Group launched its “Transform & Grow” 
plan aimed at establishing a new organization by country 
and ensuring agile and value-creating portfolio 
management. 
In 2019, Saint-Gobain acquired Continental Building 
Products, the first step in strengthening its positions 
in the construction market in North America.
Saint-Gobain established its corporate purpose, 
“Making the world a better home”.
The 2021 acquisition of Chryso made Saint-Gobain a 
major player in construction chemicals. In October 2021, 
Saint-Gobain launched its “Grow & Impact” strategic 
plan, setting out its vision to become the  worldwide 
leader in light and sustainable construction. 
In 2022, the Group finalized the acquisition of Kaycan – a 
specialist in exterior building materials – and of GCP 
Applied Technologies, a key step in establishing itself as 
a leader in construction chemicals. 
The following year, Saint-Gobain acquired Building 
Products of Canada, a manufacturer of roofing shingles 
for the residential sector, and wood fiber insulation 
panels. 
Saint-Gobain was certified as “Top Employer Global” for 
its 2025 fiscal year, for the 11 th consecutive year. The 
Group acquired CSR, a leader in construction materials in 
Australia and New Zealand, as well as Bailey, a specialist 
in metal frames for light construction in Canada, and 
initiated the acquisitions of Fosroc, a leading global 
player in construction chemicals, and Ovniver (Cemix 
brand) in Mexico. These constitute new strategic steps in 
establishing Saint-Gobain’s global presence in 
construction chemicals, which, once the transactions are 
complete, will bring its total sales in this sector to 
€6.5 billion (pro forma). 
In 2025, Saint-Gobain celebrates its 360th anniversary, a 
figure that also represents its global reach and its circular 
and comprehensive approach. In October 2025, the 
Group launches its “Lead & Grow” strategic plan, 
marking the beginning of a new chapter for 
Saint-Gobain, based on a clear ambition: to accelerate its 
profitable growth in a sustainable manner and 
outperform its markets, thereby enhancing the value 
created for all its stakeholders. At the end of 2025, the 
Group is present in 80 countries (1).

1.2 Strategy and value creation
1.2.1 SEIZING OPPORTUNITIES GENERATED BY MEGATRENDS
Saint-Gobain’s corporate purpose, “Making the World a 
Better Home”, is directly linked to three megatrends: 
global construction demand (in the residential, 
non-residential and infrastructure markets) due to 
urbanization, population growth, and social and 
economic challenges; climate change (due to greenhouse 
gas emissions), generating great unpredictability, as well 
as more frequent extreme weather events; and the 
scarcity of natural resources, reflected in the depletion of 
non-renewable resources. 
These three global megatrends generate key challenges 
that the Group considers to be of importance (i.e., likely 
to influence its performance) to its business model, and 
which generate immense opportunities for Saint-Gobain: 
population growth and urbanization, the aspiration of 
the middle classes for quality buildings, energy 
renovation, relocating business activities in the context 
of deglobalization, adapting buildings and infrastructure 
to climate change, and, lastly, the development of 
circularity.
In response to these major, closely related challenges, 
Saint-Gobain promotes a series of relevant responses 
throughout its value chain , involving its suppliers and 
customers, as well as its competitors, and public and 
regulatory authorities. These responses include 
regulatory measures (e.g., promoting a stable legal and 
financial framework focused on sustainable construction), 
procurement measures (e.g., marketing reusable and 
recyclable products), design measures (e.g., designing 
buildings capable of withstanding more frequent extreme 
weather events) and operational measures  
(e.g., improving the recovery of materials when buildings 
are demolished). The “Lead & Grow” strategic plan  
notably enables Saint-Gobain to contribute to these 
responses. Therefore, it aligns directly with global 
megatrends, the challenges that arise from them, and 
the market opportunities they generate.
A – Megatrends
a. Global demand for construction
The challenge 
The urban population is expected to grow by almost 
2  billion by 2050, particularly in Asia and Africa. In 
addition, around 1.1  billion people currently live in 
informal settlements and are still waiting for decent 
housing  (1). Based on this data, the World Economic 
Forum estimates that new residential construction 
needs worldwide will reach 2 billion homes over the next 
80 years, a sustainable source of  growth for all of the 
Group’s solutions.

Although new construction needs are particularly acute 
in emerging countries, developed countries are also 
affected. Housing shortages can be seen in several 
developed countries, including the United States, 
Canada, the United Kingdom and Germany. The 
deterioration in housing affordability over the past 
decade implies, in particular, the need for quality but 
affordable housing , an equation that lightweight 
construction makes it possible to solve by reducing the 
use of resources and construction time, thereby helping 
to reduce the total cost of the building.
Finally, urbanization and these global housing needs are 
accompanied by requirements for local public services, 
and more generally for improving the quality of life in 
cities, thanks to quality service buildings  and 
infrastructure. 
How does this affect 
the construction industry? 
The sector is directly affected by all these challenges, 
from building and renovating existing residential and 
non-residential buildings, to building and renovating 
infrastructure. The objective is, in particular, to increase 
productivity in the building sector in order to meet this 
quantitative challenge.
b. Climate change 
The challenge 
Since the pre-industrial era (around 1850-1900), the 
world’s average surface temperature has increased by 
around 1.34  °C to 1.41  °C, with 2024 being the hottest 
year on record, at 1.55  °C above the benchmark. It is 
scientifically established that greenhouse gas emissions, 
generated by human activity, are primarily responsible 
for this increase in average temperatures. The 
construction industry is particularly concerned , as it 
accounts for nearly 34% of annual CO 2 emissions 
worldwide. These emissions are generated primarily 
by the operation of the buildings (around 75%), together 
with the production and transport of materials 
and construction equipment (around 25%).
In addition, rising temperatures are accompanied by 
extreme weather events such as heat waves, heavy rainfall 
and floods, droughts, rires and hurricanes, which are 
becoming more frequent and severe. Between 3 and 
3.6 billion people live in areas that are highly vulnerable to 
extreme weather events, including severe water stress and 
drought. In 2024, 393 recorded disasters affected 
167.2 million people, exceeding the annual average of 371 
disasters recorded between 2004 and 2023.
How does this affect 
the construction industry? 
Reducing the carbon footprint of construction requires 
changes in construction standards: the more systematic 
use of renovation over demolition-reconstruction, the 
widespread use of lightweight construction methods 
that reduce the use of cement and concrete, the 
decarbonization of these two materials, and finally, 
energy renovation that reduces the energy consumption 
of buildings. Saint-Gobain offers solutions for all these 
techniques and is therefore perfectly positioned on the 
underlying trend of construction decarbonization.
Furthermore, the need to adapt all residential and non-
residential buildings to climate change creates immense 
needs that the construction industry must face. The aim 
is both to build new buildings that are resilient to climate 
change, and to adapt existing buildings to exceptional 
weather conditions, in order to ensure safety and 
comfort for residents and to minimize losses and repair 
and reconstruction costs, in a context where insurance 
companies are reducing their coverage of natural 
disasters. The Group’s solutions are particularly suited to 
these needs, whether it involves strengthening the 
insulation of buildings, installing solar-control glazing to 
protect against heat waves, or protecting buildings using 
waterproofing membranes.
c. Scarcity of natural resources
The challenge 
Resource scarcity refers to the growing gap between 
demand for essential natural resources (such as fresh 
water, minerals, land, and energy) and the planet’s ability 
to regenerate or provide them sustainably. This 
imbalance is intensifying as population, consumption, 
and environmental pressures converge. 
Global water demand is growing fast: it is expected to 
exceed supply by 40% and increase by another 20-30% 
after 2040, driven by urbanization, agriculture, and 
energy needs. At the same time, global commodities 
extraction has tripled over the past 50 years and is 
expected to almost double by 2050, exposing economies 
to the risks of shortages and high price volatility. 
How does this affect 
the construction industry? 
The construction industry accounts for 37% of solid 
waste and nearly 50% of natural resource consumption 
worldwide, leading to the extraction of 100 billion tonnes 
of raw materials per year. Two resources are particularly 
consumed by construction: sand, of  which 50  billion 
tonnes are consumed per year, and water, 15% of which 
is consumed by construction. Circularity ( limiting the 
consumption of resources, extending product life, and 
encouraging product recycling, taking into account 
their entire life cycle) offers a way forward, but scaling 
up requires overcoming major obstacles in  terms of 
design, regulations and logistics.

B – Challenges and opportunities
a. Population growth and urbanization: 
increasing the volume 
of new construction
The increase in the global population and the 
acceleration of urbanization (see section 1.2.1.A.a 
above) means accelerating both the production of 
new buildings and the renovation and reallocation  of 
existing buildings, in order to provide a sufficient 
volume of adequate housing. The construction industry 
faces an unprecedented challenge: meeting the 
explosive demand for housing caused by population 
growth, urbanization, and climate change, while 
addressing labor shortages , stagnant productivity , 
and sustainability imperatives . This twofold issue 
requires a fundamental transformation of traditional 
construction and renovation methods towards 
industrialized and  automated approaches. From this 
point of view, Saint-Gobain’s lightweight construction 
solutions, which  increase productivity, are perfectly 
suited to these challenges.
b. Aspiration for quality housing: 
building safe, dignified, healthy, 
comfortable, and affordable buildings
This aspiration overlaps with two developments: on the 
one hand, the middle classes are expanding in emerging 
countries, as illustrated by the 16% average annual 
growth of the Indian middle class by 2030; on the other 
hand, the acceleration required in construction to meet 
quantitative housing needs must not sacrifice quality: it 
is a question of building safe, healthy, comfortable and 
affordable housing. 
The benefits of building comfort on occupant quality of 
life have been demonstrated; for example, the thermal 
and acoustic comfort of a classroom has beneficial 
effects on student learning. Saint-Gobain offers 
lightweight construction solutions that improve thermal 
and acoustic comfort, as well as the air quality and light 
of buildings. 
Furthermore, in view of deteriorating housing 
affordability over the past decade, in both emerging and 
developed countries, the issue of affordability has also 
become more important. Saint-Gobain lightweight 
construction solutions optimize the cost of building 
construction, thanks to productivity gains estimated at 
between 20% and 70% during the construction phase, as 
well as the recurring cost of building occupancy  
(by  reducing energy bills); at the same time, these 
solutions improve the economic value of buildings for 
their owners: not only are rental yields improved, but real 
estate prices increasingly reflect housing energy 
efficiency. In many European countries, real estate price 
differentials between the most and least energy-efficient 
homes exceed 15%, even comparing homes with 
equivalent structural characteristics: this is the case in 
the Netherlands, for example, as well as in Germany, 
France, Italy and Spain. 
c. Adapting buildings and infrastructure 
to climate change: providing solutions 
that increase the resilience 
of buildings and infrastructure
The built environment faces unprecedented 
vulnerabilities related to the climate crisis (see section 
1.2.1.A.b above). The acceleration of extreme weather 
events, such as heatwaves, fires, floods, and hurricanes, 
requires cities, buildings, and infrastructure to adapt to 
a new climatic situation. These adaptation efforts must 
cover both new construction and existing buildings and 
must be adapted to the specific nature of climate 
change in each region of the world. 
Saint-Gobain’s offering, in particular in the insulation of 
partitions and roofs, glazing, shock-resistant shingles and 
waterproofing and fire protection membranes, makes it 
possible to meet the challenges of this necessary 
adaptation. Furthermore, the Group’s organization by 
country is particularly adapted to the need to determine 
local solutions for adapting buildings. 
d. Energy renovation of buildings: 
accelerating the volume of renovation 
and reallocation of existing buildings 
to increase their energy performance 
and reduce carbon emissions
Achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 requires the 
complete decarbonization of the construction industry, 
addressing not only emissions during the construction 
phase, but also during the use phase of buildings. These 
represent around three quarters of the building’s carbon 
emissions and can be drastically reduced by energy 
renovation. To  date, only 5% of buildings are carbon 
neutral, and  annual renovation rates remain low. 
Saint-Gobain’s solutions are particularly suited to energy 
renovation, whether for glazing, plasterboard solutions, 
or insulation for façades and roofs.

e. Relocation of activities 
as part of deglobalization
After decades of globalization and internationalization of 
industrial value chains, companies have faced multiple 
industrial and logistical challenges since the Covid 
pandemic, including value chain disruptions  during 
lockdowns, multiple climate hazards that have affected 
global trade routes (e.g., the Panama Canal affected by 
drought), and regional conflicts, e.g., in the Red Sea. 
Moreover, growing global geopolitical tensions are also 
affecting trade and encouraging central governments to 
increase their strategic autonomy. All of these 
developments are encouraging companies and central 
governments to implement policies of reindustrialization 
and the local development of strategic industries , 
including defense and the data centers necessary for the 
artificial intelligence revolution. The needs for industrial 
buildings are therefore increasing considerably in the 
Group’s various countries.
Saint-Gobain’s offering also targets these non-residential 
segments. In the data center sector, for example, 
solutions for technical insulation, waterproofing 
membranes, technical ceilings, low-carbon admixtures, 
and technical screeds meet the precise requirements of 
manufacturers.
f. Resource scarcity and circularity: 
building and renovating, 
using fewer resources
Resource scarcity (see section 1.2.1.A.c above) involves 
building and renovating while optimizing the use of raw 
materials and promoting the modularity and reallocation 
of buildings. As construction consumes 40% of the 
world’s raw materials and generates one -third of the 
world’s waste, circularity is both an environmental 
imperative and a strategic sovereignty issue . 
Saint-Gobain’s offering responds to this challenge. The 
reduction in the use of raw materials can reach 50% in 
lightweight construction methods: the substitution of 
heavy materials and solid façades with wood, metal or 
concrete structures naturally reduces the natural 
resources used; in addition, site waste is significantly 
reduced by the use of pre-fabricated and pre-assembled 
modules; and lastly, lightweight construction facilitates 
the deconstruction of buildings at the end of their life 
and the re-use of construction materials, to the extent 
that buildings are transformed into a “materials bank”, 
which will ultimately lead to a drastic reduction in the 
raw materials consumed by the construction industry.
1.2.2 DEFINING STRATEGIC OBJECTIVES
The “Lead & Grow” strategic plan marks the beginning of 
a new chapter for Saint-Gobain, based on a clear 
ambition: to sustainably accelerate profitable growth 
and outperform its markets , thereby increasing the 
value created for all its stakeholders. Over the 
2026-2030 period, the Group is targeting “mid -single 
digit” average annual sales growth (1), outperforming its 
markets by 1 to 2 points, an EBTIDA margin of between 
15% and 18%, ROCE above 13%, and a free cash flow 
conversion ratio of more than 50%.
Anchored in the Group’s long-term vision and corporate 
purpose – “Making the World a Better Home” – this plan 
is based on a proven model, local for local, and 
recognized leadership in light and sustainable 
construction, whether in mature or fast-growing markets. 
The megatrends that are shaping the construction 
industry today are creating an opportunity-rich 
environment. A global population that continues to 
grow and urbanize, the expansion of the middle class in 
high-growth markets, the housing crisis in fully 
developed economies, the growing need for local 
infrastructure, and the climate emergency are 
profoundly transforming demand. These developments 
reinforce the need for efficient building and 
infrastructure solutions that improve the daily lives of 
occupants, while being resource-efficient, low-carbon, 
and adapted to extreme weather conditions . In each 
region, these trends are reflected in a specific way: in 
Europe, energy renovation is becoming an imperative; in 
North America, housing shortages and resilience to 
climate change are structuring the market; in Asia and 
emerging economies, urbanization and infrastructure 
are generating increasing construction needs.
To meet these challenges, Saint-Gobain stands out with 
a unique offering of solutions covering the entire 
building envelope and infrastructure, deployed on a 
country-by-country basis, which constitutes a decisive 
competitive advantage because it precisely meets the 
complex needs of the Group’s customers. These solutions 
make it possible to address all the construction markets 
– residential as well as non-residential and infrastructure – 
offering Saint-Gobain a vast addressable market for 
sustainable, profitable growth.

A – Strengthening a sustainable, 
profitable growth profile
The “Lead & Grow” strategic plan aims to create 
a sustainable, profitable growth profile for the Group.
Continuing the geographical 
rebalancing of the Group’s activities
First, Saint-Gobain intends to fully capture the gradual 
recovery in Europe, with the objective of growing by an 
average of 3% to 5% per year (1). At the same time, 
Saint-Gobain is pursuing a clear strategy of strengthening 
its presence in higher-growth regions, including North 
America, Asia, and other high-growth markets. 
Accounting for around half of the Group’s sales, these 
regions represent key drivers of future growth. The 
Group aims to achieve, in the long term, nearly 60% of 
global sales in these regions. This trajectory is based on 
an average growth rate of 5%  to 8% (1), supported by 
demographic dynamics, infrastructure demand, and the 
upscaling of construction standards. 
Broadening the coverage
of all construction markets
The “Lead & Grow” plan also aims to significantly expand 
the Group’s presence in all construction markets, and 
more specifically in the non-residential and 
infrastructure segments. Historically more focused on 
residential, Saint-Gobain now enjoys a solid foundation 
for acceleration in these new markets, which are still 
under-penetrated, thanks to the expansion of its offering, 
its mastery of complex technical solutions, and the 
driving force of construction chemicals activities. In this 
segment, which is a prime gateway to infrastructure 
projects, the objective is to achieve over €9  billion in 
sales by 2030, through a combination of capital 
expenditure, product innovation and targeted external 
growth operations. 
Enhancing the Group’s profile in light and 
sustainable construction
More broadly, Saint -Gobain continuously enhances its 
business profile by supplementing, in a logical sequence, 
country by country, all its product lines – interior, 
exterior, and construction chemicals solutions. Thus, the 
Group is strengthening its ability to offer integrated 
solutions adapted to the needs of its customers, and 
which create value for the Group.
The strategic plan is accompanied by active, selective 
management of the business portfolio (see section 
1.2.7, p. 60). Saint-Gobain plans to increase its scope by 
about 20% between now and 2030, by combining 
targeted acquisitions and disciplined disposals. Each 
transaction is assessed according to strict criteria: 
consolidation of leadership positions, increased 
exposure to high growth countries, strengthening of 
construction chemicals activities, creation of financial 
value, with ROCE above 13%.
B – Accelerating profitable growth 
thanks to the solutions-based 
approach 
The roll-out of the “Lead & Grow” strategy relies on a 
central lever: accelerating the development of solutions. 
For several years now, Saint-Gobain has undergone a 
profound transformation of its model, moving from a 
product portfolio to an integrated logic of solutions 
capable of fully meeting customer expectations . This 
approach, which was successfully initiated in the 
previous plan, is being considerably strengthened under 
“Lead & Grow”.
Meeting customers’ needs, 
creating value for Saint-Gobain
The Group’s solutions-based approach is above all a 
response to, or even an anticipation of the needs of its 
customers, who are facing increasing complexity on 
construction sites and have greater needs for 
productivity, performance and sustainability. The major 
construction players are looking for integrated 
approaches, capable of providing guarantees of quality 
and performance with a single point of contact to 
support them on their project. Saint-Gobain has a unique 
breadth and depth of range, including the broadest low-
carbon offering on the market, capable of addressing the 
growing green building market. The Group thus stands 
out on the market by providing a  comprehensive 
response to its customers’ issues.
The deployment of solutions increases the value created 
for customers and, as a result, the Group’s financial 
performance, through three main levers:
■ Cross-selling across the entire Saint-Gobain portfolio, 
which enables the Group to increase its sales with its 
customers and thus outperform its competitors;
■ The sale of innovative, differentiated, high value-
added solutions  – such as complete EnveoVent 
lightweight façade systems – that increase the 
profit margin;
■ The services and specified sales that make it possible 
to enhance the sold product mix on large projects 
towards more value-added solutions.
Profitable growth opportunities, 
country by country
The expansion of the solutions-based approach is 
grounded in a rigorous, repeatable methodology, 
deployed locally. This implementation is structured in 
two ways: the gradual expansion of the offering in each 
country, and the comprehensive coverage of all sales 
channels.
Country by country, Saint-Gobain is systematically 
expanding and enhancing its offering to gain market 
share across the entire connected suite of the Group’s 
products, covering the entire building envelope and 
infrastructure. This model, for example, has been 
deployed in India over the last 10 years. Saint-Gobain has 
grown from two product lines to a full range of 
innovative solutions with high value-added, with leading 
positions in each category, and strong growth in sales 
and margins (see “Our strategy”, p. 19).

C – Accelerated penetration 
of non-residential and 
infrastructure markets
With €15  billion of sales already generated in the 
non-residential and infrastructure segments – in a total 
addressable market of nearly €250  billion – 
Saint-Gobain intends to significantly increase 
its penetration in these markets. This ambition is based 
on a clear strategy: relying on highly technical “hero” 
products, capable of opening access to complex 
projects, and drawing on integrated offers adapted to 
the requirements of these segments.
Differentiating technical products, 
real entry points for large 
non-residential projects
Saint-Gobain is able to differentiate itself in 
non-residential projects thanks to its highly technical 
solutions, essential to building performance, and which 
act as strategic gateways for large-scale projects. 
“X-Ray Protection” anti-radiation plasterboards, sold 
under the Placo® brand, are one particularly illustrative 
example: lighter, recyclable, simpler to install and 
bringing real health benefits, compared with traditional 
lead-based solutions, these boards have made it 
possible to meet the technical and environmental 
requirements of the Nantes University Hospital project, 
in which Saint -Gobain sold a total of 26 solutions 
(cf. section "Markets and activities", p. 9.
Saint-Gobain is implementing this same approach in 
the data center market, a fast-growing market 
characterized by high needs for thermal performance, 
fire protection and reliability guarantees. With a 
comprehensive range of dedicated partitioning systems 
– technical ceilings, floors, waterproofing membranes, 
insulation, etc. – Saint-Gobain is now identified as one of 
the leaders in this segment, used by  a significant 
proportion of operators in Europe and North America (1).
Construction chemicals 
as a growth driver in infrastructure
In just a few years, Saint-Gobain has built a global 
leadership position in construction chemicals, with no 
less than 43 new lines and plants built since 2021 
and 37 acquisitions in this market, including Chryso, GCP, 
Fosroc, and Cemix. This leadership plays a decisive role 
in the Group’s ability to grow in the infrastructure 
market, enabling it to address segments such as tunnels, 
bridges, viaducts, energy networks, and hydro 
structures, with high-performance solutions, 
specification teams, and the combination of expertise 
from several strong, globally recognized brands, offering 
an integrated approach to the customer.
A dedicated approach to capture the full 
potential of under-penetrated markets
To support its growth ambition in the non-residential 
and infrastructure segments, Saint-Gobain has set up 
a dedicated organization structured around 
comprehensive offerings by market segment (data 
centers, hospitals, schools, transport infrastructure, 
etc.). It relies on specification and technical support 
teams, with strong expertise in building sciences, 
capable of supporting architects, design offices, 
engineers, and project owners in the design and 
execution of projects.
This approach is also accompanied by a strengthened 
model for managing key accounts, making it possible to 
monitor major projects throughout their duration, 
coordinate the Group’s brands, and propose coherent 
and optimized solutions. The new Long Thanh airport in 
Vietnam perfectly illustrates this method: by  mobilizing 
15 complementary solutions from different Group 
entities, Saint-Gobain has demonstrated its ability to 
address the most demanding projects in a coherent, 
integrated manner (cf. “Our strategy”, p. 18).

D – An organization structured 
around country platforms 
to catalyze growth
To fully execute its “Lead & Grow” strategy, Saint-Gobain 
relies on a particularly robust organizational model  
based on country platforms. Built gradually over the past 
few years and proven in various economic contexts, this 
model is now a major asset for capturing growth 
opportunities, enabling rapid execution, and ensuring 
consistency of decisions as close to the markets 
as possible.
These platforms, deeply rooted in their local ecosystem, 
combine three essential dimensions to seize growth 
opportunities: daily proximity to customers and teams, 
access to the Group’s global expertise, and strong 
autonomy to manage their resources, adapt their 
priorities, and deploy the most relevant solutions at the 
local level. This combination makes them real 
commercial machines, capable of simultaneously 
activating all product lines and sales channels.
A bolt-on, proactive acquisition strategy
Country platforms play a decisive role in the Group’s 
acquisition momentum, which is one of the structuring 
levers of the “Lead & Grow” plan. They are often the 
ones who initiate discussions with targets. Their 
proximity to local players, their in-depth knowledge of 
the markets, and their established reputation facilitate 
bilateral discussions with family businesses or specialized 
players. Over the past five years, 80% of acquisitions 
made by Saint-Gobain have been concluded bilaterally, 
sometimes after several years of dialog and trust 
building. The country platforms are then responsible for 
operational integration, talent retention, and generating 
synergies. Recent successes – for example in India, 
where the margin rate of insulation activities has 
increased significantly in three years thanks to rigorous 
integration – demonstrate the relevance of this model.
Operational excellence supported 
by the Group’s expertise
Saint-Gobain’s country platforms ensure that they 
deliver the best operational performance possible, 
drawing on the Group’s expertise, whether in terms of 
industrial excellence, innovation with the regional R&D 
centers, good sales practices in key account 
management, customer loyalty or training programs, or 
monitoring the deployment of Saint-Gobain’s solutions-
based approach. This approach enables them to increase 
their competitiveness, by accelerating and optimizing 
execution.
Environmental excellence is at the heart of the 
performance model of the country platforms, which are 
working to reduce the carbon footprint of their 
operations, increase their share of recycled materials, 
reduce their water consumption, and thus deploy 
sustainable solutions for Saint-Gobain’s customers that 
give the Group a leading competitive advantage.
The progress made by Saint-Gobain in terms of 
decarbonization and circularity is recognized by all 
stakeholders. They help to increase the confidence of 
customers, investors, and public partners, and contribute 
to the Group’s sustainable growth. This environmental 
excellence is now seen as a differentiating attribute 
of Saint-Gobain in construction markets.
A culture of performance 
and accountability
Lastly, the performance of the country platforms is based 
on a culture of high standards and  accountability 
embodied by their leaders. Nearly 90% of country 
platform CEOs are native to the country they manage, 
which guarantees a thorough understanding of local 
issues and enhances the quality of operational leadership.
This performance culture is supported by an incentive 
scheme that is closely aligned with value creation. 
Managers manage their P&L independently, with specific 
targets in terms of growth, margins, ROCE, and CSR. The 
Group’s 3,000 key managers also benefit from  a  long-
term incentive system directly indexed to  financial 
performance, share-price trends and  environmental 
objectives.
This framework helps to unite the teams around a high 
level of commitment and a strong collective ambition, 
essential to ensuring the long-term success of the 
“Lead & Grow” plan.

1.2.3 STAKEHOLDERS
A – Principles of dialog with stakeholders
Saint-Gobain considers the interests of all its 
stakeholders when determining its long-term strategy. 
First of all, this involves building a dialog, and also 
ensuring that this  dialog is transparent and based on 
mutual trust. Factors such as the size of the Group, its 
global dimension, and the variety of its business lines 
mean that dialog must, above all, be organized in a 
decentralized manner, with each operational entity being 
responsible for conducting it within its own scope.
Saint-Gobain has mapped out its ecosystem, identifying 
and grouping its stakeholders by category. For each 
category, a Group position is responsible for organizing 
the reporting of information on its expectations, at the 
local or global levels, and producing a summary of them. 
Thus, dialog is established with stakeholders on a regular 
basis at both the Group and local levels. Each 
stakeholder’s preferred dialog method has also been 
noted. This dialog enables us to consider all the 
expectations of Saint-Gobain’s stakeholders.
In June 2025, the Group’s organization changed to 
further accentuate coordination by country (see sections 
1.2.2.D, p.  45 and 1.2.7.B, p.  62). Consequently, each 
country is in charge of the dialog with its local 
stakeholders and deploys a specific action plan to meet 
expectations.

1.2.4 SUSTAINABILITY CHALLENGES INTEGRATED 
INTO STRATEGY
A – The materiality of 
sustainability challenges
Since 2015, Saint-Gobain has regularly carried out 
“double materiality” assessments to identify and 
prioritize the impacts that are most significant for both 
the company and its stakeholders, and  those  with a 
major financial impact.
The update of the double materiality analysis carried out 
in 2024 is based on the ESRS (European Sustainability 
Reporting Standards). This change in methodology 
has not led to any major changes in the list of material 
challenges for Saint-Gobain. 
The matrix is a representation made based on the results 
of the double materiality analysis (see section 3.1.3, 
p.  106). Materiality challenges have been classified 
according to the contributions of the CSR roadmap.
Sustainability issues were identified based on:
■ Information and knowledge gained from previous 
financial years; 
■ Sector-specific reference frameworks specifying the 
priority issues linked to construction business lines;
■ The specific features of the Group’s business model 
and value chain;
■ Compliance with EU regulations by incorporating 
the detailed challenges listed by the ESRS.

its footprint.

1.2.5 SAINT-GOBAIN'S VALUE CHAIN
Saint-Gobain’s value chain extends from the extraction of 
raw materials to the end-user, including the end-of-life of 
products. Its four-part structure is identical, regardless of 
country or market. This value chain is deployed locally, 
i.e., raw materials come from suppliers located in the 
same region as the site that will transform them. The 
range of products and solutions is defined by the 
country, i.e., as close as possible to the markets and 
customers it serves. This is why the country platforms are 
central to the deployment of the “Lead & Grow” strategic 
plan. Exports of the Group’s products are  marginal and 
limited to specific situations, such as the supply of pipes 
for infrastructure-related projects. 
Similarly, while the principle of circularity (step 4) is 
universal, its deployment and implementation are strictly 
local. Its results are visible only if there is 
complementarity at each stage of the value chain. This 
implies effective collaboration between stakeholders in 
each country.

The synergies between the expertise of the central 
purchasing teams and the country or regional 
organizations make it possible to meet the needs of the 
sites, whether industrial or tertiary, in terms of  quality, 
quantity, regularity and service, and competitiveness. 
Group procurement is organized to combine the 
Group’s operational expertise and negotiation capacity 
with the specific needs of local business lines and sites. 
Thus, a central team, Saint-Gobain Purchasing, 
coordinates the purchasing of the major purchasing 
categories. For example, coordination is in place 
for  energy purchases in order to secure supply 
and  control energy costs and to identify more local 
sources of supply of decarbonized energy that meet 
both the requirements of site supply continuity 
and  energy cost competitiveness. These synergies 
between the central team and the local teams 
are  essential for the deployment of the “Lead & Grow” 
strategy, including the achievement of the financial 
and non-financial objectives by 2030. 
Saint-Gobain’s purchasing policy favors the establishment 
of medium- and long-term contracts and partnerships 
with its suppliers. Given the diversity of  materials, 
products, or services purchased and the number of active 
suppliers, partner companies can be large companies, 
mid-sized companies, or small and medium-sized 
companies.
The exposure to risks of suppliers’ employees is one of 
the criteria taken into account in responsible purchasing 
risk mapping (see section 3.4.6, p. 175).
The supply chain of industrial sites is mostly regional. 
This implies the management of a large number of 
suppliers. Nearly 190,000 companies supply the sites, 
with nearly 20,700 account for 90% of the Group’s non-
trade purchases (by purchase value). 
Purchases corresponding to the offering of the trading 
business lines are managed directly by the country 
platforms. They are concentrated around more than 
10,850 suppliers. Each brand develops its offering 
according to its positioning and the expectations of the 
markets in the countries in which it operates. As such, it 
manages relations with mainly local suppliers. 
The environmental and social impacts related to the 
Group’s procurement, including the exposure risks of 
employees of suppliers and subcontractors, as well as 
the responsible procurement policy, risk mapping, and 
action plans are described in section 3.4.6, p. 175.
They consist of industrial sites including quarries, 
trading or service agencies including logistics sites and 
storage areas, and other tertiary sites, such as offices or 
R&D centers. The geographic breakdown of sites and 
workforce is shown in the “Our global footprint” section 
(pp. 12 and 13). Thus, solutions for the interior, solutions 
for the exterior, solutions for construction sites and 
construction chemicals are developed, produced, and 
sold in each country in order to meet the specific needs 
of the construction market and customers. The impacts 
associated with industrial sites are closely monitored 
from an environmental perspective due to industrial 
processes and stored materials (see section 1.2.7.D.b, 
p. 64 and section 5.1.1, p. 290); from a social perspective 
through team-based work organization (see section 
3.4.2, p.  154); and in terms of relationships with local 
communities (see section 3.4.3, p. 162).
In general, Saint-Gobain employees have permanent 
contracts (91.8% in 2025). Depending on operational 
needs, employees with fixed-term contracts (8.2% in 2025) 
or temporary workers may supplement the workforce. 
Some countries make marginal use of independent 
contractors (fewer than 5,000 people in 2024).
