SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 55
Each country platform has a portfolio of sustainable and 
high-performance solutions (see section 1.2.7.A, p.  60) 
to  meet the needs of the residential construction, 
non-residential construction, infrastructure, and other 
industries markets. Saint-Gobain considers a customer to 
be any company or person having an influence on the 
purchasing decision. Depending on the market, 
customers may be segmented into three categories:
■ Direct customers: companies that acquire products or 
services for use in production or construction projects 
or to resell them;
■ Users: companies or persons who use the products in 
their industrial process, during the implementation of 
a construction or renovation project or after their 
installation.
■ Specifiers: companies or persons who do not buy 
or use the Group’s products and services, but whose 
opinion is vital to the purchasing decision process 
of  direct customers due to their technical expertise, 
reputation or any other capacity (architects, 
for example). 
At the various stages of construction projects, 
interactions with customers help determine needs and 
adapt solutions. Each country is committed to 
deploying solutions adapted to all channels: direct sales 
or through networks of distributors or e-commerce. 
Saint-Gobain’s strategy does not directly target 
consumers. Some distributors, who are direct customers 
of the Group, specialize in or develop business activities 
linked to the “do it yourself” trend. Saint-Gobain 
is  committed to adapting its offering to specific needs 
in  order to support the growth of this segment. 
Depending on the country, direct customers and users 
can be large international companies (e.g., for large new 
construction projects), trading houses, craftsmen, or sole 
proprietorships. Employees of companies, whether 
customers or users, work mainly on construction sites. 
Their working conditions depend on the country, local 
regulations, country-specific construction methods, 
the climate, and the local labor market. 
To develop circularity in the construction market, it is not 
enough to offer recyclable products or limit waste on 
construction sites, it is a question of creating new local 
ecosystems. Through their leadership and proximity to 
customers, country platforms can make circularity 
a real growth driver. Saint-Gobain integrates the circular 
economy principles into its solutions placed 
on the market right from the design stage:
■ By limiting the use of non-renewable resources and 
developing the reusability of products, the proportion 
of recycled or biosourced materials or byproducts 
incorporated into production and product packaging 
(1) + (2); 
■ By reducing the proportion of final waste throughout 
the entire value chain;
■ By ensuring the recyclability of the solutions placed 
on the market (2);
■ By collaborating with its customers to reduce the 
impact on natural resources of the construction and 
building industry in particular, to extend the lifespan 
of buildings and facilitate the collection of recyclable 
materials when buildings are demolished (3).
As part of its program to develop sustainable and 
high-performance solutions (see section 1.2.7.A, p.  60), 
Saint-Gobain strives to develop solutions that optimize 
the use of resources. Special attention is paid to the 
recyclability of products and packaging placed on the 
market. Some Saint-Gobain products, such as glass and 
gypsum products, can be recycled indefinitely in a 
closed-loop industrial process. Industrial processes are 
then adapted to replace natural raw materials with 
recycled materials derived from internal or  external 
collection. 
Depending on the markets addressed, Saint -Gobain’s 
products have a lifespan that is variable but optimized 
relative to their use. Some products, such as glazing, 
have theoretical lifespans of up to 30 years; others, such 
as additives in the construction chemicals market, 
are designed for a specific use.

1.2.6 THE GROUP'S VALUE CREATION MODEL
The value creation model shows the consistency of the 
Group’s strategy. The “Grow & Impact” (2020 – 2025) 
and then "Lead & Grow" (2025 – 2030) strategic plans 
are aligned both with the purpose of “Making the world a 
better home” and with the vision of being the leader in 
light and sustainable construction. Saint-Gobain guides 
its efforts on the megatrends of global demand for 
construction, the fight against climate change, and 
resource scarcity (see section 1.2.1, p. 39). Based on the 
challenges and opportunities associated with these 
megatrends, the Group has defined strategic objectives 
to accelerate sustainable profitable growth and 
outperform the markets (see section 1.2.2, p. 42). 
As part of its “Lead & Grow” strategic plan, Saint-Gobain 
confirms its vision of a construction market that it 
approaches in a decentralized and local manner through 
its country platforms (see section 1.2.5, p.  53), its 
commitment to meeting customer expectations by 
adopting a solutions-based approach (see section 1.1.3, 
p.  29) and its ambition to increase its presence in the 
non-residential construction and infrastructure markets 
(see section 1.2.2, p. 42).
To this end, the country platforms will be able to draw 
on the Group’s expertise (1.2.7.F, p.  67) in terms of 
industrial excellence, innovation, best commercial 
practices and environmental performance. 
Saint-Gobain integrates its stakeholders into its model 
through mapping (see section 1.2.3, p. 46).

1.2.7 CROSS-FUNCTIONAL STRENGTHS AND LEVERS
A – Offering solutions that 
combine performance 
and sustainability
Saint-Gobain adopts a customer-centric approach with 
a view to developing complete, innovative solutions 
(see “Solutions-based approach”, p.  6). In each of the 
countries in which it operates, the teams offer their 
customers solutions combining performance and 
contribution to sustainable development, in particular 
promoting the acceleration towards a decarbonized 
and more circular economy. 
As well as providing high-performance solutions, the 
Group’s offering must enable its customers to make 
progress on their own sustainable development goals, 
thereby accelerating the transition of the construction, 
mobility and industry sectors to a “low-carbon” economy 
that consumes fewer natural resources, while improving 
the health, safety, and well-being of users. 
To measure its progress in this respect, since 2020 
Saint-Gobain has implemented a methodology that takes 
into account local markets and contexts to estimate the 
share of its sales generated by solutions offering 
benefits in terms of performance and sustainability.
Beyond the traditional approach of meeting a specific 
need with a suitable product, the aim is to offer clients 
comprehensive, end-to-end support in addressing 
complex challenges, modeled as a series of “use cases” –
illustrations of particular scenarios such as building a 
single-family home or renovating a hospital. Examples of 
how these solutions are implemented in different 
countries are presented in section 1.1.3, p. 29.
To measure the performance of solutions , the Group 
assesses the increase in economic value for the customer 
based on criteria such as productivity and financial 
benefits, as well as the user experience. 
To measure the sustainability impacts of solutions, the 
methodology relies on performance assessments of 
solutions in terms of environmental or health 
and well-being impacts. 
The performance of a solution is assessed across the 
entire value chain and for the main stakeholders 
involved, right through to the end user. 
In addition to measuring its overall effort, this approach – 
which covers more than 90% of Saint-Gobain’s sales – 
aims to align the sustainability benefit assessment 
methods, and guide the work of the Group’s teams, 
particularly in terms of innovation, customer relations, 
sales, marketing, and the design of solutions.
The share of sales generated with sustainable solutions 
was 73% in 2025.
a. Product innovation 
and customer proximity
Creating more value for its customers, strengthening its 
offering of more sustainable solutions, taking full 
advantage of its local and global presence and expertise, 
and reducing time-to-market: these are the objectives to 
which Saint-Gobain’s teams are committed. 
The offering of solutions is defined by the country 
platforms (see section 1.2.5, p.  53) as close as possible 
to the needs of customers and local markets. 
The in-depth knowledge of the markets, the proximity of 
the teams with its customers (see pp. 6 and 7), the design 
of a residential, non-residential, or infrastructure project 
(see value chain 1.2.5, p. 53), allows the teams to propose 
innovations developed locally or adapted from solutions 
that have proven their worth in other countries; possibly 
with the technical support and expertise of the central 
teams by business line – “performance segments”.

Regulatory and normative requirements are integrated 
into the innovation process from the earliest stage of the 
marketing brief, and marketing teams in each country of 
commercialization ensure product compliance with 
regulations.
Lastly, the “World Class Manufacturing” (WCM) 
industrial excellence program  (see section 1.2.7.F.a, 
p. 67) ensures the deployment of best practices in terms 
of quality and product compliance at industrial sites, 
based on the ISO 9001 standard.
Technical products are launched after sales force 
training and reinforced support by product managers 
and technical trainers. In several countries, they 
intervene directly at worksites when installers use a 
differentiating innovation for the first time, throughout 
the launch phases until the sales organization reaches a 
sufficient level of maturity. 
In addition, a monitoring procedure incorporating every 
step in the innovation process allows for the rapid 
identification and consideration of potential difficulties 
prompting attention to potential problems. Close 
monitoring of the progress achieved and product 
performance means that the process of innovation is 
faster and more secure.
Saint-Gobain University’s “Unicampus” program  (see 
section 1.2.7.F.b, p.  70) offers five training courses 
associated with the innovation process. These training 
courses are primarily intended for marketing and R&D 
functions but also aim to raise awareness across 
all functions. A product compliance training module has 
also been incorporated into the program. Practical 
courses combining theory, practice, and experience 
sharing are offered widely to the principal offices 
involved in the innovation process, such as marketing, 
R&D, purchasing, production, and industrial efficiency.
The process for launching new products, systems and 
services is verified as part of internal control (see section 
1.2.7.F.a, p.  67). It is regularly updated to improve the 
quality management system procedures and associated 
monitoring indicators. 
b. Toward more sustainable 
products and solutions
Saint-Gobain has incorporated an environmental, health 
and safety impact verification dimension into the 
innovation process since 2008 in the form of a checklist. 
Since 2023, a new standard has been developed and a 
tool for integrating sustainability issues into the 
innovation process is available to the teams. 
The main objectives of the new standard for innovation are:
■ Eliminating or limiting the presence of substances of 
very high concern in new products marketed by 
Saint-Gobain and used in the downstream value chain;
■ Eliminating or limiting and controlling potential health 
and environmental risks during production processes 
at Saint-Gobain sites.
■ select relevant sustainability indicators to measure 
performance throughout the innovation process, 
based on product categories and market needs.
At each stage of the innovation process, this tool makes 
it possible to define and monitor objectives for reducing 
the environmental footprint and maximizing health and 
well-being benefits in accordance with the approach to 
propose efficient and sustainable solutions (see section 
1.2.7.A, p. 60). 
c. Informing customers 
through to end users
To provide clients with information on the environmental 
benefits of products and solutions, Saint -Gobain is 
committed to the development and  promotion of life 
cycle analyses (LCAs).
These analyses are useful internally to guide innovation, 
and to meet growing market demand for greater 
transparency. Saint-Gobain is committed to ensuring 
that, by 2030, 100% of the Group’s sales, excluding 
distribution activities, will be generated by products 
covered by verified LCAs (life cycle analyses) or EPDs 
(environmental product declarations). 
As of late 2025, 57% (stable vs 2024) of sales were 
generated by products covered by verified LCAs or 
EPDs, either specific (produced by Saint -Gobain) or 
generic (produced by professional associations).
This represents more than 5.000 EPDs (2,700 in 2024) 
verified EPDs published in close to 40 countries; the 
Group is positioned as the world’s leading provider of 
verified EPDs – by number – in the construction industry.
Saint-Gobain’s customers also rely on sustainable 
construction certifications, such as BREEAM and LEED, 
to assess and enhance the overall performance of their 
buildings. They seek products whose features help 
achieve the desired levels of performance.
To support country platform teams in leveraging this 
opportunity, dedicated tools have been made available 
for three segments – gypsum, insulation, and glass. 
These include checklists to identify the potential 
contributions of products to the main sustainability 
standards, as well as evidence that can be provided to 
customers (documents, data). These tools are 
supplemented by locally adaptable presentations to 
share this information with customers. 
For example, the contribution of Saint-Gobain glazing is 
available on the Saint -Gobain Glass website: https://
www.saint-gobain-glass.com/green-building-labelling-
schemes. 
According to Group’s estimates, the number of projects 
supported by a sustainable construction certification is 
rising in the main countries where it operates.

With regard to information on users, the Group’s 
products comply with current regulations, such as CE 
marking in Europe, or the requirement for chemical 
products to have labels and safety data sheets (SDS). 
Saint-Gobain also provides non-mandatory information 
specific to some of its products, such as:
■ Voluntary safety data declaration sheets for 
unclassified articles or substances;
■ The declaration of the composition of components 
and materials via the IMDS (International Material Data 
System) database in the case of the automotive 
industry;
■ Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs) for 
construction products (or Environmental and  Health 
Declaration Forms (FDES) in France);
■ Voluntary certifications obtained through 
independent national laboratories – or, failing that, 
international laboratories close to these markets – 
when innovative products or systems are not covered 
by international or national standards.
Specific measures relating to the product compliance 
program are presented in section 1.2.7.F.a, p. 67.
B – Creating the conditions 
for success: organization 
for performance
Established in June 2025 to create the conditions 
required for the deployment of the “Lead & Grow” 
strategic plan, Saint-Gobain’s new organization is part of 
a strategy aimed at strengthening profitable growth, 
simplifying the structure, and asserting the Group’s 
worldwide leadership in light and sustainable 
construction. This development is not a break, but a 
natural step that draws on the strengths of the existing 
model in order to go further. It aims to  strengthen 
Saint-Gobain’s ability to efficiently execute its strategic 
plan by combining proximity, agility, and expertise.
For several years, the multi-local model has enabled 
the Group to get closer to the markets and customers. 
Today, this model is being expanded : each country is 
becoming fully responsible for all business lines, with 
greater autonomy to coordinate commercial and 
operational performance. This empowerment makes it 
possible to act faster, seize opportunities in markets that 
are still partially addressed, and expand Saint -Gobain’s 
offering to create more value. It also promotes a 
solutions-based approach, tailored to the needs of 
customers, whether for key accounts, distribution 
networks, or direct sales.
To support this change, Saint-Gobain has created a 
Group Operational Performance Department. Its role is 
to guide, challenge and support countries in the 
implementation of their growth plans. This Department 
relies on two complementary levers. On the one hand, 
the Performance Segments provide business expertise 
to enrich the offering , maximize synergies and ensure 
strategic consistency. On the other hand, the shared 
Expertise Platforms provide innovation, digital, 
purchasing and industrial and commercial excellence 
solutions. This ensures that each country has  the 
resources and skills to succeed.
This organization also simplifies the Group’s structure. 
This integration promotes strategic coherence, the 
pooling of resources, and the achievement of economies 
of scale, which will be reinvested in  growth. This is an 
operational lever to aim for significant cost reduction. 
This organization also strengthens the perception of the 
consistency of offers and stimulates the culture of 
collaboration within Saint-Gobain. 
The expected benefits are concrete and measurable. The 
Group will be able to offer a more comprehensive and 
better-deployed offering, improve its operational 
efficiency, strengthen its proximity to customers and act 
quickly in an economic environment marked by 
regionalization. This organization is designed to 
accelerate profitable growth , simplify processes to 
become more competitive, and assert Saint-Gobain as a 
worldwide leader in light and sustainable construction 
across its entire scope.
This change comes at a key moment. The current 
organization has reached maturity: its strengths 
are known and its areas for improvement are identified. 
The global context is shifting towards deglobalization, 
which requires more agility and flexibility. By deepening 
the multi-local model and mobilizing 100% of the Group’s 
scope in the countries, Saint-Gobain is giving itself the 
means to respond to these challenges and seize 
opportunities. This organization is designed as a 
powerful lever to execute the new “Lead & Grow” 
strategic plan.
C – Rigorously allocating 
financial resources
Saint-Gobain rigorously applies its dynamic capital 
allocation approach, adhering to strict criteria in terms of 
value creation potential. As part of its “Lead & Grow” 
strategic plan, the Group plans to deploy approximately 
€20 billion of capital between now and 2030, combining 
growth and attractive returns for shareholders, while 
maintaining a solid balance sheet with a net debt to 
EBITDA ratio of between 1.5x and 2.0x. Of this total, 
Saint-Gobain plans to allocate $12  billion in growth 
investments  (1) over the 2025-2030 period , giving 
priority to high-growth markets (North America, Asia-
Pacific, growth countries, construction chemicals) as well 
as consolidating its leading positions and enriching its 
offering for each regional platform, country by country. 
The Group also plans to increase shareholder returns to 
around €8 billion: approximately €6 billion distributed in 
dividends, targeting steady growth in the dividend per 
share; and €2 billion in share buybacks.

a. Supporting the Group’s growth 
and commitments
In 2025, Saint-Gobain continued its investment policy, 
allocating resources to strengthen its industrial base  
with 24 new lines or plants coming on stream during the 
year. These investments cover all continents (Americas, 
Europe, Asia-Pacific, Middle East, and Africa) and a very 
large part of the Group’s activities, from plaster to 
insulation, construction chemicals, mortars, and solutions 
for industry and mobility. In addition, in 2025, the Group 
committed €213  million in investments (CAPEX and 
R&D) to support its carbon roadmap, with the goal of 
spending at least €100  million per year on these 
expenses until 2030.
b. Ensuring agile, value-creating 
portfolio management
Saint-Gobain is consistently pursuing a strategy to 
optimize the Group’s profile in order to continue to 
strengthen growth, profitability, and value creation. 
From 2018 through December 31, 2025, Saint-Gobain has 
made acquisitions representing approximately €7 billion 
in revenue and divestments representing around 
€10  billion in revenue. As part of its “Lead & Grow” 
strategic plan, the Group is targeting an asset rotation of 
more than 20% of revenue over the 2026-2030 period.
Continuing to pursue a strategy
of value-creating acquisitions
In 2025, Saint-Gobain completed 17 acquisitions, 
generating additional sales of €862  million. These 
acquisitions consolidate Saint-Gobain’s position as the 
worldwide leader in light and sustainable construction 
and accelerate its growth.
In the construction chemicals sector, the Group 
completed the acquisition of the Ovniver Group (Cemix 
brand), a major player in the construction chemicals 
sector in Mexico and Central America. Saint-Gobain also 
completed the acquisition of Fosroc, a leading company 
in construction chemicals with a strong presence in India, 
the Middle East, and Asia-Pacific. This acquisition 
strengthens the Group’s presence in high-growth 
emerging markets and consolidates its worldwide 
leadership in light and sustainable construction. 
Saint-Gobain also strengthened its digital platform 
dedicated to construction chemicals with the acquisition 
of Maturix, a Danish company offering digital solutions 
for real-time monitoring of concrete manufacturing. This 
transaction expands the Group’s digital offering, 
complements its VERIFI® system, and enables smarter 
and more sustainable construction processes.
Conducting regular reviews of the portfolio 
in order to concentrate the Group’s strengths
In 2025, the Group completed 6 divestments, generating 
€352  million in revenue. Saint-Gobain signed an 
agreement to sell Brüggemann, a German specialist in 
prefabrication solutions, to the Köster Group. The Group 
also finalized the sale of SFIC Belgium, a distributor of 
building materials specializing in plaster, insulation, and 
ceilings on the Belgian market, as well as the sale of 
Tumelero, a building materials distribution chain in Brazil 
with a strong presence in the south of the country.
D – Creating a culture 
of innovation, serving 
industrial performance
a. Developing a culture of innovation 
Innovation is the lever on which Saint-Gobain relies to 
develop new products and solutions. It is both a 
condition and an accelerator of growth. Innovation 
makes it possible:
■ to meet the evolving customer expectations (in 
particular for more performance and sustainability) in 
order to continuously adjust the Group’s offering; 
■ to stand out from its competitors; 
■ to take advantage of opportunities created by global 
megatrends (see section 1.2.1, p. 39); 
■ to anticipate the rapid evolution of the role of digital 
and artificial intelligence , which are transforming 
Saint-Gobain’s markets; 
■ to stay ahead of increased competition; 
■ to respond effectively to the rapid growth and issues 
of certain markets  (for example, the need for 
increased productivity for installers, due to a growing 
shortage of skilled construction and renovation 
workers). 
In this context, innovation is a cross-functional asset 
that permeates all the Group’s activities and enables 
the success of its “Lead & Grow” strategic plan  
(see  section 1.2.2, p.  42). To make the most of it, 
Saint-Gobain defines priorities and aims to find the right 
balance between the different innovation horizons; links 
innovation to the expectations of its markets, 
maintaining the greatest proximity to its customers (see 
above, section 1.2.7.A.a, p.  60); and tends to make 
progress to reduce the time-to-market for innovative 
solutions.

For the Group, innovation is an open process, involving 
both resources and research and development teams 
present around the world (8 transversal R&D centers, 
3,600 researchers and 450+ patents filed in 2025) as well 
as external partners such as start-ups (30+ agreements 
signed in 2025 via its NOVA entity), universities, 
customers and suppliers of the Group. Saint -Gobain 
implements innovation through a structured, Group-wide 
system, based on clear strategic priorities, a unified 
Innovation Framework, and strong coordination between 
central and regional teams.  Innovation is driven by 
customer centricity, sustainability, and the transition of 
products to complete solutions, supported by methods, 
tools, and learning loops that improve success rates and 
shorten time-to-market. A central Innovation 
Development team maintains and deploys this 
framework, while the regions gradually take responsibility 
in order to maximize the impact as close as possible to 
the activities. Skills are strengthened through extensive 
training programs, including the network of Innovation 
Catalysts – employees formally trained to stimulate 
innovation locally – as well as through digital tools such 
as the Innovation Project Companion, which offers 
secure, personalized support. Together, these elements 
create a shared mindset, harmonized practices, and 
execution discipline that enable Saint-Gobain to innovate 
consistently and effectively across the Group. 
Saint-Gobain uses AI and digital tools to accelerate 
innovation, facilitating faster experimentation, more 
informed decision-making, and better access to 
knowledge. Generative AI contributes to the 
development of new materials, while secure internal tools 
increase productivity and support teams. Together, these 
technologies optimize workflows, reduce time-to-market, 
and drive data-driven innovation. 
b. Integrating innovation 
into industrial processes 
Innovation is central to Saint-Gobain’s industrial 
operations. By relying on innovation the Group makes 
progress in terms of operational excellence, 
decarbonization, and circularity . Year after year, 
investments in industrial facilities have increased 
productivity and safety, reduced carbon emissions, raw 
material consumption and waste production. 
This modernization involves the integration of digital 
technologies (in particular via IoT sensors for real-time 
monitoring of energy production and consumption); 
predictive maintenance through data analysis 
(vibrations, temperatures, pressures) in order to reduce 
unplanned shutdowns; and digital twinning to simulate 
and optimize production lines. This also involves 
replacing energy sources , such as biogas or 
hydroelectricity, rather than fossil fuels. It also involves 
automation and robotification , deploying robots for 
repetitive, dangerous or delicate tasks (glass handling, 
packaging) and automated quality control systems to 
immediately detect defects. It is also a question of 
reducing the carbon footprint , through the energy 
optimization of glass furnaces (new geometries, heat 
recovery); the use of alternative fuels (hydrogen, 
electricity) to replace natural gas; or by integrating 
waste or end-of-life products into the production 
process. Saint-Gobain is also working on deploying tools 
based on artificial intelligence , for example in its 
automotive glazing plants – to improve product quality – 
or to optimize the operation of its fiberglass furnaces, in 
order to reduce costs, the quantity of resources and 
energy used, and CO 2 emissions. Finally, the Group is 
making progress thanks to new materials  and the 
optimization of formulations, through more efficient and 
sustainable materials (insulation, smart glazing), less 
energy-intensive melting and transformation processes, 
as well as additives and formulations that improve 
quality, while accelerating rates.
E – Developing a culture of trust
a. Building trust with stakeholders
Values shared with Saint-Gobain’s 
stakeholders
The Group bases its development on its corporate 
purpose and draws on strong values firmly rooted in 
Saint-Gobain’s culture: the Principles of Conduct and 
Action. They constitute the Group’s code of ethics and 
guide Saint-Gobain’s decisions.
This code of ethics is the foundation of all Saint-Gobain 
policies and commitments, specifically the compliance 
policies, the human rights policy, the Environmental, 
Health and Safety Charter, and the “Buyer” and “Supplier” 
Charters of the Purchasing Department. This code of 
ethics applies to all Group entities and employees, as well 
as subcontractors in their work on Saint-Gobain sites, and 
suppliers (see section 1.2.3.A, p. 46). 
The Principles of Conduct and Action are translated into 
31 languages and available on the Group’s website for 
wide distribution to external as well as internal 
stakeholders. During the recruitment process or at the 
time of onboarding, they are communicated to each new 
employee, including those with fixed-term contracts and 
temporary workers, in the local language of the country. 
This communication may take various forms, depending 
on the country:
■ A welcome brochure with comments from the Human 
Resources representative or the manager;
■ The code of ethics directly incorporated into the 
employment contract or the job offer letter.

Participation in public debate
> Advocacy
Saint-Gobain participates in public debates on the 
strategic challenges  for its business activity and 
environment. This participation takes place directly, via 
professional associations, and via global, regional, or local 
alliances. The Group’s advocacy activities aim to 
constructively feed into discussions and bring together 
value chain players and stakeholders. Inspired by its 
corporate purpose “Making the world a better home ,” 
Saint-Gobain regularly works on the priority themes of 
decarbonization of the economy, circularity, and well-
being in the construction sector (see section 1.3.2, p. 74). 
Saint-Gobain and the majority of its subsidiaries belong 
to professional associations representing their industry 
at the national or supranational levels. For example, in 
France, the Group is involved in professional associations 
representing companies, such as Afep and Medef. 
Saint-Gobain’s subsidiaries also cooperate with various 
local associations or organizations involved in normative 
or regulatory issues, or related to  environmental, social, 
societal or economic issues. The subsidiaries have internal 
procedures in place to ensure that their participation in 
associations is recognized and referenced, and that 
employees who represent them in associations are 
trained in the rules of antitrust law. In 2025, Saint-Gobain 
published a Lobbying Policy.

> Multi-stakeholder partnerships
Saint-Gobain has been a member of the United Nations 
Global Compact since 2003 and regularly reports on its 
progress in the areas covered by the Compact. 
Saint-Gobain also encourages its partners, particularly its 
suppliers, to commit to the Global Compact’s ten 
principles.
Likewise, the Group pays special attention to the United 
Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), so as to 
make progress in evaluating the real impacts that 
companies can have in working towards a fairer, more 
sustainable world. These goals also make possible new 
multi-stakeholder collaborations, in which companies are 
engaged locally and globally. 
Finally, the Group is a member of the forum of committed 
companies with the organization Transparency 
International France. In this respect, Saint -Gobain has 
committed to rejecting and combating corruption, in all 
its forms. The Group undertakes to make its best efforts 
to implement a solid prevention mechanism, inspired by 
the current best practices of the business world. 
A list of the Group’s main partnerships and investments is 
available on the website (https://www.saint-gobain.com/
en/corporate-responsibility/our-responsibility/our-
commitments-partnerships-and-recognitions).
The Group refrains from financing any political party.
b. Committed employees
Building a culture of trust, 
responsibility and collaboration
Saint-Gobain’s new organization, aiming to empower 
countries and at the local level, entails building trust, as a 
condition for the effective delegation of authority and 
fostering cross-functional collaboration between all the 
Group’s functions and business lines at the global level. 
The Trust, Empowerment and Collaboration (TEC) 
approach represents a significant change in corporate 
culture within the Group , which primarily concerns 
managerial culture: the aim is to establish, by default, 
the  principle of trust and thus move from a vertical, 
traditional structure, to an open, learning organization, 
leaving the freedom of action at the local management 
level in the 80 countries (1) where Saint-Gobain operates. 
It also responds to the underlying trends affecting the 
world in which the Group operates, and in particular to 
the disintermediation brought about by new 
technologies, which makes managerial methods obsolete 
and promotes profound changes in the relationship 
between individuals and work. The successive lockdowns 
associated with Covid-19, the development of 
teleworking, and the adaptation of working hours at the 
production sites have called for greater autonomy on 
the part of employees and required them to be more 
flexible and adaptable. In this respect, the TEC approach 
is a way of aligning Saint-Gobain’s strategy with changes 
in the expectations of employees and strongly supports 
the development of its employer brand.
The TEC culture also helps to make the innovation 
process more efficient, to align it with customer needs 
by fostering collaboration between countries and 
business lines (for example, to provide an offering of 
complete solutions to Saint-Gobain’s customers) and 
between functions (for example, between researchers, 
marketing specialists and technicians). 
To implement this approach on the ground, the Group is 
relying increasingly on its training program (see section 
1.2.7.F.b, p. 70) and on approaches such as collective and 
individual coaching, made accessible to a greater 
number of employees, as well as the gradual roll-out of 
360° assessments. The development of feedback is 
encouraged to strengthen collaboration and trust, both 
at the Group level (for example, via the annual 
me@Saint-Gobain survey), as well as in project 
management, and at the individual level (by developing 
the ability to request and receive feedback).
Each manager is therefore encouraged to promote 
the TEC culture within their scope and monitor progress 
on its implementation. 
Employee satisfaction
Increasing employees’ involvement in a context of 
change, both generational and technological, is an 
essential challenge for the Group. To meet this challenge, 
the Group places managerial attitude and involvement at 
the heart of this approach: managers motivate and 
develop the loyalty of employees by giving more 
meaning to their everyday work and by favoring a spirit 
of initiative.
Since 2019, a unique tool to measure employee 
commitment has been developed. It makes it possible to 
conduct surveys targeted to particular populations and/
or themes, for example, such as the specific 
responsiveness of managers during transformation 
phases. This platform is also used to conduct the annual 
global survey sent to all employees: “me@Saint-Gobain”. 
Employees are asked questions covering the seven main 
focus areas of the HR policy and the current 
transformation programs:
■ Team: a positive and collaborative working environment;
■ Actor: an organization that values employees;
■ Talent: an HR organization focused on upskilling;
■ Management: a participatory management style;
■ Inspiration: a clear focus on the future;
■ CSR: a responsible company;
■ Innovation, excellence, and customer focus.
With a participation rate of 88% in 2025, 
127,311  employees took part. In particular, 85% of them 
would recommend Saint-Gobain as a good place to work.
The engagement index reached a score of 83%.

F – Deploying an expertise 
platform
a. Ensuring the Group’s operational 
performance
The "WCM" Program for industrial excellence
Saint-Gobain’s “World Class Manufacturing” (WCM) 
program, deployed at industrial sites, combines the 
standardization of methods, tools, and best practices  
with the modularity required to adapt to a wide variety 
of industrial processes and site sizes. It is based on 
continuous performance improvement methods such as 
Lean, Six Sigma, TPM (Total Productive Maintenance), 
and 5S. This program defines the logic, the objective of 
rigor, and the actions to achieve continuous 
improvements in terms of quality, performance, and 
sustainability by integrating a high level of service and 
customer satisfaction. 
The “WCM” program is based on certification procedures 
such as ISO 9001 for quality, ISO 14001 and 50001 for the 
environment, ILO OSH 2001 and ISO 45001 for health and 
safety. This is a program of cultural transformation of 
sites, aimed at involving as many people as possible in 
improving performance. Digital tools are made available 
to help this transformation. Its management, monitoring 
its execution, and improving the performance of the sites 
are managed across the businesses in coordination with 
the Management of the sites.
The deployment of the “WCM” program at a site is 
adapted to its priorities, size, strengths, and weaknesses 
and its objectives in terms of financial and environmental 
performance, quality, and customer satisfaction. Thus, 
each site establishes its own roadmap, in accordance 
with international guidelines, standards specific to its 
business line, the expectations of its customers and the 
improvement objectives set. A “WCM” expertise network 
has been set up to better disseminate the program, 
optimize resources by country, region, or business line, 
and share expertise on each of the program pillars. A 
central team heads up the WCM network, trains the 
teams, creates and applies the program standards, 
circulates the tools, and provides site-specific assistance 
on request. They rely on local teams to increase the 
maturity of the sites.
Saint-Gobain’s “WCM” program is based on eight pillars, 
each one representing an area of excellence.
The foundations of the program define the methods 
and tools:
■ Analyzing losses to determine the priority of actions;
■ Resolving problems with logic, rigor and precision for 
lasting improvement;
■ Involving and engaging employees in a proactive 
approach;
■ Improving standards to make progress easier to 
deploy and more robust over time.
Achieving industrial excellence is a demanding process 
that requires gradual, methodical and constant 
implementation. To support the sites in this process, 
training programs are rolled out during sessions led 
either by the central teams or by local trainers. These 
trainers are trained and certified by the central team. In 
2025, more than 2,200 employees were trained. The 
methods developed under the “people development” 
pillar to ensure the management of  Saint -Gobain’s 
technical skills by adapting training programs, employee 
career paths, and, when necessary, the search for external 
skills. This pillar also plays a vital role in strengthening the 
TEC culture (see section 1.2.7.E.b, p. 66). 
The benefits in terms of competitiveness, improvement 
of customer service, stability of performance, and 
employee commitment can be measured at each stage 
of the site path. Stringency levels have been established 
to set principles shared by the entire organization. Each 
of these levels corresponds both to a performance 
objective set by the business and to a maturity milestone 
in the approach. Audits verify the robustness of the 
actions implemented and the sustainability of the results 
obtained. As of late 2025, 45 “Foundations” sites, 
181 sites were certified “Bronze”, 60 “Silver” and 6 “Gold”.

The “WCM” program accelerates the digital 
transformation of the sites , a significant reduction in 
production costs, while minimizing risks in terms of 
health, safety, environmental, and industrial risks. The 
“Quality”, “Industrial Performance” and “Environment” 
pillars contribute significantly to reducing Saint-Gobain’s 
environmental footprint by reducing production waste 
and water consumption and by improving energy 
efficiency. The “WCM” program and its extension to the 
supply chain represent a change of culture and 
management system, with the aim of bringing a high 
level of service to customers, better competitiveness, 
and greater efficiency, while continuously improving the 
health and safety of all Group employees and also of its 
partners. It fosters and promotes employee commitment 
and mobility. Finally, it contributes to the success of the 
digital transformation of plants and to the adoption 
of its methods and tools by user.
In the Industry 5.0 era, the Group’s operational 
performance is based on the ability of Saint-Gobain’s 
sites to integrate digital technology across the entire 
value chain. To meet this challenge, a strategic program 
has been launched to accelerate the digital 
transformation of all the Group’s sites. Its goal is to 
increase operational efficiency, reduce costs, and drive 
product innovation through a unified governance 
framework and state-of-the-art technology assets. This 
initiative is part of a global ambition, in line with the 
“Lead & Grow” strategy: to make each site, by 2030, a 
model of performance and sustainable development on 
a global scale, based on an integrated, lean, and resilient 
digital ecosystem capable of supporting competitiveness 
and operational excellence.
To achieve this ambition, it is essential to establish 
a  Group baseline to assess the digital maturity of each 
site and incorporate it into the existing WCM program. 
The objective assessment of this digital maturity on five 
levels makes it possible to develop personalized 
digitalization roadmaps, taking into account the specific 
needs and potential of each site, in order to support 
them step by step in their progress.
Saint-Gobain is embarking on a bold transformation to 
reinvent the future of its operations. By combining 
innovation and standardization, Saint-Gobain’s initial 
priorities focus on key areas: streamlining solutions, 
consolidating data platforms, expanding IoT 
connectivity, integrating AI (classic, generative, agentic), 
and deploying computer vision and digital twinning. 
These levers will allow the Group to rethink its processes 
and increase operational excellence to a new level, but 
also to continuously improve the performance of its 
products in terms of  quality, reliability, and efficiency. 
This ambition is also driven by a Digital Transformation 
Accelerator, which ensures strategic consistency and 
catalyzes synergies.
Training programs organized by technical business line 
ensure the management and updating of the skills 
required to offer customers high-performance, 
competitive, and innovative products and services. These 
programs are generally developed and implemented by 
training teams organized by business line: glass, gypsum, 
insulation, mortars, pipe, etc. The Glass Technical 
Academy thus incorporated all glass manufacturing 
training, as well as technical glass transformation training 
for construction and automotive applications. Designed 
and delivered by around 70 experts, the training sessions 
provide in-depth technical content, practical exercises, 
and site visits. This constitution of a center of excellence 
around the businesses enables the transfer of knowledge, 
sharing of best practices, and the alignment of methods 
within the business lines.
Optimizing the supply chain
Ensuring optimized management of the supply chain, 
from supplier to customer, is an essential part of both 
industrial efficiency and customer service. By helping 
optimize inventory levels, supply chain efficiency is also a 
crucial factor in cash management. Lastly, the Supply 
Chain makes it possible to develop innovation in logistics 
services, the shared management of products, and their 
sales forecasts (Sales & Operations Planning), which are 
levers of profitable growth in Saint-Gobain’s existing and 
future markets of Saint-Gobain. All of these missions 
make the supply chain a major contributor to the 
company’s sustainable development.
The Group’s supply chains may be local or global 
and are managed by the entities’ internal organizations. 
Global coordination and a team of experts allow 
common logistics optimization tools, dedicated training, 
and customized supply chain improvement programs to 
be provided. These teams of experts also work directly in 
the countries with the support of the general 
management bodies to raise awareness of all functions, 
identify potential for improvement and draw up action 
plans to be implemented by the country teams. 
Depending on the maturity of local supply chains, 
actions may involve optimizing the management of 
product lines by the marketing teams, implementing 
collaborative processes, developing the customer culture 
at the sites, adapting planning (customer forecasts such 
as plant scheduling) or optimizing transport. The 
objective is to maximize customer satisfaction while 
optimizing financial and environmental impacts.
Saint-Gobain has also developed “Supply Chain 4.0” 
digital programs to optimize distribution networks, 
measure transport CO₂ emissions, and then take action to 
reduce them, and reduce the lead times in order or 
procurement processes. Whether it is for its purchases or 
customer delivery, the Group has programs for the 
optimization of processes, routes, and vehicle loading 
as well as more efficient travel planning by coordinating 
inbound and outbound transport to prevent empty miles.

Quality and the product compliance program
The Group’s Quality Excellence Department supports 
countries and local teams in order to boost customer 
satisfaction by improving the quality culture and Group 
product compliance and reducing the costs stemming 
from poor quality. 
It relies on the ISO  9001 or IATF  16494 certification 
standards, the “Quality & Process Control” pillar of the 
“WCM” program, and the “Internal Quality Control” 
guidelines (see section 5.2.5, p. 313). Training programs 
on the tools relating to product quality and compliance 
are also organized as part of “UniCampus” (see section 
1.2.7.F.b, p. 70) or via e-learning courses available on the 
Group’s training platform.
The purpose of the product compliance program is to 
challenge and improve organizations’ processes in order 
to ensure that products:
■ comply with applicable regulations and product 
standards;
■ meet the customer promise.
The customer promise includes the functionalities or 
performances announced and communicated to the 
customer. 
Product compliance is a fundamental requirement . 
Procedures and processes are adapted in step with 
changes in the organization of the Group, which 
supplemented the measures already in place by 
launching a program in 2021 to further strengthen the 
culture of quality and resilience of organizations 
concerning product compliance. The program was 
designed to remind countries and local teams of the key 
principles and processes related to product quality and 
compliance throughout the product life cycle, from 
design to production, marketing, use, and end of life.
This program includes four steps:
■ Awareness campaigns at all Group levels;
■ The definition of a roadmap by local management 
teams;
■ An assessment of the effectiveness of organizations 
and processes in the countries for each business line;
■ The definition and implementation of continuous 
improvement plans where necessary.
A network of local facilitators and supports comprising 
over 200 people at end-2025 has been set up and 
trained to support local teams in the implementation of 
the program and ensure the sharing of best practices, 
thus fostering the continuous improvement of 
procedures and processes. 
Country and regional CEOs demonstrate their 
commitment to promoting and implementing the 
program through the annual self-assessment process 
and job offer letters implemented at the Group level by 
internal audit. 
Lastly, the smooth running of the program is monitored 
by a committee created for this purpose consisting of 
two members of the Group’s General Management, and 
the results are presented regularly to the members of the 
Executive Committee. The Group’s internal control teams 
also assess the effective implementation of the program 
through the general audit process and  annual targeted 
audit campaigns.
Industrial and distribution risk prevention
The aim of the industrial and distribution risk prevention 
policy is to reduce the likelihood of accidental events, 
minimize their severity if  they do occur, and preserve 
the continuity of business operations. This policy applies 
to all Saint-Gobain sites.
Defined and led by the Risk and Insurance Department, 
this policy is rolled out within the organization to the sites 
by a network of  prevention coordinators. The Group’s 
reference framework is a risk prevention manual. It 
includes the applicable standards, procedures, and 
technical rules, methods for identifying and reducing risks, 
including natural risks, and the drafting of emergency and 
business continuity plans. This  manual may be shared 
with the relevant stakeholders, such as permanent on-site 
subcontractors. The risk assessment tool is used by all 
operational sites and provides an objective assessment of 
the protection and prevention level. It takes into account 
both human factors (organization, procedures, 
communication, training, etc.) and physical facilities. This 
means that each site is able to identify its areas for 
improvement, develop action plans including investments, 
and use this tool to measure progress. The tool is 
accompanied by periodic site visits by the risk prevention 
engineering team: a total of 387 sites were visited in 2025. 
A total of 119 sites have the HPR (Highly Protected Risk) 
label, 47% of which are priority sites.
The Group is rolling out business continuity plans for 
each site according to the risk assessment and the 
vulnerability of processes to unforeseen interruptions 
including an anticipation of the impacts of an accident, so 
as to limit its effects. The aim is to fully or partially ensure 
customer service and recover operational capabilities 
as quickly as possible. The subcontractors working on the 
sites are involved in the process and must commit to a 
prevention plan. In 2025, 21 sites were visited by the 
prevention engineering team, specifically to verify the 
quality of their continuity plans with regard to the 
Group’s guidelines in this area.

Saint-Gobain constantly adapts its risk management 
system to better anticipate the potential risks associated 
with the effects of climate change. Action plans to 
further increase prevention, particularly in the face of 
natural disaster risks, are being rolled out. In particular, 
they include changes in the design of certain sites to 
reduce, where necessary, the impacts of these natural 
events, especially flooding. In 2025, 14 at-risk sites were 
visited to specifically check their exposure to  natural 
disasters, especially flooding.
Environmental management system, 
industrial hygiene, occupational health 
and safety (EHS)
The EHS management system is based on an internal 
reference framework that describes the process for 
identifying and managing environmental and 
occupational health and safety impacts and risks to be 
implemented by each of the Saint-Gobain sites. The 
description of this system is available in chapter 5 “Risks 
and Control” in section 5.2.5, p. 313.
Each Group site conducts its own assessment of 
environmental, health and safety risks  under the Site 
Manager’s responsibility. To do this, a standardized 
method has been deployed and is regularly updated. 
Training courses are organized for site teams, and a 
digital application has been developed incorporating risk 
analysis, assessment, and management actions. This tool 
facilitates the deployment, reliability and monitoring of 
risk management action plans at all the Group’s sites.
Each site has tools to facilitate the continuous 
improvement of its performance by reducing negative 
impacts and anticipating risks:
■ Thematic policies accompanied by standards 
and application guides;
■ Thematic training and webinars on the main EHS 
issues;
■ Tools for monitoring action plans and reporting 
to drive performance improvement.
A support team of experts, in the regions and centrally, 
support the sites in this process.
The action plans of the sites are part of the “WCM” 
approach (see section 1.2.7.F.a, p.  67), in particular the 
“Environment and risk prevention” and “Health & Safety” 
pillars. 
Audits of the environmental, health, and safety 
management system are conducted by the functional 
division concerned. These audits are conducted as a 
priority at sites with ISO or equivalent certification. In 
addition to such audits, a version of the audit 
methodology has been developed for smaller sites 
for which ISO certification is less suitable.
Lastly, a training matrix specifies the training courses on 
managing environmental, health, and safety risks for the 
teams according to the position held. It is a particularly 
relevant tool to use to define employee training courses.
b. Developing human capital
Saint-Gobain’s development depends first and foremost 
on the quality and expertise of the women and men who 
comprise the Group. This is reflected first and foremost in 
the attention paid to recruiting the best talents in all 
specialties, including engineers, digital & data scientists, 
sales and marketing staff, product managers, supply 
chain, and sustainable development specialists. Beyond 
the recruitment process and the attention paid to  its 
brand as an employer, it is Saint -Gobain’s collective 
ability to train, nurture, and constantly develop these 
talents that will enable it to stand out. With digital 
technology and refined data processing, career paths can 
be more easily individualized and the HR support policy 
customized (see section 1.2.7.E.b, p. 66).
Training provided by Saint -Gobain must ensure the 
employability and success of all employees throughout 
their working lives. The objective is to facilitate access to 
training through formats that correspond to their needs 
and expectations.
Training is part of the Group’s major transformations, as 
it provides support for employees and availability of the 
skills necessary for the success of operational teams.
Particular emphasis is placed on the skills that are 
the most critical for the future of the Group and that will 
therefore strengthen the employability of  employees in 
the medium and long term.
The training policy is structured as follows:
■ Supporting the transformation of leadership based on 
trust, empowerment and collaboration, and 
promoting ways of working that generate greater 
efficiency and flexibility. This includes managerial 
training and talent development;
■ Fostering growth and focus on customers: sales and 
marketing performance, product innovation, services, 
and business models;
■ Ensuring efficiency and operational excellence: 
industrial performance, and programs dedicated to 
Saint-Gobain’s major support functions (finance, HR, 
purchasing, marketing, etc.) in order to improve and 
adapt skills;
■ Implementing mandatory training (on compliance, 
ethics, cybersecurity, etc.).
All programs are in digital or hybrid format (in-person 
and digital) and the majority of in-person programs are 
regional, in order to maximize inclusion for all the 
employees worldwide, and to reduce the number 
of  business trips and minimize the CO 2 emissions and 
carbon footprint. This applies in particular to the 
“Unicampus” program, the objective of which is to 
enable the  dissemination of a common culture of 
operational excellence focused on the expectations 
and  needs of  customers. To that end, the training 
sessions focus mainly on marketing, sales, and customer 
services or  innovation. The only global in-person 
programs are  reserved for employees identified as 
having high potential.

c. Striving for commercial excellence
Striving for commercial excellence is a priority for 
Saint-Gobain, and is one of the priority objectives of 
its  “Lead & Grow” strategic plan (see section 1.2.2.C, 
p.  42). The idea is to foster a winning mindset in the 
Group’s customer approach, to be the best commercially 
and  operationally on every line in Saint -Gobain’s 
portfolio, leveraging innovation and digital platforms. 
The aim is to outperform the Group’s competitors and 
underlying end markets.
For several years, Saint-Gobain has developed a 
structured customer approach, with an organization that 
places knowledge and listening to customers at the heart 
of its strategy. This requirement translates into an 
approach based on detailed segmentation of its markets 
and customization of its offerings, in a “go-to-partner” 
logic. The Group provides its teams with effective 
methods and tools to strengthen their operational 
efficiency over the long term. It also makes a special 
effort to intervene as early as possible in the value chain, 
in particular by recommending comprehensive solutions 
and working closely with architects and specifiers. This 
integrated approach enables Saint-Gobain to consistently 
outperform its competitors across all of its markets.
Identifying customer expectations and needs makes it 
possible to improve the existing product and service 
offering, drive innovation (see section 1.2.7.A.a, p. 60), and 
adapt sales approaches to generate customer loyalty.
The development of this corporate culture – in which 
every employee focuses squarely on making customers’ 
every lives easier – is one of the fundamental levers for 
generating sustainable growth.
Knowledge of current and future market expectations is 
essential in order to achieve Saint-Gobain’s medium- and 
long-term targets. For this reason, the satisfaction of its 
customers is a priority for the Group, whose objective is 
to be an organization focused on their expectations. 
To measure customer satisfaction, several practices have 
been extended to all Group operations:
■ On the one hand, the provision of tools and 
methodologies to detect the main points of 
satisfaction and dissatisfaction among actual and 
potential customers, both direct and indirect, and to 
determine the net promoter score, the only measure 
common to all; this refined measure will eventually 
make all customers the Group’s primary specifiers;
■ On the other hand, the regular deployment of 
operational action plans to visibly improve the 
customer experience throughout the customer 
journey. 
Thus, customer satisfaction measurements are carried 
out on a regular basis for all operations.
In the field, the brands are increasingly collecting 
feedback from customers on an interpersonal and 
transactional level, with the dissemination, internally and 
across functions, of best practices in the area. These data 
are cross-referenced with the context of the relationship, 
as well as with the type of customers, in order to assess 
the degree of satisfaction throughout their journey, i.e., 
across the entire chain of interactions between them and 
the Group’s brands. In this context, the satisfaction 
questionnaires already implemented have shown that 
compliance and punctuality are  the  most frequently 
cited negative points. Every piece of customer feedback 
is useful in improving the  quality of Saint -Gobain’s 
performance in concrete, operational ways.
Expertise developed at the central level enables local 
teams to accelerate the implementation of best practices 
while adapting them to the specificities of their markets, 
thus creating an ability to know and respond rapidly to 
customer needs which, among other things, enables 
Saint-Gobain to deliver commercial excellence and 
outperform markets.
The aim is to generate growth by creating the conditions 
that facilitate the experience and satisfaction of 
customers. In addition to tools, it is essential to involve all 
employees in this approach. A network of “Customer 
Experience Champions” facilitates the deployment of 
this customer culture at the local level.

To go even further, Saint-Gobain invests in tools, training 
and programs to help its employees better understand 
its customers’ needs. The aim is to implement a 
widespread culture of commercial excellence and a spirit 
of conquest, covering various aspects of the customer 
relationship, from devising offers and  setting prices to 
digitalizing the customer journey, analyzing margins, and 
seizing opportunities specific to certain markets, such as 
energy renovation. The aim is to develop a corporate 
culture in which the obsession of each employee is to 
make the day-to-day lives of  customers easier and 
create the conditions for greater proximity, so as to 
detect all the customer’s needs and  respond to them 
through offers that mobilize the  Group’s full range of 
expertise. One of the Group’s areas of excellence and 
progress is training, in order to  build a growing 
community of customer experience experts, through 
training in “customer experience” methods and concepts 
through the “Unicampus” program. In addition, a 
platform called “Pulse” has been created to centralize 
and make available to Saint -Gobain countries and 
entities methodologies and tools for  managing the 
customer experience, such as  “personas”, i.e., the 
definition of groups of customers whose behaviors and 
preferences are merged into  a  single predictive model 
and interview guides to  encourage each employee to 
develop a culture of customer feedback.
All the aspects of this approach have the virtue of 
positioning Saint-Gobain as a provider of complete 
solutions to its customers , and constitute a powerful 
lever for development, differentiation and growth 
for the Group. 
Looking beyond the measurement of satisfaction in the 
strictest sense, all these systems create the basis for a 
co-development approach; based on customer opinions, 
a shared innovation process can be implemented.
Actions aimed at specifiers are also carried out. In 
construction markets, architects play a key role in the 
choice of solutions chosen by direct customers. In 
addition, local and central teams work regularly with 
them to analyze existing products, identify avenues for 
innovation, and develop construction techniques. For 
nearly 20 years, Saint -Gobain has organized an 
architecture competition for students, the aim being to 
develop a project that incorporates the principles of 
sustainable construction. Every year, Saint-Gobain selects 
a country with an architectural challenge and works 
closely with the local municipality to develop a task that 
will respond to real social and cultural issues. Students 
from universities around the world submit their best ideas 
to compete and win one of the prizes in this international 
competition. The 2025 competition was organized in 
close collaboration with the city of Villefontaine, France, 
Les Grands Ateliers, the village of Chimilin, and the 
Alliance HQE-GBC. The challenge was to develop a 
residential area (for students and visiting professors) near 
Les Grands Ateliers, and to renovate a former school 
building in Chimilin into a multipurpose building for local 
associations and organizations. More than 1,300 students 
from over 200 universities in 33 countries submitted 
projects. Thirty-three projects were selected for the final 
phase and the awarding of five prizes.
To meet the specific expectations of specifiers  
(architects, project owners, or project managers), 
dedicated teams are set up in numerous countries. 
They  support customers and facilitate the optimization 
of construction projects. These teams also participate in 
the development of technical Business Units such as the 
“Façades” Business Units or pre-manufacturing. This 
collaboration, essential to generating innovation and 
developing more sustainable, high-performance 
products, solutions and construction methods, is built 
right from the start of architects’ training.
To help the Group stand out more and increase the value 
provided on the market, Saint-Gobain aims to adopt a 
one-stop-shop approach enabling them to find all the 
solutions they need in one place. This approach simplifies 
the customer journey and improves their  overall 
experience. In this respect, Saint-Gobain’s organization, 
which places the priority on the local level, constitutes a 
high-value operational driver, as it enables greater agility 
and in-depth knowledge of each region, along with its 
regulatory context and economic fabric. The 
adjustments made in the summer of 2025 to 
Saint-Gobain’s organization reinforce this dynamic, 
placing all business lines under the responsibility of the 
country and regional CEOs and setting up specialized 
central teams to support them. 
The Group also uses artificial intelligence to improve its 
sales performance, for example by automating the 
large-scale analysis of tenders.

1.3.2 SAINT-GOBAIN'S CONTRIBUTIONS
Saint-Gobain’s CSR strategy (cf.  section 3.1.4 B, p.  114) 
relies on two levers for action:
■ deploying high-performant and sustainable solutions 
that deliver benefits to stakeholders by maximizing 
its contribution in terms of environmental impact, 
health, and well-being;
■ mobilizing for sustainability by minimizing the 
environmental and social footprint of its operations 
across its value chain and with potentially affected 
local communities.
A – A decarbonated home
Combating climate change and advancing the transition 
toward a decarbonated world require the collective 
mobilization and collaboration of all stakeholders: 
customers and suppliers, citizens and employees, 
governments and major institutions. Through solutions 
that help reduce the construction sector’s environmental 
footprint and its commitment to achieving net-zero 
emissions by 2050, Saint-Gobain is making a significant 
contribution to the fight against global warming.
Solutions to reduce the carbon 
impact of construction
Saint-Gobain is deploying a global strategy aimed at 
accelerating the reduction of the construction sector’s 
carbon footprint throughout the life cycle of buildings 
and infrastructure by developing a growing range of 
sustainable solutions. This involves designing and 
distributing solutions that are low in carbon emissions 
during production, but that also facilitate energy 
efficiency during the use phase (reducing heating, air 
conditioning, and energy consumption requirements). 
In addition to the greenhouse gas emissions avoided by 
integrating these solutions into buildings, they also 
reduce energy consumption and associated costs for 
occupants, as well as reducing overall energy demand 
both during peak periods and on average. 
These solutions reduce CO₂ emissions, optimize the use 
of natural resources, and improve the comfort, safety 
and quality of life of occupants.
Adaptation and resilience solutions
Through its adaptation solutions, Saint-Gobain also 
contributes to the resilience of its customers and end 
users by responding to the growing needs of 
construction markets facing more intense climatic 
phenomena. 
Thanks to the diversity of its businesses and expertise, its 
partnerships and innovations, Saint-Gobain offers 
solutions to address the dangers associated with the 
effects of climate change (droughts, floods, fires, storms 
and rising temperatures).
Country platforms play an essential role in offering 
adaptation solutions specific to the effects of climate 
change in their territory. In this way, in countries 
experiencing an increase in the number of heatwave 
days, demand is shifting towards insulation solutions 
and, more broadly, changes in building design to better 
protect occupants from the effects of the sun. For 
countries more exposed to the risk of storms, solutions 
to reinforce roofs in particular can be offered.
In addition to the need to adapt buildings and 
infrastructure, Saint-Gobain’s approach also takes into 
account the potential impact of climatic phenomena on 
its customers’ construction sites. Solutions to improve 
productivity or prefabrication can be proposed to better 
organize construction sites and improve productivity.
2030 roadmap towards 
net zero emissions in 2050
Saint-Gobain is committed to a long-term trajectory 
aimed at achieving net zero emissions by 2050, 
structured around ambitious intermediate milestones. 
This roadmap relies on several complementary levers to 
reduce scope  1 and 2 emissions: actions on products 
(eco-design, weight reduction, composition, etc.), 
industrial excellence (productivity, energy efficiency, 
etc.), innovation (creating sites of zero scope  1 and 2 
emissions in particular), and decarbonated energy 
(electricity or other decarbonated energy sources). 
Through its effective actions on these four levers, the 
Group has reduced its emissions by 35% in 2025 
compared to 2017, in line with its target of -33% 
emissions in 2030 compared to 2017, in a context where 
Saint-Gobain is developing a growth strategy for 2030 
with the rollout of its “Lead & Grow” plan.
In this context, a new target has been set and the Group 
is now aiming for a reduction of -40% to -45% by 2035.
For scope  3, decarbonization is progressing more 
gradually, as it involves a large ecosystem of 
stakeholders. The most significant categories are 
purchasing and transportation, with three key levers for 
reduction: reformulating product compositions, 
improving logistics performance, and decarbonizing 
purchases linked to actions taken directly by suppliers.
Saint-Gobain has also implemented a plan to adapt its 
industrial sites, which strengthens the Group’s resilience 
to the physical risks associated with climate change: 
adapting industrial sites and the supply chain to climate 
events, but also protecting its employees from extreme 
working conditions.
The Group’s efforts and the quality of its actions have 
once again been rewarded with its inclusion in the CDP’s 
“Climate A List.”

B – More performance with less
The construction sector has a major impact on the 
environment, accounting for 40% of solid waste and 
almost 50% of the consumption of natural resources. 
Circular models contribute to environmental protection 
and the preservation of resources and nature.
Proposing solutions that promote 
the development of circular flows 
Saint-Gobain invests in innovation and eco-design in 
order to offer increasingly sustainable products , 
particularly in the field of lightweight construction. The 
Group is therefore continuing its efforts in terms of both 
its products and solutions, while also working with its 
customers to anticipate the use and demolition phases 
of residential and non-residential buildings: optimizing 
formulations to incorporate more recycled or renewable 
raw materials, simulating the optimal deconstruction of a 
building to predict which materials can be recycled and 
facilitate their recovery, increasing the modularity of 
buildings to facilitate changes in use and thus extend 
their occupancy time…
Developing circularity drawing on the 
Group’s country platforms and expertise
Saint-Gobain draws on both the Group’s expertise, which 
drives a global vision, know-how and operational 
excellence, and on country platforms with in-depth 
knowledge of markets and customers, to respond locally 
to the challenges on the ground. This combination of 
global expertise and local presence enables Saint-Gobain 
to implement concrete solutions tailored to customer 
expectations and the specific characteristics of each 
market (such as distribution channels, regulations, 
customer expectations, and construction market 
characteristics). This is essential for developing circularity, 
which by its very nature can only be achieved at the local 
level. Local production, local markets and customers and 
leadership, that brings stakeholders together, are all 
assets that country platforms can leverage to seize 
growth opportunities linked to circularity.
Optimizing resources through 
the creation of recycling channels
To optimize the use of raw materials, Saint-Gobain takes 
action on several fronts. The Group first seeks to reduce 
waste generation, whether from internal industrial 
processes, construction sites, or demolition. Organizing 
waste recovery along the value chain, setting up 
collection channels (reuse, repair, recycling, or energy 
recovery), and initiating waste treatment solutions for 
reuse in production are all examples of partnerships and 
solutions offered by country platforms. These local 
partnerships enable us to work in synergy with other 
players in the construction sector to recover and 
reintroduce reused or recycled materials or products, 
which also requires close dialog with stakeholders. In 
parallel with this hands-on management, the Group’s 
expertise plays an essential role in product innovation, 
the promotion of the circular economy, and R&D aimed 
at accelerating the development of recycling channels 
and the capacity for reuse or recycling in the 
construction sector.
Reducing the use 
of non-renewable raw materials
To reduce the use of non-renewable raw materials, 
Saint-Gobain is taking action by reducing the natural 
resource intensity of its products through eco-design: 
making products and solutions lighter, changing 
formulations and substituting non-renewable materials 
with recycled or renewable materials, facilitating 
recyclability, etc. 
Beyond this reduction, Saint-Gobain’s approach is part of 
the goal to reduce the intensity of non-renewable raw 
materials in the construction sector: developing 
modularity that limits waste at source and facilitates 
waste management, seeking to increase the lifespan of 
materials such as buildings and infrastructure, or 
promoting lightweight construction that halves the 
amount of materials required compared to traditional 
methods.
These resources, which are recyclable, recycled, 
renewable, biosourced, or derived from co-products, are 
directly integrated into the Group’s solutions. Thanks to 
this dual approach, Saint-Gobain designs solutions that 
are more economical, lighter, and incorporate a 
growing proportion of alternative materials , thereby 
helping to preserve natural resources and reduce the 
environmental impact of the construction sector.
Preserving water
Faced with increasing water stress and rising demand for 
water, Saint-Gobain is strengthening its responsible 
water management, particularly with regard to 
withdrawals and discharges in areas under water stress 
and taking into account the water needs of local 
stakeholders. The Group has set ambitious targets, 
aiming to achieve zero liquid discharge by 2030 in areas 
of extremely high water risk and to minimize water 
withdrawals at all its sites, particularly those located in 
regions subject to water stress. As a result, 86% of the 
water consumed is reused thanks to closed-loop water 
reuse systems. An internal water price has been in place 
since 2024 and differentiates investments made in areas 
under water stress.
Protecting biodiversity 
and combating deforestation
Saint-Gobain is committed to Act4Nature International 
(commitment renewed in 2025), reaffirming its 
willingness to integrate biodiversity issues into all its 
activities. Saint-Gobain has made a commitment to non-
deforestation and is implementing a “Forest” policy, 
supplemented by two specific policies published or 
updated in 2025 (Timber Policy and Wood Pulp Policy). 
In 2025, the Group published its Sustainability Briefs 
entitled “Forests, Our Commitment,” which presents the 
new Forest Policy and the concrete actions Saint-Gobain 
is implementing to preserve forest ecosystems.
