C – A better living for all 
Saint-Gobain bases its development on its purpose – 
Making the world a better home – and on strong values. 
Through its business model and, in particular, thanks to 
the solutions it provides, Saint-Gobain contributes to 
having a tangible positive impact on all its stakeholders, 
including individuals, local communities, and the 
environment. In practice, this translates into respect for 
human rights, a responsible purchasing policy, and the 
preservation of people’s health and safety throughout 
the value chain.
Well-being and comfort solutions
Saint-Gobain is developing a range of solutions 
designed to improve comfort, convenience, and well-
being for end users. The Group’s innovations and choice 
of suitable materials can help improve cleanliness, 
hygiene, air quality, and comfort in living spaces while 
limiting health risks. These solutions are particularly 
relevant in non-residential buildings such as schools and 
hospitals, where indoor environmental quality is 
essential. Through this offering, Saint-Gobain provides a 
concrete and sustainable response to users’ needs. 
When designing products, Saint-Gobain also takes into 
account the working conditions of users. Improving 
ergonomics for installers and anticipating risks on 
construction sites are two key aspects of Saint-Gobain’s 
product innovation approach.
Employee commitments 
For the 11 th consecutive year, Saint-Gobain has been 
awarded the “Top Employer Global” certification, which 
highlights the quality of the company’s commitment to 
its employees, particularly in terms of diversity, inclusion, 
and development of opportunities and skills. The high 
participation rate in the annual me@Saint-Gobain survey 
(88%) and the high level of recommendation of the 
company as a good place to work (85%) reflect a 
relationship of mutual trust, based on listening and the 
involvement of everyone. 
In addition, the Saint-Gobain Foundation supports Group 
employees in their personal commitments to local 
communities. Since its creation in 2008, the Foundation 
has supported more than 400 projects sponsored by 
employees in 44 countries promoting social housing and 
the professional integration of excluded people. 
Preserving employees’ health 
and security
The health and safety of employees are top priorities, 
and Saint-Gobain places them at the heart of its 
corporate culture. While the frequency rate of accidents 
with and without lost time among employees, temporary 
workers and permanent subcontractors has been halved 
since 2017, Saint-Gobain is strengthening its measures 
for managing critical situations at all levels of the 
organization. 
Eliminating all workplace accidents, everywhere, for 
everyone, at all times, is Saint-Gobain’s daily priority. In 
this context, the Group reiterates its strong commitment 
to making the long-term absence of fatal accidents a 
priority objective and is rolling out numerous awareness-
raising and prevention initiatives targeting work 
situations that could lead to serious accidents on its 
sites, for its employees as well as temporary workers and 
subcontractors.
Responsible purchasing
Saint-Gobain is continuing the sustainable transformation 
of its supply chain by strengthening the management of 
risks related to natural raw materials, in particular through 
its “Forest” policy. In addition, Saint-Gobain is mobilizing 
its suppliers around ambitious environmental and social 
requirements, supported by the development of 
recycling channels, such as those for paper, which in 
many countries achieve very high rates of recycled 
material integration. The Group regularly conducts CSR 
audits, particularly in the most sensitive regions, in 
accordance with international standards, and implements 
corrective action plans with suppliers when necessary.

America (31%);

developed markets (US, France, UK, Spain, Italy) and 
emerging countries (India, South-East Asia, Brazil, 
Mexico). Perfectly adapted to the current geopolitical 
environment, this model enables us to accelerate 
growth in solutions, while sourcing and integrating 
value-creative acquisitions: combined EBITDA margin 
of 20% for Chryso and GCP (up 600 basis points in 
three years), 18% for Canadian acquisitions (Bailey, 
Building Products of Canada and Kaycan), over 17%

a competitive advantage –

■ Constant innovation: climate-resilient offering in the

emissions;

glass wool, stone wool and glass), contributing to a 
35% reduction in scope 1 & 2 CO2 emissions in 2025 
compared with 2017, with 70% of decarbonized 
electricity in 2025 (versus 39% in 2021).

of Group sales), Saint-Gobain is ideally placed to

spending plans in the region.

noticeably in the second half, up 1.7% , but were

improvement in new construction; Saint-Gobain 
outperformed both the new construction and

range of innovative solutions and its specification

infrastructure connecting Ramhan Island to Abu 
Dhabi, the Dubai Metro Blue Line) – as well as 
residential and tourist complexes.

2.1.7 STRATEGIC PRIORITIES 
In 2026, the Group will focus on strong execution to 
decisively implement the strategic priorities of its 
“Lead & Grow” plan:
1) Outperform markets by 1 to 2 percentage points 
thanks to:
■ Saint-Gobain’s complete range of solutions offering 
customers performance and sustainability;
■ Country platforms based on local value chains, 
optimized by CEOs native to their country who are 
fully accountable for their perimeter;
■ An expanded presence in non-residential and 
infrastructure thanks to the development of tailored 
offers and dedicated teams for each end market 
(particularly hotels, data centers, healthcare and 
educational facilities, transport infrastructure);
■ Saint-Gobain’s industry-leading role as worldwide 
leader in light and sustainable construction.
2) Continue to pursue excellence in execution in order 
to deliver the Group’s ambitious trajectory, with an 
EBITDA margin of between 15% and 18% over the period 
2026-2030 and a free cash flow conversion ratio above 
50%, thanks to:
■ Disciplined management of the price-cost spread;
■ Strict measures to reduce costs and deliver 
productivity gains in order to proactively adapt to 
market conditions.
3) Continue to actively optimize the Group’s profile, 
with asset rotation to represent over 20% of sales by 
2030, in terms of both acquisitions and divestments.
4) Disciplined capital allocation to deliver growth and 
value creation for shareholders:
■ Investments focused on consolidating leadership 
positions, high-growth countries and construction 
chemicals; 
■ Capital expenditure around 4.5% of sales in 2026;
■ Attractive shareholder returns, targeting regular 
growth in dividends per share and €2  billion in net 
share buybacks (2026-2030).
2.1.8 2026 OUTLOOK
In a contrasted macroeconomic environment and 
uncertain geopolitical landscape, the Group expects 
the following trends for 2026:
■ Europe: gradual improvement, with contrasted trends 
by country;
■ North America: continued market weakness in the first 
half, gradually improving outlook in the second half 
with an easier comparison basis; 
■ Asia-Pacific and Latin America: growth led notably by 
India, South-East Asia and Mexico. 
Saint-Gobain expects an EBITDA margin of more than 
15.0% in 2026, with the first half affected by the 
extreme weather conditions in Europe and North 
America since the start of the year.

B – Environment 
The data show a continuous and significant 
improvement in the Group’s environmental performance. 
Most of the 2025 performance targets are in line with the 
2030 and 2035 targets. While the integration of 
acquisitions into environmental reporting is rapid, the 
alignment of practices and the implementation of action 
plans may, depending on the environmental issues, 
require more time to set up.
Reducing Climate Change
■ CO2e emissions:
– CO2e (scope  1 and 2): The absolute reduction in 
emissions reached 35% compared to 2017, in line 
with the 2030 roadmap for the net-zero emissions 
trajectory by 2050. This result incorporates the 
effect of acquisitions completed in 2024, 
particularly CSR in Australia and BP Canada, and is 
an improvement compared to 2024 (8.7  million 
tonnes of CO2e in 2025 vs. 8.9  million tonnes of 
CO2e in 2024, considering the full-year effect of 
the acquisitions).
– CO2e (scope  3): In 2025, Saint-Gobain continued 
to improve the reliability and scope of reporting. 
The Group is focusing its efforts on the most 
significant scope  3 categories, particularly on 
the  decarbonization of procurement, which is a 
gradual process requiring a strong commitment 
from suppliers.
■ Carbon intensity: The carbon intensity of emissions 
remains stable between 2024 and 2025 at 0.19 kg 
CO2e per euro of revenue and 1.21 kg CO2e per euro 
of EBITDA; this marks a significant reduction 
compared to 2017, with a decrease of 76% for revenue 
and 58% for EBITDA, reflecting the Group’s 
decarbonization efforts.
■ Energy consumption, including decarbonized energy: 
In absolute terms, total energy consumption has 
slightly increased in 2025 compared to 2024 (+5%). 
However, changes in the energy mix have rendered 
the impact on overall energy consumption difficult to 
assess. Fossil fuels, primarily natural gas, continue to 
play a decisive role in the Group’s energy mix, yet the 
share of renewable energy in total energy 
consumption has now reached 18.3%, an increase of 2% 
compared to 2024. The proportion of decarbonized 
electricity in total electricity consumption reached 70% 
in 2025, up from 67% in 2024.
■ Life cycle analysis: Saint-Gobain is enhancing the 
information it provides to customers about its 
products by increasing the proportion of solutions 
equipped with a life cycle analysis (LCA) or an 
environmental product declaration (EPD). This 
coverage rate reaches nearly 57% of revenue in 2025, 
in line with the 2030 target, thanks to the publication 
of more than 5,000 EPDs.

Other environmental issues
■ Water management: Water withdrawals remain stable 
compared to 2024, reflecting a 26% reduction versus 
2017, which aligns with the trajectory toward a 50% 
reduction by 2030. In 2025, 303 sites are located in 
areas of high and very high water stress, compared to 
274 in 2024. This increase is attributable to the 
integration of recent acquisitions. Consequently, the 
Group’s withdrawals in these sensitive areas have 
risen by 11% between 2024 and 2025.
■ Waste management: Improved data quality and the 
inclusion of recent acquisitions in the results have led 
to an increase – in mass – of non-recovered waste 
compared to 2024. By the end of 2025, non-
recovered waste was reduced by 27% compared to 
2017. More than two-thirds of the waste generated is 
recycled, reused, or converted into energy.
■ Biodiversity: The impact on biodiversity is primarily 
concentrated around quarries. Of the Group’s 
108quarries, 85 are currently active. The number of 
industrial sites, including quarries, located in 
protected areas is very low relative to the Group’s 
overall activities – 45 sites, including quarries, 
representing less than 5% of industrial locations. By 
the end of 2025, the ambitious goal of covering 100% 
of active quarries with a BMap (including a site 
biodiversity inventory and identification of priority 
actions) was only achieved for 35%. Nevertheless, 
quarries are operated and subsequently restored with 
the aim of preserving the environment in accordance 
with local regulations, minimizing visual, acoustic, and 
ecological impacts as much as possible. The Group 
continues its efforts and reaffirms its commitment to 
biodiversity through the redefinition of its Act4Nature 
objectives, published in 2025.
■ Combating deforestation: In 2025, Saint-Gobain 
finalized its Forest Policy and published a CSR 
booklet, “Forest: Our Commitment,” which details the 
impact of the Group’s procurement activities and the 
action plans implemented.

C – Social
Employment indicators show steady and overall positive 
progress, in line with the Group’s 2025 commitments to 
guarantee the safety and well-being of all.
Social indicators show progress in line with the Group’s 
commitments for 2025:
■ Headcount and breakdown by region: At the end of 
2025, the distribution of the Group’s workforce 
remains stable compared to 2024 and is consistent 
with its strategic development.
■ Diversity and leadership: The proportion of women in 
senior management has reached 27%, surpassing the 
target of 25%, while women represent 29.6% of 
managers, nearly achieving the 30% goal set for 2025. 
These outcomes reflect the Group’s steady progress 
over the past 15 years.
■ Social responsibility: In 2025, 100% of the Group’s 
countries have implemented programs to support 
local communities.
■ Employee engagement and development: The “CARE 
by Saint-Gobain” social protection program has been 
deployed across all countries since 2022, in line with 
the Group’s commitment to support essential health 
needs as well as significant family milestones. 
Employee engagement remains well above the 
industry benchmark (83% compared to 76%), 
ensuring a fulfilling professional environment.

D – Governance
The Principles of Conduct and Action, which serve as the 
Group’s true code of ethics, are the benchmark for 
business conduct.
■ Diversity in leadership bodies: Women represent 44% 
of the Group Executive Committee and 30% of 
Business Unit Executive Committees, exceeding the 
30% targets set for 2025.
■ Responsible sourcing: The proportion of responsibly 
certified wood purchases remains high at 95%, 
approaching the 100% goal for 2025, reaffirming the 
Group’s commitment to a sustainable supply chain.
■ Ethics and compliance: Training for new managers on 
the code of ethics within their first year remains nearly 
comprehensive (98% in 2025), close to the annual 
target of 100%. Thanks to this onboarding initiative, 
nearly all (99.6%) of the Group’s managers have been 
trained on the code of ethics. The same holds true for 
anti-corruption training (99.1% of new hires and 99.7% 
of managers) and compliance with competition rules 
(99.1% of new hires and 99.7% of all managers).

2.2.2 INTEGRATION OF THE UNITED NATIONS SUSTAINABLE 
DEVELOPMENT GOALS
To embed the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) within its CSR approach, Saint -Gobain draws upon the 
materiality analysis (see section 1.2.4, p. 49), the Group’s stakeholder dialog and its understanding of its value chain. 
Saint-Gobain generally actively follows the debates on SDGs and reporting, especially the working group initiated by 
the Global Compact. The 17 SDGs have been subdivided into different levels: SDGs aligned with the strategy, 
moderately aligned SDGs (limited scope of influence or associated with a specific activity) and non-priority SDGs 
where the Group has little or no impact. 
The Group is especially committed to 14 Sustainable Development Goals aligned with the strategy:
2025 RESULTS AND OUTLOOK FOR 2026
NON-FINANCIAL RESULTS
96 SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 Ë www.saint-gobain.com
No poverty
Creating inclusive growth in the countries where 
Saint-Gobain operates:
■ for employees: the Group ensures fair compensation 
to its employees (see section 3.4.2, p. 154);
■ for end users: by increasing the lifespan of buildings 
and reducing operating costs and electricity bills 
through its sustainable and efficient solutions, 
Saint-Gobain makes housing more affordable and 
reduces end-user costs (see section 1.2.7.A, p. 60);
■ for local communities: Saint -Gobain contributes to 
economic development, improving access to decent 
housing and local employment (see  section 3.4.3, 
p. 162).
Good health and well-being
Ensuring healthy lives and promote well-being for all at 
all ages:
■ for employees: health and safety are central concerns, 
covered by an EHS policy and charter, and are top 
priorities at the heart of Saint-Gobain’s corporate 
culture (see section 1.2.7.F, p. 67);
■ for suppliers: the Group encourages its suppliers to 
improve the workplace health and safety of its 
employees through its Responsible Purchasing policy 
(see section 3.4.6, p. 175);
■ for direct customers and end users: one of the Group’s 
priorities is to design convenient, sustainable products. 
By facilitating fast, high-quality construction with 
lighter, ergonomic products, Saint-Gobain reduces the 
risk of accidents for workers on construction sites. 
They also make it possible to address sustainable 
construction through an approach more focused on 
people’s basic needs: health (clean air), safety 
(reliability and protection against external hazards), 
comfort (thermal, acoustic, ease of maintenance) and 
economy (productivity gains and reduction of users’ 
energy spending). (see section 1.2.7.A, p. 60);
■ for local communities: in the context of emergency 
situations, Saint-Gobain’s local teams are mobilized to 
assist affected populations (see section 3.4.3, p. 162).
Quality education
Promoting lifelong learning opportunities: for employees:
■ Saint-Gobain’s ambition is to be a benchmark 
employer, known and recognized for the wealth of 
career paths it offers. Saint -Gobain is committed to 
facilitating access to training for all its employees, 
using formats that meet their needs and expectations 
(see section 1.2.7.F, p. 67);
■ for customers: the Group develops training programs 
for customers’ employees, some of which lead to 
certification (see section 3.4.3, p. 162);
■ for local communities: the Group maintains 
relationships with local partners in many countries 
where it operates to boost local employment and 
support disadvantaged populations with their career 
aspirations. Saint-Gobain also contributes to major 
societal issues through sponsorship and philanthropy, 
in particular the Saint-Gobain Foundation (see section 
3.4.3, p. 162);
■ for civil society: support for young people is a priority 
in all the countries where the Group operates, 
particularly the professional integration of young 
adults in difficulty in the construction industry through 
the Build Change program (see section 3.4.3, p. 162).
Gender equality
Being inclusive by promoting equal opportunities:
■ for employees: Saint-Gobain is working to create an 
environment that fosters fairness and equality, which 
are essential for genuine professional development, 
while facilitating the formation and cohesion of high-
performance operational teams. Exemplary 
management and a policy of equal treatment in 
recruitment, professional training and compensation 
are the main levers for action (see section 3.4.2, p. 154);
■ for civil society: Saint-Gobain is working to promote a 
more inclusive environment through its membership 
of the UN’s Women Empowerment Principles (WEPs); 
■ for local communities: the Saint -Gobain India 
Foundation has set itself the task of improving the 
living conditions of the most underprivileged by 
supporting education-related projects, in particular by 
accompanying approximately 9,500 young girls 
(see section 3.4.3, p. 162).

Clean water and sanitation
Ensuring the sustainable management of water 
resources:
■ for civil society: reduce the impacts of the Group’s 
activities on water resources as much as possible, 
whether in terms of abstraction or discharges. The 
long-term objectives are to take as little water as 
possible and aim for “zero discharges” of industrial 
water in liquid form while avoiding generating new 
impacts for other natural environments and/or for 
other stakeholders (see section 1.2.7.F, p. 67);
■ for suppliers: the Group pays particular attention to 
the quality of its supplies and suppliers’ performance 
in terms of sustainable resource management. Risks 
related to purchasing categories include 
environmental performance and in particular those 
related to water (see section 3.4.6, p. 175);
■ for local communities: manage these issues locally. 
Needs and risks related to water access for local 
populations are systematically taken into account in 
the Group’s action plans (see section 1.2.7.F, p. 67).
Affordable and clean energy
Using Saint-Gobain’s potential for local consumption to 
foster the development of local renewable energy 
networks:
■ for civil society: Saint-Gobain is a member of the ETC 
(Energy Transition Commission), the aim of which is 
to accelerate the transition to a decarbonated energy 
system (see section 3.2.1, p. 116).
Decent work and economic growth
Creating conditions guaranteeing quality jobs for 
employees, suppliers and direct customers:
■ for employees: the development of a TEC. (Trust, 
Empowerment, Collaboration) culture is an important 
catalyst for successful employee development 
(see section 1.2.7.E.b, p. 66). All the actions undertaken 
have made it possible to achieve a record employee 
engagement index of 84% in 2025, with 86% of 
employees considering their working conditions to be 
good (see section 1.2.7.F, p. 67);
■ for suppliers: the Group’s suppliers are committed to 
ensuring decent working conditions. Ethical criteria on 
human rights, working conditions and compliance 
with standards, health and safety and the 
environment are incorporated into the procurement 
process (see section 3.4.6, p. 175);
■ for direct customers: Saint-Gobain’s solutions 
optimize the work of its professional customers and 
generate maximum returns for them. They streamline 
implementation and reduce errors and the risk of 
accidents, while optimizing overall project costs. This 
makes it possible to deliver buildings and 
infrastructure faster, increase project values, and 
make construction more accessible (see section 
1.2.7.F, p. 67).
Industry, innovation and infrastructure
Engaging Saint-Gobain’s innovation at the service of 
sustainable development and the circular economy:
■ for employees: to develop solutions that anticipate 
market trends, the Group has introduced an 
innovation approach that includes the challenges of 
sustainable development by design, adapted to any 
specific local factors, and deployed worldwide. It is 
thanks to innovation and solution performance 
evaluation that the Group is able to increase avoided 
CO2 emissions and to adapt its offering to the new 
opportunities linked to a fair and sustainable transition 
(see section 1.2.7.B, p. 62);
■ for civil society: Saint-Gobain has been a member of 
the WBCSD Board with responsibility for “climate, 
energy, the circular economy, towns and cities, and 
mobility” since 2017 (see section 3.2.1, p. 116).
Reduced inequalities
Being inclusive by promoting equal opportunities:
■ for employees: Saint-Gobain is working to create an 
environment conducive to fairness and equality, 
which  is crucial to employees’ professional 
growth,  while fostering training and the cohesion of 
high-performance operational teams (see  section 
3.4.2, p. 154);
■ for local communities: wherever it is present, the 
Group is committed to promoting inclusion and 
diversity in all its forms: gender, nationalities, training, 
career paths, generational diversity, disabilities and 
ethnic and social origins (see section 3.4.2, p. 154).
Sustainable cities and communities
Offering sustainable and affordable solutions in response 
to lifestyle changes in line with increasing urbanization, 
and building “more” and “better”:
■ for customers: for Saint -Gobain, it is imperative to 
design sustainable solutions and to contribute to the 
construction and renovation of resilient cities, 
guaranteeing the well-being of individuals against a 
backdrop of increasing resource scarcity and climate 
change (see section 3.2.2, p. 122);

3
INTRODUCTION
In accordance with the CSRD regulations to which Saint-Gobain is subject, this chapter three contains the four parts of 
its Sustainability Report as defined in ESRS 1. 
Saint-Gobain considers sustainability issues to be strategic and wishes to maintain communication of its issues, action 
plans and ESG performance aligned and consistent with its commitments, organization and operational action plans. 
The presentation of its roadmap in three pillars (see section 1.3.2, p. 74) enables the Group’s stakeholders to identify its 
long-term contributions and ensures this alignment between its commitments and what it actually achieves. The three 
pillars of the roadmap are also consistent with the results of the double materiality assessment (see section 3.1.3, p. 106).
The regulations require the Environment, Social and Governance sections in the Sustainability Report to be identified. It 
should also be noted that the four sections of the Sustainability Report within the meaning of the CSRD regulation are:
■ General provisions (ESRS 1 and ESRS 2), included in section 3.1, p. 103;
■ the Environment section, covered by sections 3.2, p. 116. (information related to climate change) and 3.3, p. 138 
(other environmental issues);
■ the Social section, included in sections 3.4.2, p. 154 and 3.4.3, p. 162;
■ the Governance section, available in sections 3.4.5, p. 172, 3.4.6, p. 175 and 3.4.7, p. 178.
To ensure compliance with regulations, this chapter separates the environmental, social and governance aspects but 
without any specific numbering. It should be noted that sections 3.4.5, p. 172 – Human Rights – and 3.4.6, p. 175 – 
Responsible Purchasing – are included in the Governance section but contain a significant amount of information 
required in the Social section. 
Chapter  8 contains the correlation tables used to assess Saint -Gobain’s performance against other regulations, 
standards and benchmarks, in particular the vigilance plan, the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures 
(TCFD) and standards developed by the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB).

3.1.1 BASIS FOR PREPARATION
Context
This Sustainability Statement for the 2025 fiscal year has 
been prepared on the basis of the consolidated scope. 
It was approved by the Board of Directors on 
February 26, 2026.
It was drawn up within the framework of the application 
of the European Corporate Sustainability Reporting 
Directive (CSRD), transposed into French law in 
December 2023, and prepared in application of the 
European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS).
This second year of application comes against a 
backdrop of uncertainties regarding the interpretation of 
texts and limitations in the preparation of the 
information inherent in the work to simplify regulations 
initiated in January 2025. 
In preparing the 2025 Sustainability Statement, no use 
was made of the options for omitting certain information 
relating to intellectual property, know-how and 
innovation results, or to upcoming developments and 
business under negotiation. 
Medium- and long-term timescales are set on the basis 
of each impact and the time required for the results of 
the action plans implemented to start influencing 
performance monitoring indicators. 
Scope
The scope covered is based on that of the financial 
statements (see chapter  7 – Financial and accounting 
information, Note 4 – scope of consolidation). The scope 
of the Group’s “own operations” therefore includes 
companies over which the Group exercises control and 
which are fully consolidated in the financial statements.
Some indicators show partial coverage rates. These are 
specified in the methodological note:
■ for social indicators in section 3.7.1.B.b, p. 209;
■ for environmental indicators in section 3.7.1.B.a, p. 206.
The Group is taking steps to improve these coverage 
rates. 
The upstream and downstream value chain, as described 
in section 1.2.5, p. 53, was considered during the double 
materiality analysis, which led to the identification 
of certain impacts, risks or opportunities directly related 
to  all or part of the Group’s value chain (see section 
1.2.4.B, p.  50 for more details on the impacts, risks 
and  opportunities identified). Among the main 
topics  identified and developed in this Sustainability 
Statement are: 
■ greenhouse gas emissions in the Group’s value chain 
that contribute to global warming and threaten 
biodiversity and ecosystems (see section 3.2.1.B, p. 118);
■ respect for the rights and working conditions of 
workers in the Group’s value chain (see section 3.4.5, 
p. 172);
■ the safety of users of the Group’s products and 
services and provision of correct information to them;
■ positive impacts related to sustainable and high-
performance solutions sold (see section 1.2.7.A, p. 60).
Calculation methods; main 
estimates and unpublished 
information
The methodologies for the indicators are described in 
section 3.7.1, p. 204 of this report, along with the scopes 
of application of the indicator calculations, proxies used 
and the degree of uncertainty and accuracy. 
Despite the efforts made by the Group, certain 
information has not been published: 
■ amounts of pollutants in water (E2-4 §28): the Group 
is present in over 80 countries. Industrial sites are 
subject to local regulation. To require from each site 
to communicate information based according to a 
pollutants list established by the European authorities 
requires important means. The Group gives priority to 
implementing the action plan for reaching the 
objective of pollutants limitation in water discharges;
■ information on substances of concern and very high 
concern (E2-5 §33 and §34); in particular, the request 
to provide volumes in units of mass does not directly 
serve the Group’s objectives and constitutes a 
significant effort to be carried out over several years;
■ the disclosure of materials present in waste and 
breakdown of waste disposed of (E5-5 §37c, §38b); 
This consolidated information is of little relevance to 
the Group given the large number of businesses and 
countries of operation. Reporting efforts are focused 
at this stage on assessing the waste generated and 
monitoring recycling networks development.

3.1.3 DOUBLE MATERIALITY
Saint-Gobain regularly performs double materiality 
analyses. Each of the updates resulted in an adaptation 
to the methodology based firstly on changes in the 
Group’s scope, strategy and value chain, and secondly 
on changes in existing practices and standards. The 
exercise conducted in 2024 was based on the ESRS 
established for the application of the European CSRD. 
Saint-Gobain may change the methodology or 
assessment of certain issues in the coming years. 
Saint-Gobain assessed the potential impact of the 
changes in 2025 on the results of the materiality analysis. 
This applies in particular to changes in scope, 
organizational changes, and changes in results. The 
Group concluded that the results of the materiality 
analysis published in 2024 remain relevant. 
A – Methodology
Adopted in 2022 and entered into force in January 2024, 
the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) 
is a European directive aimed at improving and 
harmonizing the disclosure of environmental, social and 
governance (ESG) information by companies.
A cornerstone of the CSRD, the double materiality 
analysis aims to identify sustainability themes reflecting:
■ the potential or actual positive and negative material 
impacts
 of a company’s activities and value chain on 
society and the environment;
■ the material positive financial effects (opportunities) 
and negative financial effects (risks) of sustainability 
matters that affect or could affect the Group’s 
financial performance.
Saint-Gobain has been conducting materiality analyses 
since 2015. Prior to the CSRD, Saint -Gobain’s material 
challenges were identified and assessed on the basis of 
stakeholder expectations and management’s vision. This 
process has been strengthened to incorporate the new 
CSRD requirements. 
In 2024, Saint-Gobain published the results of the 
analysis carried out in accordance with the requirements 
of the European Sustainability Reporting Standards 
(ESRS) published in July 2023. As no major changes 
were identified in 2025, the results of the analysis remain 
unchanged from the 2024 financial year.
The process for identifying and assessing impacts, risks 
and opportunities (IROs) described below reflects the 
steps applied during the initial assessment and 
subsequent update. 
General approach
The double materiality analysis is broken down into four main stages: 
a. Identification of sustainability stakes
Saint-Gobain’s sustainability stakes were determined 
based on (1) the stakes previously identified by the 
Group, (2) industry-specific reference frameworks 
specifying the priority stakes related to the construction 
business lines, (3) the Group’s business model and value 
chains, and (4) alignment with ESG stakes, sub-stakes 
and sub-sub-stakes listed by the ESRS.
b. Identification of impacts, 
risks and opportunities (IROs)
Subsequently, each sustainability stake was translated 
into IROs.
The identification of IROs was based on: 
■ industry information sources: studies, peer practices, 
reference frameworks, etc. (e.g. SASB, rating agency 
questionnaires, etc.);
■ internal sources of information analyzing the Group’s 
activities, products and services: risk mapping 
(transition risks, physical risks, risks related to 
operations, etc.) stakeholders, geographical areas of 
operation, etc.;
■ consolidation of the viewpoints and interests of 
external stakeholders (consumers, local communities, 
civil society, nature, etc.) through an in-depth review 
of the literature, and interviews conducted with the 
functional departments in charge of relations with 
these stakeholders;
■ this dual approach (documentation and qualitative 
interviews) ensures that a wide range of stakeholders 
are represented while maintaining a strategic balance 
between the different expectations. This consultation 
methodology, already tried and tested by the Group, 
will be used in future exercises;
■ support from an external firm of consultants.
The IROs have been identified so as to cover all the 
Group’s activities and its entire value chain, both 
upstream and downstream. Parties in the value chain 
beyond the top tier have also been included and thus 
cover materials sourcing, subcontracting and all 
downstream users. 
A COMMITTED GROUP
SUSTAINABILITY STAKES INTEGRATED INTO STRATEGY
106 SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 Ë www.saint-gobain.com
This approach has ensured that the impacts for which 
Saint-Gobain was responsible and those resulting from 
its business relations were identified and thus that all 
activities, business relations and geographical areas that 
might be concerned by negative impacts on the 
environment and society were taken into account. 
In accordance with the requirements of the ESRS, the 
following methodological presumptions have been used:
■ impacts, risks and opportunities are identified “gross”, 
i.e. without taking into consideration any action plans 
implemented by the Group;
■ the search for correlation between impacts and risks/
opportunities: for each impact identified, the Group 
considered whether there might be a counterpart in 
terms of financial effects, and vice versa. 
The final list, which includes more than 120 IROs , has 
been ratified by the Saint-Gobain CSR Department.
c. Evaluation of IROs
A specific methodology has been defined to assess the 
material nature of IROs. 
Impact materiality assessment
In accordance with the ESRS 1 guidance, the impact 
materiality assessment is based on four variables: the 
severity of the impact (scale and scope), its irremediable 
character (for negative impacts only) and the likelihood 
of its occurrence. This analysis incorporates the potential 
change in long-term impacts by calculating an 
aggravation/improvement coefficient. Combining the 
scores and coefficients applied to these variables gave a 
final score ranging from 1 to 4, which makes it possible 
to rank the impacts relative to each other.
The impact materiality assessment was based on:
■ the assessment of the functional divisions  
responsible for stakeholder dialog, as representing the 
expectations of the stakeholders concerned (i.e. 
employees, civil society, investors, consumers, 
regulatory authorities, suppliers and local 
communities, nature);
■ internal sources, notably existing impact and risk 
analyses;
■ external sources, in particular controversies, sector 
studies, international reference frameworks and 
industry benchmarks. The document reference base 
includes numerous reports and studies from 
organizations such as: United Nations Environment 
Program, Yale Center for Ecosystems + Architecture, 
IPCC, International Energy Agency, European 
Environment Agency, OECD, World Green Building 
Council, CDP Water, Encore Nature, World Economic 
Forum, WRI, ILO;
■ the expertise of the CSR Department;
■ support from an external firm of consultants.
Financial materiality assessment
In accordance with the ESRS guidance, financial 
materiality was assessed using two variables: severity 
and likelihood. This analysis incorporates the potential 
change in long-term risks and opportunities by 
calculating a deterioration/improvement coefficient for 
the financial impact. The severity scale was determined 
by the Finance, Risk and Internal Audit departments in 
order to capitalize on existing work and ensure 
consistency with the Group’s other risk management 
exercises. Each variable was given a score of 1 to 4 or 
was used as a coefficient. Combining these scores and 
coefficients gave a final score ranging from 1 to 4, which 
was used to prioritize risks and opportunities.
The financial materiality assessment was undertaken:
■ financial risks: by the Saint -Gobain Audit & Risks  
team. The involvement of the Audit & Risk team 
ensured consistency with the Group’s overall risk 
management process;
■ financial opportunities: by the CSR team.
Although the majority of material risks identified during 
the analysis are already included in the Group risk 
mapping, and the Audit & Risk team has ensured 
consistency with the overall risk management process, 
identifying and assessing risks and opportunities as part 
of the double materiality analysis remains a specific 
procedure. This process is not currently integrated with 
the Group’s overall risk management process. However, 
for risks that have already been integrated, the 
prioritization of sustainability risks follows the same 
process as for other risks.
As regards opportunities, these have already been 
identified, assessed and managed within the Group’s 
overall management process since they have been 
determined and are aligned with the Group’s strategy. 
Setting materiality thresholds
Each score in the impact materiality assessment and 
financial materiality assessment has been reviewed and 
validated by Saint-Gobain’s CSR Department.
The setting of the materiality threshold was based on the 
definition of a number of scenarios built around the 
following criteria:
■ alignment and continuity with the Group’s strategy 
and previous materiality assessments;
■ the materiality of the information for impacted 
stakeholders and users of sustainability information.
Setting this threshold made it possible to validate a list 
of material impacts, risks and opportunities  and 
consequently to determine the priority sustainability 
themes to be included within the CSRD reporting scope. 
d. Final approval
The results of the double materiality assessment were 
approved by the Group’s Senior Management. These 
results are also submitted for approval to the CSR 
Committee and to the Board of Directors.

B – Material challenges
Saint-Gobain has prioritized material challenges 
according to their level of priority, the location of the 
impact, risk or opportunity on the value chain.

BOARD OF DIRECTORS
■ Examines and establishes the Group’s strategic 
orientations annually and ensures their 
implementation, taking into consideration the social 
and environmental challenges of its activity
■ Determines, on the proposal of the General 
Management, the multi-annual ESG strategic 
orientations 
■ Reviews results annually (climate or ESG)
EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE
■ Defines strategies in line with the Group’s 
commitments and stakeholder expectations
■ Ensures implementation methods
CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY COMMITTEE 
OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
■ Reviews the Group’s CSR strategy, commitments 
and roadmap

with the annual review of non-financial risks conducted 
by the Audit and Risk Committee
■ Reviews sustainability information and results
■ Reviews, in conjunction with the Nomination 
and Remuneration Committee, the criteria for CSR 
performance metrics in the long-term compensation 
and variable compensation of corporate officers
■ Monitors the non-financial ratings 
and sustainability expectations of rating agencies 
THE BOARD’S AUDIT AND RISK COMMITTEE
■ Ensures the sustainability information preparation 
process is monitored 
■ Ensures the internal control and risk management

CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY DEPARTMENT
The control of sustainability information is the 
responsibility of the Corporate Social Responsibility 
Department, with the support of the functional 
Departments. Each functional Department (e.g. Human 
Resources, Legal Affairs, Purchasing, Environment, 
Security and Health) with the support of country or 
Business Unit organizations, is responsible for producing, 
consolidating, analyzing and reporting social, 
environmental and governance-related data. Internal 
procedures, including internal control procedures, are 
updated and widely communicated via an information 
tool that compiles the procedures related to financial 
and non-financial information.
For each of the material stakes, action plans are 
prepared, drawing on the expertise of the functional 
departments. They are deployed in the countries under 
the responsibility of local managers. 
The Group has not reported any current financial impact 
related to the risks and opportunities of sustainability 
stakes. Specific items related to combating climate 
change are presented in the note to the consolidated 
financial statements 3 “Climate issues” (see section 7, 
p. 350).
B – CSR strategy
For Saint-Gobain, sustainable growth is conceived within 
its ecosystem, in other words, taking into account the 
interests of all its stakeholders. It is therefore a question 
of pursuing a growth trajectory that integrates financial 
performance and shareholder value objectives as well as 
the Group’s Corporate Social Responsibility. 
Saint-Gobain has a perfect alignment between its 
corporate purpose, “Making the world a better home”, its 
vision, to be the leader in light and sustainable 
construction, and its strategic plan, “Grow & Impact”, 
from 2021 to 2025, and “Lead & Grow”, since 
October 2025.
Stakeholders’ expectations and the impact of operations 
(see  section 1.2.3.B, p.  48) are thus translated into 
sustainability stakes incorporated into the Group’s 
strategy. Saint-Gobain has growth opportunities linked 
to short-, medium- and long-term sustainability stakes. 
These include in particular opportunities related 
to  adaptation to climate change and the development 
of circularity. 
Its CSR roadmap is based on two levers of action 
systematically implemented for each of the sustainability 
stakes:
■ Deploy high-performance and sustainable solutions 
that bring benefits to stakeholders while maximizing 
its contribution to environmental impact, health or 
well-being;
■ Work towards sustainability by minimizing the 
adverse environmental and social effects of its 
operations across its value chain and with 
communities potentially affected.
Saint-Gobain makes use of its code of ethics, the 
Principles of Conduct and Action, responsible business 
practices (see section 1.2.7.E.a, p.  64) and the values 
shared with its partners to make decisions that maximize 
its positive impact and minimize the adverse effects on 
the environment, human beings and local communities, 
including residents in the vicinity of Group sites. 
In addition to, and as part of, the “Lead & Grow” 
strategic plan, Saint-Gobain is committed to accelerating 
the transition of the construction sector towards a more 
sustainable model. This transition requires the collective 
commitment of all stakeholders – professionals, 
institutions and citizens – both at the global level and in 
each of the countries where the Group operates.
This is why Saint-Gobain launched the Sustainable 
Construction Observatory in 2023, positioning itself as a 
benchmark company, both a pioneer and a driving force, 
to accelerate sustainable construction worldwide by 
bringing together all stakeholders. 
A barometer of sustainable construction, based on a 
quantitative study, was conducted in 22 countries 
among professionals, students, elected officials, and 
members of associations. While all respondents agreed 
that implementing sustainable construction is a priority, 
the understanding of sustainable construction often 
remains limited to environmental issues: the energy 
efficiency of buildings or the carbon footprint of 
construction. The concepts of resilience and occupant 
comfort are often still considered secondary. 
In 2025, an Action Paper was published. This document 
is the result of collaboration between international 
leaders and experts. It proposes 13 priority actions and a 
framework for reflection to accelerate the transformation 
towards a more sustainable construction model. It draws 
on the analyses and discussions conducted by the 
Sustainable Construction Observatory since its creation.
Beyond this barometer and publications, events are 
organized to bring stakeholders together on topics 
related to sustainable construction. In 2025, “Sustainable 
Construction Talks” were held, notably in Belém during 
COP 30 to present the Sustainable Construction 
Observatory’s Action Paper and to discuss collective 
mobilization and priority actions to address the climate 
crisis; in Venice for the Architecture Biennale on 
reconciling creativity and sustainability; in Cape Town to 
share the challenges of inclusion and just transition 
during World Environment Day; and in Davos during the 
World Economic Forum in January 2026 to highlight the 
power and opportunity of resilience and adaptation in 
sustainable construction.
This approach is accompanied by the creation of an 
information platform on sustainable construction 
challenges, “Constructing a sustainable future by 
Saint-Gobain”, to share the opinions or analyses of 
stakeholder representatives and theme-based 
presentations including innovative solutions and inspiring 
projects ( https://www.constructing-sustainable-
future.com/).
These levers of action are implemented with the 
objective of contributing to three long-term ambitions:
■ “a decarbonated home”, encompassing all the 
initiatives implemented for the Group’s contribution to 
the decarbonization of economies and reducing 
global carbon emissions on a trajectory aligned with 
the Paris Agreement;
A COMMITTED GROUP
SUSTAINABILITY STAKES INTEGRATED INTO STRATEGY
114 SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 Ë www.saint-gobain.com
■ “more performance with less”, representing actions in 
favor of an economy that is more frugal in its use of 
resources, raw materials and water, avoiding waste 
throughout the value chain of Saint -Gobain’s 
operations and favoring reuse or recycling; 
■ “a better living for all”, aiming to create a safe, 
engaging working environment for Group employees 
and those of its partners operating in its value chain 
and to contribute to the development of local 
communities, based on Saint-Gobain’s code of ethics, 
the Principles of Conduct and Action.
Internal and external stakeholders are involved in these 
action plans as part of an ongoing dialog at both country 
organization and Group support function levels (see 
section 1.2.3, p. 46).
Medium-term objectives are set to monitor Saint-Gobain’s 
ESG performance. As part of the implementation of the 
“Lead & Grow” strategic plan, the dashboard of CSR 
objectives for 2030 was reviewed (see section 3.2.4.A, 
p. 129).
Saint-Gobain’s CSR strategy and the corresponding 
objectives have been presented to and approved by the 
Board of Directors and its CSR Committee.
a. Maximize the contribution 
to sustainability stakes 
The dual materiality analysis identified material 
opportunities for the Group, whether financial or impact-
related, in the short, medium or long term (see section 
3.1.3 B, p. 108). 
By 2030, the main challenges and opportunities under 
the “Lead & Grow” strategic plan are linked to 
sustainability stakes (see section 1.2.1, p.  39). Growth 
opportunities lie in solutions for adapting buildings and 
infrastructure to climate change and developing 
circularity. 
Country platforms are an ideal form of organization for 
specifying and adapting solutions to the expectations 
and needs of customers who are specific to a given 
country and rolling them out in local markets that are 
involved in all the stages of the execution of a 
construction project, from design, to operation and even 
use (see value chain in section 1.2.5, p. 53)
The solution-based approach makes it possible to 
anticipate the needs of customers through in-depth 
knowledge of their expectations and technical expertise 
in interior solutions, exterior solutions, construction 
chemicals and services including trade and service 
agencies. (see section Solutions-based approach and 
Markets and activities, pp. 6 to 9)
The Group’s approach to developing high-performing 
and sustainable solutions is described in section 1.2.7.A, 
p.  60. The integration of sustainability considerations 
into the innovation process (see section 1.2.7.A.b, p. 61) is 
systematic. The impact and footprint of the solutions 
developed are assessed throughout their entire lifecycle 
and for their main stakeholders involved across the 
entire value chain, up to the end user.
The share of revenue generated with solutions assessed 
as sustainable according to the Group’s methodology 
published is 73% in 2025. This revenue includes 
operations which are not assessed under European 
Regulation 2020/852 Taxonomy Regulation (see section 
3.6, p. 200), such as trade and services activities, as well 
as impacts and benefits not integrated into the 
regulation such as resources and circular economy or 
other benefits related to health, safety and comfort 
which will potentially be eligible for the social taxonomy 
in the future.
b. Minimize the Group’s footprint
The reduction of the environmental footprint of its 
operations, responsible management of its value chain, 
and the implementation of its HR policy (see section 
3.4.2, p.  154) are the pillars of the Group’s objective to 
minimize its operational footprint.
To achieve this, Saint-Gobain relies on the efficiency of 
its operational excellence program (see section 1.2.7.F.a, 
p. 67). To accelerate the reduction of its environmental 
footprint, the Group has identified a list of priority 
industrial sites called “Focus Groups.” For each theme, 
these “Focus Group” sites represent approximately 80% 
of the impact. Of Saint-Gobain’s 1,100 industrial sites, the 
number of “Focus Group” sites remains limited, fewer 
than 200 whatever the topic.
The follow-up of the implementation of the 
environmental impact management system for 
operations and the ones for health and safety is 
accompanied by performance monitoring, in particular 
the recording of events related to health and safety, 
especially accidents or exposure to health risks and 
those having an impact on the environment such as 
accidental pollution.
Saint-Gobain has thus implemented a system for 
monitoring environmental incidents based on a 
classification that takes into account the nature of the 
accident, the type of accidental impact (air, water, or soil 
pollution, nuisances, particularly those related to odors 
or noise, or any other environmental impact with 
consequences for nature or local residents), its intensity, 
and its consequences.
This approach also relies on the principle of sharing best 
practices between sites. For many years, “EHS Awards” 
have been organized. Each site can present an 
innovative project recently implemented that has 
reduced the site’s environmental footprint or improved 
health and safety.
In 2025, the 35th edition of the “EHS Awards” received 115 
projects, which were evaluated by an international jury 
composed of Saint-Gobain employees and external 
experts. Four main criteria were considered: the project’s 
impact (risk reduction, energy savings, reputation, 
improvement of EHS culture, replicability, etc.), project 
management (participation of staff or external 
stakeholders such as associations, cross-site collaboration, 
etc.), innovation taking into account the local context, and 
communication about the project, both internally and 
externally. Fourteen winners were recognized.

3.2 A decarbonated home
3.2.1 GOVERNANCE AND STRATEGY
Faced with the challenge of climate change and the risks related to the increase in average temperatures, 
Saint-Gobain aims to contribute to the decarbonization of the construction sector, which accounts for nearly 40% of 
global CO2 emissions. In September 2019, Saint-Gobain responded to a call for action issued by a broad coalition of 
business leaders, civil society representatives and United Nations leaders to help limit the rise in global temperature to 
1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. 
In concrete terms, the objective is to bring the Group’s customers solutions to reduce their carbon emissions or to 
facilitate their adaptation to climate change while reducing the carbon impact of its operations across the value chain 
and thus achieving its goal of net zero emissions by 2050. 
A – Governance
A COMMITTED GROUP
A DECARBONATED HOME
116 SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 Ë www.saint-gobain.com
The “Carbon” roadmap (see section 3.2.4, p. 129) corresponds to Saint-Gobain’s commitment to “net zero 
emissions” by 2050. As a result, Saint-Gobain will reduce its CO2 emissions as much as possible in scope 1, 2 
and 3 by 2050 and will implement measures to absorb all the residual emissions. The success of the 
“net zero emissions” objective is based on intermediate objectives for 2030 and 2035 and on several levers 
of action. The roadmap is coordinated by the Sustainable Development Department. 
The Senior Vice President, Human Resources and Corporate Social 
Responsibility is in charge of corporate social responsibility. She oversees 
the incorporation of ESG challenges into strategy, coordinates the CSR roadmap, 
and ratifies the objectives.
The Sustainable Development department manages climate-related challenges, 
which represent both a risk and an opportunity for the Group.
The organizational chart for governance of CSR challenges by the Board 
of Directors and the Executive Committee is defined in section 3.1.4.A, p. 113.
THE “CARBON” ROADMAP
At Group level:
■ the Strategy Department supports 
Saint-Gobain’s ambition to be a leader 
in sustainability by including sustainable 
development as a key pillar of the Group’s 
growth and differentiation strategy. 
It monitors and implements the internal 
carbon price, including updating its level;
■ the Innovation Department coordinates

B – Strategy
Buildings and construction account for nearly 40% of 
annual CO2 emissions worldwide (1). Two thirds of the 
sector’s carbon impact comes from the operation of 
buildings, while the remaining one third comes from the 
emissions contained in building products in particular. 
The transition of buildings and the construction industry 
to carbon neutrality is therefore vital to the fight against 
climate change (see section 1.3.2.B, p. 76). Saint-Gobain’s 
objective is to contribute to a fair and sustainable 
transition towards a low-carbon economy. The 
implementation and results of this strategy are 
incorporated into scenarios that limit global warming to 
below a 1.5 °C rise compared with the pre-industrial era, 
so that they are compatible with the Paris Agreement. 
Saint-Gobain is thus seeking to decouple the growth of its 
sales and financial performance from its carbon impact. 
In response to climate risks, taking action as closely as 
possible to the areas concerned (countries, regions, etc.) 
makes it possible to make use of resilient local 
ecosystems that are more favorable to the development 
of a “low-carbon” economy. Country platforms (see 
section 1.2.5, p.  53) are an ideal organization in this 
context and their ability to initiate local partnerships is an 
asset both in risk management and in the development 
of growth opportunities.
In addition, Saint -Gobain’s organizational structure is 
based on a unique combination of local and global, 
which makes it possible to benefit from new 
opportunities that meet local needs while being part of a 
worldwide dynamic, including in terms of energy-
efficient building renovation and the development of 
light construction (see  section 1.2.2.A, p.  43) and in 
anticipating the effects of climate change.

a. Working with stakeholders 
for a just transition
The fight against climate change requires the 
cooperation of all stakeholders as part of a demanding 
international framework. Saint-Gobain is committed to 
implementing rapid action plans based on a common 
goal of limiting the rise in temperature to 1.5 °C. To that 
end, the Group has developed programs to involve its 
employees, the entire construction sector, public entities 
and NGOs.
Enhancing employee commitment
As part of a just transition, the transformation of 
Saint-Gobain’s industrial processes under the 
implementation of its “Carbon 2030” roadmap (see 
section 3.2.4, p. 129) does not result in any major change 
in the business lines or organization of industrial sites. 
The training programs set up by the Group already 
anticipate this transition (see section 1.2.7.A.a, p. 60), in 
particular those aiming to:
■ ensure efficiency and operational excellence; 
■ accelerate the digital transformation in operations, 
business models and skills.
In addition, Saint-Gobain is seeking to inform and train 
its employees on the challenges of climate change for 
the planet and for human beings. 
To meet this broad objective, it has provided employees 
with access to a set of e-learning training courses called 
the “Climate Academy”, regardless of their level of skills 
on the subject or their role at the company. The Climate 
Academy has been designed in two stages. In the first 
stage, employees learn about climate change impacts 
and challenges through modules of no more than five 
minutes. In the second, the Climate Academy presents 
eight themes describing the various means of acting to 
protect the environment and contribute to carbon 
neutrality in 2050. In addition to these online training 
courses, “Climate Fresco” workshops are organized 
around the world, with more than 75% of employees 
having been trained in the climate fresco at end-2025. 
To engage all its employees on the road to the 
contribution to carbon neutrality by 2050, and to 
contribute to achieving the objective of reducing the 
Group’s CO2 emissions between now and 2035, in April 
2021, Saint-Gobain launched an internal “Carbon Fund”. 
First implemented in a pilot region, Northern Europe, it 
aims to accelerate the reduction of non-industrial CO 2 
emissions through the daily actions of employees and 
targeted investments in sites. The areas covered by 
these investments are mainly related to the sustainable 
mobility of employees, renewable energies and the 
improvement of comfort and energy efficiency at 
Saint-Gobain sites. These projects proposed and 
selected by employees mainly concern their working 
environment. Organizational methods, thematic choices 
and priorities are defined by local organizations.
Engage the transition 
of the construction sector
The 2025 sustainable construction barometer, published 
as part of the sustainable construction observatory, 
shows significant global progress in knowledge and 
understanding of the concept of sustainable construction. 
Among the challenges, issues related to climate change 
(energy efficiency, carbon neutrality, and adaptation to 
climate hazards in particular) are particularly recognized 
by all stakeholders. Resilience to climate hazards has 
thus seen significant progress since the previous edition.

Saint-Gobain is committed to guiding the construction

sustainable construction and energy efficiency: 
■ the Group is a founding member of the steering

■ Saint-Gobain is fully committed as a non-state player

b. Solutions to reduce the carbon impact 
of the construction sector and support 
its adaptation
Saint-Gobain’s solutions help to reduce the negative 
climate impact of the construction sector and adapt 
buildings to the effects of climate change. The Group is 
focusing its action plans on the following areas:
■ offering low-carbon solutions by reducing emissions 
in Group operations (scope  1 and 2) and emissions 
related to its value chain (scope  3) to reduce the 
carbon content of buildings. (see section 3.2.4.B, 
p. 129);
■ offering solutions for decarbonizing industrial 
processes and manufactured products, such as the 
admixtures developed by Construction Chemicals to 
reduce the carbon impact of cement and concrete for 
buildings and infrastructure alike;
■ offering solutions that provide benefits during the 
building operation phase (use phase): the design, 
production and distribution of high-performance 
solutions with a positive contribution to the 
environment, i.e., solutions that promote energy 
efficiency and reduce CO 2 emissions during the use 
phase of buildings.

A DECARBONATED HOME
 
SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 119
Solutions to improve the energy performance of 
buildings help to reduce both the negative impact of 
buildings and construction on the environment and their 
occupants’ energy bills, while also enhancing occupant 
well-being. In addition, the solutions developed by 
Saint-Gobain help reduce energy demand, both during 
peak periods and on average, for heating and electricity, 
lower energy costs for industries and households, reduce 
associated carbon emissions, and optimize investments 
in energy production and transportation infrastructure. 
They therefore play an important role in the fight against 
climate change, because by reducing energy demand 
they decrease the quantity of greenhouse gases emitted. 
Since 2015, Saint -Gobain regularly updates the 
methodology used to calculate the quantity of 
greenhouse gases avoided thanks to the use of its own 
solutions in order to:
■ comply with the most recent and recognized 
international recommendations for the calculation of 
avoided greenhouse gas emissions;
■ extend the geographic coverage of the assessment;
■ update the operating conditions of the buildings 
taken into account, such as the heating systems, the 
distribution of energy used and the associated 
emission factors, and the efforts made to renovate the 
stocks.
Saint-Gobain has estimated that some 1, 043  million 
tonnes of emissions have been avoided thanks to the 
solutions produced and sold in one year in 2023 
throughout their entire life cycle. This research was 
conducted for the residential and non-residential 
buildings segment and for technical insulation activities 
(insulation in an industrial environment or insulation of 
ducts and pipes). 
The evaluation of avoided emissions is assessed based 
on the benefits provided by the installation of 
Saint-Gobain solutions compared with an installation 
meeting the standard or regulation. When current 
construction standards are demanding in terms of 
reducing buildings’ impact and are therefore aligned with 
the principles of more sustainable construction, the 
emissions avoided by the solutions installed by 
Saint-Gobain are low or even zero. In this case, it is the 
emissions of the entire construction sector that are being 
reduced. The gradual reduction in the amount of 
emissions avoided related to the products sold is a 
favorable sign of the transition of the construction sector, 
to which the Group is committed (see section 1.2.1, p. 39). 
The updated methodology is available to all stakeholders 
on the Saint-Gobain website. This calculation has been 
reviewed by an independent third party. The assessment 
is based on collecting country-by-country information 
from marketing teams, in particular on the condition of 
the building stock, the standards in force for new 
construction, and the use of recognized external sources, 
in particular for evaluating the impact of the country’s 
existing energy mix.
c. Achieve “net zero emissions” 
(scope 1, 2 and 3) by 2050
Ambitious interim targets to support growth 
Saint-Gobain set its first decarbonization targets in the 
early 2010s and ever since has incorporated plans to 
reduce its carbon footprint. In 2019, the Group set a 
target of net zero emissions by 2050, validated by the 
Science Based Targets initiative and aligned with the 
Paris Agreement and a 1.5 °C trajectory.
The action plan for reducing carbon emissions (scope 1, 2 
and 3) is divided into three periods:
■ 2020 to 2030: Saint-Gobain is rolling out its carbon 
roadmap, with an action plan and targets for the end 
of 2030 (see section 3.2.4.A.a, p. 130). This roadmap 
has two ambitions:
– reduce (in absolute terms) CO2e emissions in 
scope  1 and 2 by 33% and in scope  3 by 16% 
between 2017 and 2030, and do so without using 
carbon offsetting or sequestration measures;
– innovate and test industrial processes to achieve 
net zero emissions in the three scopes.
■ 2025 to 2035 (medium term): when launching its 
“Lead & Grow” strategic plan, Saint-Gobain published 
a new objective to reduce scope 1 and 2 emissions in 
the medium term. Given the uncertainties of changes 
in valuation standards for scope  1, 2 and 3, and the 
extension by SBTi of the validity of its objectives to 
2030, the Group has chosen to propose a new 
objective that will be revised if necessary: a reduction 
of between 40% and 45% in scope 1 and 2 emissions 
between 2017 and 2035, in absolute value;
■ 2035 to 2050 (long term): the roadmap will be 
adapted on the basis of the results obtained during 
the previous period. The innovations identified when 
implementing the action plans will be rolled out. 
Carbon capture projects may be activated at the end 
of the period to supplement the transformation 
measures up to a maximum of 10% of emissions 
(scope 1, 2 and 3).
The Group’s action plan does not, at this stage, include 
carbon credits or offsetting, or avoided emissions.
To support this carbon roadmap, Saint -Gobain has 
committed to investing at least €100  million a year in 
CAPEX and R&D over the period 2020 to 2030.
Saint-Gobain’s operations, in particular its industrial 
assets (asset base replaced over a period of 20 years), 
but also the solutions that the Group puts on the market, 
will not generate significant locked-in CO 2 emissions 
by 2050.

Integrating carbon impact 
into operational decision-making tools 
to accelerate the transition
Since 2016, Saint-Gobain has used an internal carbon price 
to assess the current or potential impact that a regulatory 
carbon price would have on all of Saint -Gobain’s 
operations, identify growth opportunities, refocusing 
capital expenditure towards manufacturing and R&D, and 
prioritizing actions to reduce CO2 emissions. The objective 
of the internal carbon price is consequently to influence 
investment decisions. The Group has set two levels of 
internal carbon prices. The first internal carbon price level 
per tonne is applied to capital expenditure above, 
investments associated with a change in energy source, 
energy investments on an existing or greenfield site. The 
second carbon price level is used for R&D investment in 
breakthrough technology. The second carbon price level 
is used for R&D investments in technological disruptions. 
This price level has proved its relevance in supporting 
low-carbon R&D projects.
The internal carbon price levels are regularly updated in 
line with market trends and are applicable to all 
countries in which the Group operates. At end-2025, the 
prices applicable were €100 per tonne of CO2 for CAPEX 
and €200 per tonne for R&D projects. In addition, a 
specific approach applicable to significant acquisitions 
has been defined. It includes any effort required to 
ensure that the carbon impact of this acquisition is 
compatible with Saint -Gobain’s direct and indirect 
emissions target trajectory.
The carbon impact is also integrated into the processes 
for establishing annual budgets or strategic plans. 
Information on the carbon impact of planned investments 
is available to technical teams at sites and to the industrial 
departments of each business. Technical innovations such 
as investments in more mature technologies are identified 
according to their cost, technical maturity and potential 
for reducing CO2 emissions. 
Scope  1 and scope  2 emissions are automatically 
measured monthly for nearly 90% of the Group’s impact. 
This reporting is based on computerized management 
systems (ERP). The management controllers are 
responsible for updating the information used to 
calculate scope 1, such as consumption of raw material 
or energy. PPA (Purchase Power Agreement) contracts 
are updated by the purchasing teams and integrated 
into the reporting tools for monitoring scope 2.
In addition, the Board’s CSR Committee ensures that 
Corporate Social Responsibility issues are taken into 
consideration when defining Saint-Gobain’s strategy and 
in its implementation (see organizational chart and for a 
description of the Corporate Social Responsibility 
Committee’s remit and activities in section 3.1.4.A, p. 113). 
Considering the challenge of climate change as strategic 
for the Group, the reduction of CO 2 emissions is a 
performance metric included within the short- and long-
term compensation plans for Group executives (see 
section 4.2.3, p. 275 and section 4.2.4.B, p. 276). 
Lastly, between 2022 and 2024, financing tools linked 
to  ESG performance criteria such as the Sustainability 
Link Bond, the Sustainability Link Loan and Green Bond 
were issued.

3.2.2 RISKS, OPPORTUNITIES AND SOLUTIONS
Saint-Gobain is committed to understanding and 
anticipating the impacts of climate change on its business 
activities. The “Risks and opportunities” section reflects 
the Group’s proactive approach to climate risk analysis. 
The analysis is based on three future climate scenarios, 
which identify relevant risks for Saint-Gobain, such as 
extreme weather events and new environmental 
regulations. At the same time, Saint-Gobain is exploring 
the opportunities that may arise from these 
developments, particularly in terms of technological 
innovation, low-carbon offerings and solutions for 
adapting to climate change. This approach helps to 
prepare the Group for an uncertain future while actively 
contributing to the transition to a more sustainable world.
A – Analysis of climate scenarios for 2050
For strategic planning purposes, Saint-Gobain has built three qualitative “climate scenarios” that incorporate political, 
technological, economic and societal assumptions. Each scenario is associated with an increase in average 
temperature of between 1.5 °C and 4.5 °C before the end of the century and is based on the work of the IPCC.

METHOD OF CONSTRUCTION
■ Collective buildings are designed for near-zero energy performance.
■ Household appliances are shared and efficient while excess heat is shared between connected buildings.
■ Apartments are easy to reconfigure and refurbish to optimize space and reuse.
■ Builders favor natural lighting, passive cooling and solar protection.
■ To improve their resilience, the buildings are equipped with green walls and roofs, wastewater and rainwater harvesting 
systems, reflective materials, and the foundations are adapted to heat waves and clay shrinkage.
■ The use of bio-sourced, reused and recycled materials is becoming widespread to mitigate the effects of climate change. 
Likewise, energy self-production, waste sorting and composting systems are installed: innovations (particularly 3D printing, 
AI assistance) are thus used to optimize energy efficiency.
■ The installation of smart meters and sensors makes it possible to monitor consumption and automatically regulate lighting, 
ventilation, cooling and heating.
■ Real estate markets favor low-carbon, high-performance assets, and the infrastructure sector is sacrificing productivity gains 
in favor of a lighter environmental footprint.
THE SHOW MIGHT GO ON SCENARIO
SUSTAINABLE CITY
Model of existing city Nairobi, Buenos Aires, Beijing and some other Asian cities.
Size Rapid growth due to intensive industrialization.
Mobility Public transit does not cover the entire city and does not make it 
possible to optimize travel. Most people continue to travel by car.
METHOD OF CONSTRUCTION
■ Two models emerge: firstly, the European model, and secondly, the US model.
■ In Europe, the majority of the population lives in office buildings built in 2000 and converted into residential buildings in 
2030. The individual apartments are small, but benefit from large shared spaces (workspaces, fitness, high-tech kitchens). 
The appliances shared in the kitchens and laundry rooms, which are gradually being introduced into a circular economy 
system, are highly efficient and consume little energy. The roof is equipped with photovoltaic panels, heat pumps are used 
for heating, and insulation has been reinforced with recycled materials. A centralized monitoring system automatically 
adjusts heating, lighting, ventilation, and cooling.
■ In the United States, the majority of the population lives in apartment buildings and private condominiums in the suburbs of a 
large city, in buildings dating from the 1970s. Only a minority of individual apartments have been renovated. Most devices are 
programmable, but none are shared. Energy consumption is not systematically monitored. However, facilities have been put in 
place to increase the energy efficiency of buildings and mitigate the effects of climate change on residents’ comfort: the 
electrification of heating is slowly developing, wall and roof insulation has been improved, double-glazed windows have been 
installed, and passive cooling systems have been put in place.
■ With greater exposure to natural disasters, cities are taking reactive measures, but green infrastructure is being introduced late. 
HIGHWAY TO CLIMATE HELL SCENARIO
SUSTAINABLE CITY
Model of existing city London, Rio de Janeiro, some US cities, Lagos, Lima, New Cairo.
Size These immense cities occupy a vast territory and are home to 
3  to 5  million inhabitants. In less developed countries, these 
growing cities are surrounded by large slums.
Mobility The majority of the population lives in the suburbs, and driving is 
the most used mode of transportation thanks to the extent of the 
road network.
METHOD OF CONSTRUCTION
■ Subsidized, affordable but low-quality housing is built to contain the endless expansion of slums in emerging countries. Poor 
quality is often accompanied by raised living spaces, a lack of daylight, thermal discomfort, high levels of noise pollution and 
inadequate ventilation of fresh air. 
■ Emergency renovations in response to natural disasters or the increasing use of air conditioning, which has become the only 
recourse to global warming in a self-perpetuating process, do not ensure systemic resilience. Basic insulation solutions are 
still incompatible with the affordability required for such “slum sanitation” approaches. 
■ Access to basic services (wastewater, drinking water, electricity, sanitation, waste disposal) is an important step towards 
achieving the fundamental objectives of human development. Recycling, reuse and the circular economy can only be 
considered when these basic services have been fully realized or when resource scarcity forces innovation, around 2050.
