B – Risks and opportunities 
across the value chain
The identification and assessment of risks and 
opportunities related to climate change is an integral 
part of Saint -Gobain’s global risk management and 
innovation processes. 
Saint-Gobain distinguishes between two types of risk:
■ physical risks, which are the direct consequences of 
climate change, such as floods or heat waves, which 
can damage infrastructure and affect human health; 
■ transition risks, which are related to the economic and 
regulatory changes required to move to a low-carbon 
economy, such as the closure of coal-fired power 
plants and the increase in carbon taxes. 
The major risks linked to climate disruption identified on 
the basis of the sixth IPCC report are the increased 
frequency and/or intensity of potentially destructive 
events, resource scarcity, and the increase in global 
temperatures. 
The Group has identified five strategic risks and five 
strategic opportunities related to climate change. Each 
risk and opportunity affects each segment of 
Saint-Gobain’s value chain differently, from raw material 
extraction to end-of-life. 
The analysis of exposure to transition risks was carried 
out based on the 1.5 °C scenario, Wind of Change. The 
risks analyzed by Saint-Gobain are political and legal, 
technological, reputational, and market risks. The 
analysis covered the entire value chain. There are 
significant disparities between regions, linked in 
particular to the varying pace of development of 
ambitious policies and regulatory frameworks, local 
investment to ensure the availability of carbon-free 
energy at a competitive price, and the capacity to 
develop circular material flows within a given territory. 
The Group’s opportunities are linked both to the effects 
of climate events and to the adaptation of buildings and 
infrastructure. 
The Risk and Insurance Department continuously 
assesses the risks to which the Group’s sites are exposed 
worldwide and, in particular, the risks related to the 
effects of climate change (see section 3.2.3, p. 127). 
In order to evaluate the financial impact of these risks and 
opportunities, Saint-Gobain conducted a further study 
with an external firm to identify its exposure to physical 
risks related to the impact of climate change (floods, 
forest fires, cyclones, storms, drought and heat stress), as 
well as earthquakes, on its operations. Exposure and 
vulnerability to climate issues were analyzed for assets at 
approximately 500 of the largest industrial and logistics 
sites (covering more than 80% of the Group’s sales and 
net book value of its assets), using three scenarios based 
on the work of the IPCC: SSP1-2.6 – Wind of Change; 
SSP2-4.5 – The Show Might Go On; SSP5-8.5 – Highway 
to Climate Hell; and three time horizons: 2030 (medium 
term), 2040 and 2050 (long term). 
This study served to assess the financial impact for each 
site and for the Group as a whole, after factoring in the 
following impacts:
■ direct impacts: the immediate effects of climate 
change on sites, infrastructure, and living and working 
conditions;
■ indirect impacts: the consequences of climate change 
on business activity and the financial statements, and 
the impact on the workforce, including business 
interruptions.
Heat stress, floods and storms would represent the bulk 
of the estimated risks, which would mainly arise not as a 
result of direct damage but from business interruption. 
The impact would be more significant in Asia and India, 
while Europe would not be materially affected. 
Potential adaptation measures were then examined to 
reduce the vulnerability of the sites, taking into account 
their cost, feasibility and ease of implementation. This 
study confirms that the risks identified do not present 
significant financial materiality for the Group on its own 
operations, including in the most extreme scenario and 
by 2050 (scenario SSP5-8.5 – Highway to Climate Hell) 
(see Note 3 Climate issues in chapter 7).
This study was supplemented in 2024 by a comparable 
analysis of 51 Australian sites of the CSR Australia entity. 
The risks identified during this additional analysis also 
appear to be insignificant for CSR and Saint -Gobain 
overall. The update of the entirety of this study 
conducted in 2024 confirmed the conclusions of the 
initial 2023 study.
In parallel with this physical risk assessment for its assets, 
the Group has begun analyzing the growth opportunities 
for its solutions resulting from the impact of climate 
change in several regions. 
Saint-Gobain’s solutions are designed to limit their 
impact on the climate. The Group’s analysis of 
opportunities focused on three risks in four strategic 
countries, covering 38% of its revenue and focusing on 
the construction and renovation markets. Heat waves 
were analyzed in France and Brazil, floods in India, and 
cyclones in the United States, according to the three 
IPCC scenarios: SSP1-2.6 – Wind of Change; SSP2-4.5 – 
The Show Might Go On; and SSP5-8.5 – Highway to 
Climate Hell. 
The tables below show how the opportunities and risks 
identified by Saint -Gobain impact each stage of the 
value chain while being part of global market dynamics 
and meeting the expectations of end users. This 
approach has also been aligned with TCFD 
recommendations. The risks identified do not present 
significant financial materiality for the Group, even over 
the long-term, worst-case scenario based on current 
knowledge.
The Group takes these climate challenges fully into 
account, incorporating them into its financial statements 
and their short-, medium- and long-term projections 
(economic forecasts, energy mix, discount rate, etc. (see 
Note 3 Climate issues in chapter 7).

3.2.3 ADAPTATION PLAN
A – Adaptation to physical risks
In addition to developing an offering linked to market 
adaptation needs, Saint -Gobain is preparing its 
operations for the risks associated with climate change 
and is developing:
■ programs to adapt its operations, particularly its 
industrial sites, to climatic events (see section 1.2.7.F.a 
“Industrial and distribution risk prevention policy”, 
p. 67);
■ programs to adapt working conditions to rising 
temperatures;
■ adaptation programs linked to the potential impact of 
climate change on the supply chain.
The “World Class Manufacturing” (WCM) industrial 
excellence program (see section 1.2.7.F.a, p. 67) ensures 
the implementation of best practices in terms of 
methods and tools at industrial sites and facilitates the 
implementation of adaptation measures.
In 2022, a specific study of the exposure of the main 
sites was conducted. These risks are managed by the 
sites concerned, which draw up and implement action 
plans to reduce their risk exposure, updating business 
continuity plans to take account of climatic risks. The 
technical and industrial performance department, in 
particular the industrial and R&D departments of each 
activity, coordinates actions involving changes to 
industrial processes or plant design. However, as 
specified in paragraph 3.2.2.B, the risks identified do not 
present significant financial materiality for the Group 
(even over the long-term, in the worst-case scenario 
based on current knowledge). 
Saint-Gobain is implementing concrete measures to 
respond to physical risks at its sites. For example, the 
new furnaces installed on the sites are designed to 
better take into account the risk of flooding. All 
Saint-Gobain industrial sites exceed local seismic 
standards. To mitigate the risk of drought, particularly in 
water-stressed areas, Saint-Gobain is working to adapt 
its most water-intensive sites to operate them in a closed 
loop and potentially invest in rainwater capture systems. 
These measures are accompanied by training programs 
for site teams that enable the rapid implementation of 
preventive measures in the event of climate events such 
as rising water levels or floods. 
The HR and Environment, Health and Safety (EHS) teams 
have worked on prevention tools to anticipate the 
deterioration of working conditions during heat waves 
and periods of intense cold. 
B – Adaptation to transition risks
All of Saint-Gobain’s activities are compatible with 
climate transition and the goal of achieving net zero 
emissions by 2025.
a. Political and legal
At the local level, monitoring and compliance programs 
have been implemented in the countries coordinated by 
the EHS Department, while the Legal Department 
monitors new environmental regulations. In addition, the 
marketing teams ensure that the Group’s products 
comply with local environmental regulations. Similarly, 
the risks of climate change disputes are assessed as part 
of the existing risk management process. Saint -Gobain 
monitors changes in climate reporting requirements in 
order to meet the expectations of its stakeholders, 
particularly regulatory requirements and investor 
expectations.
b. Technological
The Group anticipates the technological risk linked to the 
substitution of existing products with low-carbon 
options by investing in the development of disruptive 
technologies and eco-innovative solutions to meet the 
expectations of its customers. Two internal carbon prices 
were set up in 2016 to support the viability of 
Saint-Gobain’s projects and strategy (see section 
3.2.1.B.c, p. 120). 
c. Market
Saint-Gobain anticipates the risk of raw materials 
scarcity by actively promoting the transition towards a 
circular economy (see section 3.3.3, p.  143) and by 
reducing its water consumption (see section 3.3.2, 
p.  140). The substitution of non-renewable virgin raw 
materials with renewable or recycled raw materials, the 
extension of the lifespan or use of Saint-Gobain’s 
products or systems, and the reduction of the intensity 
of materials are at the heart of the Group’s innovation 
process and enable it to ensure the competitiveness of 
its solutions while anticipating changes in the 
preferences of its end users and legislation.
Saint-Gobain is also working to optimize and reduce its 
energy consumption through such means as investing in 
digital tools to adjust energy consumption as closely as 
possible to needs.
A COMMITTED GROUP
A DECARBONATED HOME
 
SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 127
Anticipation of the increase in the cost of high-emission 
products, which would follow the tightening of 
regulations and the change in preferences expected by 
end users and customers, encourages Saint -Gobain to 
support the development of low-carbon materials and 
methods throughout its value chain. In addition to its 
efforts to contribute to carbon neutrality in its 
operations, the Group promotes renewable energies 
and develops solutions to improve the energy efficiency 
of its customers to enable them to meet the climate 
and  environmental challenges they face (see section 
3.2.2.B, p. 124). 
Lastly, the Purchasing Department factors the risk of an 
increase in the price of raw materials or of energy and 
greenhouse gas emissions into its purchasing strategies. 
As part of its Responsible Purchasing program, 
Saint-Gobain relies on a diversity of suppliers and supply 
sources to reduce the risk of transportation difficulties 
and supply chain disruptions.
d. Reputational
Mindful of the impact of a bad reputation on 
environmental matters, the Group fully integrates 
reputational risk into its risk management policy. 
Saint-Gobain is demonstrating its commitment to the 
climate through its climate policy and concrete targets 
for reducing its CO2 emissions and energy consumption. 
Lastly, the needs and risks related to access to water 
for  local populations are also taken into account in its 
action plans.
C – Opportunities related 
to adaptation 
Regardless of the predictive scenarios on the effects of 
climate change (see section 3.2.2.A, p.  122), the 
combined effects of temperature rises and climate 
events (droughts, floods, fires, storms, etc.) will have a 
strong impact on construction market growth:
■ destruction of homes caused by the increase in 
climatic phenomena, resulting in increased demand 
for reconstruction in the geographical areas affected;
■ buildings damaged by drought and shrinkage in clay 
soils, for example in France the percentage of 
buildings reckoned to be exposed or highly exposed 
to risks varies from 35% to 78% for temperature 
increases between 1.8 °C and 4.4 °C (source I4CE).
At the same time, construction methods will have to 
change to incorporate new constraints to preserve the 
value of buildings and/or to ensure the comfort of 
building users, both residential and non-residential, in 
response to rising temperatures and the growing 
number of days of heatwave. 
Saint-Gobain is thus orienting its offering towards 
sustainable construction markets. Saint-Gobain’s portfolio 
of businesses and expertise in insulation, materials 
reinforcement with construction chemicals, and building 
science, ensures that it is particularly well positioned to 
meet the adaptation needs of construction markets. By 
leveraging existing expertise and building on its culture 
of innovation (see section 1.2.7.D.a, p. 63), Saint-Gobain’s 
range of solutions can be extended to meet the perils 
associated with the effects of climate change, in 
particular adapting housing to rising temperatures or 
protecting buildings from storms and flooding.
Thanks to its strong exposure to the renovation market, 
the Group is ideally situated to play a decisive role in the 
national and European “green recovery” plans for the 
energy transition, which should support Saint -Gobain’s 
structural growth. Saint-Gobain’s portfolio of expertise 
and solutions provides it with a particularly favorable 
positioning in the face of the need to adapt construction 
markets, and resource scarcity. The program to develop 
the range of sustainable and high-performance solutions 
also includes a component on improving customer 
productivity.
The organization structure based on country platforms 
(see section 1.2.5, p.  53) makes it possible to develop 
solutions that meet the specific needs of the region 
concerned and to be part of local building resilience 
programs.
Specific offers for adapting buildings are being 
developed in many countries, for example, in the US 
CertainTeed has partnered with the Insurance Institute 
for Business & Home Safety (IBHS) to offer roofing 
solutions that meet their FORTIFIED™ Roof standard. 
FORTIFIED™ Roof is a nationally recognized standard 
designed to strengthen homes against extreme weather 
conditions, including high winds, hail, and heavy rain. It 
goes beyond typical building codes and offers a unified 
system of products and installation methods that have 
been proven to increase the resilience of homes and 
reduce potential damage. 
In some parts of the world, rising temperatures combined 
with high humidity levels will have a significant effect on 
working conditions at construction sites, which may even 
lead to a shutdown of construction sites for an increasing 
number of days. Saint -Gobain’s customers will have to 
change their methods and find productivity drivers. Since 
its launch in 2021, the program to develop the range of 
sustainable and high-performance solutions (see 
section  1.2.7.A, p.  60) has included a customer 
productivity improvement component through 
digitalization service proposals designed to improve 
anticipation of worksite organization or prefabrication, 
optimizing assembly time on the worksite.

3.2.4 TRANSITION PLAN 
A – 2030 to 2050 trajectory
Saint-Gobain’s medium- and long-term growth ambitions 
require a reduction in the carbon intensity of its 
operations and solutions. The Group has set a target of 
net zero emissions by 2050 in scope 1, 2 and 3, validated 
by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) and 
aligned with the Paris Agreement and a 1.5 °C trajectory.
In 2020, SBTi validated Saint -Gobain’s 2030 target: 
8.9 million tonnes of CO2 in scope 1 and 2 in 2030, i.e., a 
33% reduction in absolute terms between 2017 and 2030, 
and a 16% reduction in scope 3 over the same period. 
While the Group has rotated its business portfolio, the 
cumulative effects on the original baseline are not 
significant, at under 5%. The Group has invested in new 
business activities, mainly in the construction chemicals 
sector, and has sold trading and glass processing 
activities. Saint-Gobain has also made acquisitions to 
step up growth in new regions, investing in the 
Australian company CSR in 2024 as well as in Canada, in 
Kaycan, Bailey and BP Canada. 
In addition, Saint-Gobain has implemented a set of 
indicators to monitor its performance in terms of climate 
change. Emissions reduction performance is therefore an 
operational performance indicator in the same way as 
financial performance indicators.
By the end of 2025, the Group had reduced its emissions 
in scope 1 and 2 by 35% since 2017.
Assessing scope 3 emissions remains a challenge for all 
companies due to methodological changes, the 
complexity of value chains, and disparities in the quality 
of data provided by partners. Since 2021, Saint-Gobain 
has implemented a program to improve the quality of 
data collected and expand the scope and categories of 
scope 3 emissions considered. 
This is why the update of Saint-Gobain’s scope  3 
emissions assessment in 2021 was accompanied by a 
more specific assessment of emission factors and a more 
granular analysis of the impacts on the three most 
significant categories, representing more than 80% of 
total scope 3 emissions. The calculation was updated in 
2023 to more accurately reflect the impact of end-of-life 
products and based on more recent emission factors. 
The methodology used to measure Saint-Gobain’s 
scope  3 emissions is available in the resource center 
section of its website ( https://www.saint-gobain.com/
en/corporate-responsibility/resource-center).
A database has also been created to track the emission 
factors of materials and products purchased by the 
Group. The ideal and most reliable approach is to obtain 
a life cycle analysis from suppliers for the materials and 
products they have delivered to the Group. If this 
information is not available, the assessment is based on 
values from recognized databases, such as Gabi or 
EcoInvent.
This collective effort to improve data results in an 
automatic increase in the Group’s scope  3 emissions 
assessment, but it is an essential prerequisite for 
ensuring the effectiveness of the collective action plans 
implemented. 
At the end of 2025, scope 3 emissions were estimated at 
23.4 million tonnes for the scope considered in the 2030 
target validated by SBTi (24.4 million tonnes at the end 
of 2023), as detailed in section 3.2.4.A, p.  129. This 
increase is largely due to improved coverage of 
estimates, particularly the inclusion of end-of-life 
emissions from products.
The scope 3 reduction target between 2017 and 2030 is 
measured on a reduced scope in accordance with the 
methodology validated by SBTi. Nevertheless, 
Saint-Gobain assesses all categories and action plans are 
implemented across all of its operations. scope  3 
reporting tables for all categories and for the scope of 
the target validated by SBTi are available at section 
3.5.3, p. 197.
The scope  3 impact of Saint -Gobain’s operations is 
concentrated on the three most significant categories: 
■ purchases of raw materials (category 1) and energy 
(category 3); 
■ transport and logistics (categories 4 and 9); 
■ purchases related to trading operations (category 1). 
Each country is responsible for its own roadmap 
incorporating emissions from scope  1, 2 and 3. Each 
year’s financial budgets include an assessment of carbon 
emission reductions based on planned investments. The 
carbon roadmap is supported by a CAPEX and R&D 
investment plan of at least €100  million per year until 
2030. In 2025, €213 million had been invested in capital 
expenditure and R&D related to the carbon roadmap. 
Under European Taxonomy Regulation 2020/852, a 
limited number of the Group’s activities have been 
assessed. As a result, only 16.4% of its revenue is eligible 
in 2025. Furthermore, the methods used to calculate 
indicators, particularly Capex and Opex as defined by 
the regulation, differ from the operational rules for 
monitoring the carbon roadmap. The Capex amounts 
published in accordance with the European Taxonomy 
Regulation are available in section 3.6, p. 200.
The carbon roadmap, and the action plans in general, 
addressing the commitment to achieve net zero carbon 
emissions by 2050 are regularly monitored by the 
governance bodies (cf. section 3.2.1.A, p. 116).

B – Scope 1 and 2 carbon emissions 
and decarbonization levers
The 2030 roadmap relies on four main levers to reduce 
scope 1 and 2 emissions:
■ actions on products  (A): product optimization and 
eco-design, including recycling efforts and the 
integration of recycled materials; 
■ industrial excellence  (B): industrial process 
improvements and productivity efforts;
■ innovation  (C): new technologies and new 
compositions;
■ the use of carbon-free energies (D). The quantification 
of the importance of each of these levers in achieving 
the 2030 target is estimated and excludes the effect 
of production volume. 
The CO₂ emissions reduction target is calculated by 
absolute value and not by intensity. In addition, 
variations in production volume to adapt to market 
demand, and changes in scope  related to acquisitions 
and disposals, have a significant impact on the 
measurement of progress towards the 2030 target. 
The success of this roadmap requires the involvement of 
all employees and a change of mentality. Carbon 
reduction objectives are included in all operational 
processes: the WCM program for ongoing productivity 
efforts, energy purchases that include securing supplies 
of carbon-free energies (renewable electricity or biogas, 
for example), and increased use of recycled materials, 
which involves the development of collection channels in 
all countries or the evolution of products through eco-
design (such as lightening and optimizing packaging to 
reduce the impact of transport).
The future availability of decarbonized and economically 
viable energy in sufficient quantities is an indispensable 
factor in achieving zero net emissions by 2050. However, 
access to this energy remains uncertain owing to 
challenges in the production, distribution and growing 
demand for low-carbon energy. Energy transport and 
the connection of sites also remain key factors to be 
included in the roadmap, certainly since the security of 
supply is not fully guaranteed.

C – Scope 3 emissions and 
decarbonization levers
The deployment of the 2030 carbon roadmap also 
includes the scope 3 reduction target. The first step is to 
improve the identification and measurement of impacts, 
while raising awareness among internal players, in 
particular buyers and logistics experts, and external 
partners, primarily suppliers. 
Actions are taken in each of the 15 categories according 
to the materiality of their impact.
Three categories are crucial to achieving the reduction 
target:
■ category 1: purchased goods and services;
■ categories 4 and 9: transport.
While scope  3 decarbonization levers are clearly 
identified, the Group’s ability to reduce its scope  3 
emissions largely depends on the ability of the Group’s 
partners to decarbonize their own operations. 
The action plan addresses three main areas:
■ product reformulation, which will contribute 
approximately 30% to achieving the target;
■ innovation and logistics performance, which will 
contribute approximately 10% to achieving the target.
■ the decarbonization of purchases through supplier-led 
initiatives, which will contribute approximately 60% to 
achieving the target.
These figures exclude any changes in methodology, 
changes in scope, improvements in information systems 
and the quality of information about emission factors. 
SBTi commitment 
and presentation of scope 3 
Category 11 of scope  3, “Use of products sold”, is not 
material for Saint-Gobain according to SBTi criteria and 
therefore does not need to be reported. The main 
components of this category are the use of boilers and 
windshields sold by the Group.
For each of these activities, the Group’s direct influence 
on reducing this category is limited and does not prevent 
the transition of these industries. Nevertheless, Mobility 
Business Unit teams are developing specific products for 
electric vehicles and are involved in their customers’ 
action plans for sustainable mobility. Similarly, the 
purchasing teams of Saint-Gobain’s distribution 
businesses work with their suppliers to reduce the carbon 
impact of heating during the use phase of buildings. The 
brands are also contributing to efforts to transform the 
construction industry by training trade professionals and 
informing users (see section 3.4.3.B, p. 163).

Other scope 3 categories
The impact of category 11, on the use of sold products, is 
concentrated on two operations: the sale of automotive 
glazing and the sale of air-conditioning and heating 
equipment by the heating equipment building trading 
brands. 
With regard to category 3 (fuel and energy-related 
emissions not included in scope  1 and 2), efforts to 
reduce fossil fuel consumption and promote the use of 
decarbonated energy sources will have a positive impact 
on the reduction of scope 3 emissions.
Regarding category 6 on business travel, the travel 
policy was updated in 2023 to:
■ check and significantly reduce the number of trips, 
including international trips;
■ systematically review the advisability of postponing or 
switching seminars and other meetings into virtual 
meetings;
■ travel by train is mandatory for all journeys of less 
than 4 hours. 
Methodology, Volume
Saint-Gobain expects an increase in scope 3 emissions as 
a result of the increase in production, and also as a result 
of actions to improve the reliability of the scope  3 
assessment carried out with suppliers.
Five principles are implemented by the purchasing 
teams and environmental experts: 
■ a digital tool available to teams at local level and by 
category to enable them to estimate scope  3 
emissions; 
■ communication kits to share the challenges and 
targets of the fight against climate change with 
suppliers;
■ the collection of information by suppliers on their 
emissions on the basis of life cycle analyses verified 
by independent third parties;
■ the integration of the maturity of suppliers regarding 
their climate commitment into the overall assessment 
of their performance; 
■ the creation of joint action plans with suppliers to 
reduce their carbon impact.
This systematization will continue to make scope  3 
assessments more reliable. It also structures action plans 
to accelerate the reduction of emissions. 
Best practices have been identified and shared with all 
Group buyers.

D – The objectives beyond 2030
a. Objective 2035
In October 2025, for Capital Markets Day and the launch 
of its “Lead & Grow” strategic plan, Saint-Gobain 
announced new targets for 2035, with an absolute 
reduction in scope  1 and 2 emissions of between 40% 
and 45% (2017 basis).
This objective was determined by taking into account 
the Group’s growth objectives, the effects of measures 
and investments linked to the “Carbon 2030” roadmap, 
and the uncertainties linked to the availability of low-
carbon and competitive energy in the countries where 
the Group operates. 
This objective was set on a voluntary basis. SBTi 
extended the validity of scope  1 and 2 and scope  3 
objectives through to 2030. A process to approve new 
objectives beyond 2030 has been initiated as part of the 
revision of methodologies, which impacts trajectory 
calculations in particular. 
At the same time, the standards and methodologies for 
assessing scope  3 are being revised by the reference 
bodies. In addition, pending an assessment of the effect 
of these changes, Saint-Gobain is moving ahead with its 
in-depth work to improve data quality and the reliability 
of the methodology implemented. 
b. Objective 2050
A new roadmap for 2050 will be established following 
the “Carbon 2030” roadmap. It will incorporate the 
technical advances identified thanks to the innovation 
efforts made over the 2020-2030 period. While in the 
2020-2030 period, innovation efforts will not produce 
much by way of tangible results in terms of reducing 
scope 1 and 2 emissions, their implementation will be the 
most significant contributor to reducing emissions in the 
2030-2050 period. 
The development of a circular economy in all countries 
where the Group is present and is also a determining 
factor in achieving the reduction target for scope  1, 2 
and 3.
The availability of decarbonized and economically viable 
energy in sufficient quantities will be an indispensable 
factor in achieving zero net emissions by 2050.
The associated financial resources will also be assessed.

3.3 More performance with less
3.3.1 GOVERNANCE AND STRATEGY
The construction sector is responsible for the consumption of 50% of natural resources and generates 40% of solid 
waste every year. Transforming the industry toward more sustainable building practices is essential to lessen its 
impact on the environment – especially considering that 50% of the buildings that will exist in 2050 have yet to be 
constructed.

that have been set. Each industrial department

B – Strategy
Construction markets are responding both to the need 
for buildings driven by demographics and growing 
urbanization in developing countries, and to the need for 
renovation, the benefits of which in terms of energy 
efficiency and CO2 emissions reduction are essential in 
the fight against climate change, under transition or 
adaptation plans alike. In this context, the number of 
geographical areas exposed to water stress is increasing, 
while water demand is constantly rising.
The circular economy is a model that helps reduce 
pressure on non-renewable natural resources. Circularity 
combined with an efficient and responsible use of 
resources is definitely a response to sustainable 
development issues, in particular the fight against climate 
change and pollution, and the preservation of 
biodiversity. For example, a study published by the 
World Economic Forum in December 2023 indicates that 
the circularity of materials can contribute to a reduction 
of around 75% in emissions linked to the materials used in 
the construction of a building by 2050, while creating 
significant economic value. 
Developing circularity is applied closer to markets and at 
country and regional level. A successful transition 
towards the circular economy will make it possible to 
offer solutions and services over the long term which 
take into account environmental, social and societal 
expectations and which balance well-being, sustainability 
and performance for stakeholders. Saint-Gobain is 
actively and collaboratively involved in discussions on 
the evolution of construction methods towards 
lightweight construction solutions that use fewer 
materials for at least the same performance. In this way, 
the Group is participating in the transformation of the 
sector towards more sustainable construction in all the 
countries where it operates.
Country platforms (cf. section 1.2.5, p. 53) and the “local 
for local” model (see section 1.2.2.D, p.45) make it 
possible to seize growth opportunities and develop the 
partnerships essential to implementing circularity: 
innovation in building design to increase the lifespan and 
modularity of constructions, waste collection and 
treatment channels throughout the value chain to create 
circular material flows, integration of these alternative 
raw materials into production, and proposals for reusable 
or recyclable solutions. Success depends on the ability of 
local players to mobilize.
Operational excellence supported by the Group’s 
expertise in innovation, industrial excellence, and 
environmental performance enables country platforms 
to further strengthen the confidence of customers and 
other partners. 
3.3.2 PRESERVING WATER
A – Strategy
The world’s water resources are finite and depend on the 
geographical area under consideration. The effects of 
climate change have a significant impact on the renewal 
of water resources. As a result, the number of areas with 
high and very high water stress continues to grow. 
Depending on the location, access to water will have to 
be divided between use by populations, agriculture or 
industry. According to the World Resources Institute 
(WRI), some 4  billion people are already exposed to 
water stress for at least one month of the year. At the 
same time, demand for water is set to increase by 30% 
by 2050. 
Reducing water withdrawals from Saint-Gobain sites is 
therefore essential to safeguarding resources, 
particularly in areas identified as water stress areas, while 
preserving water quality, particularly to ensure access to 
drinking water for populations. 
The Group’s water policy confirms its desire to minimize 
the impact of its operations on water resources and 
establishes four resources for action and prevention: 
■ mobilize internal and external stakeholders;
■ implement action plans based on assessed risks; 
■ measure progress;
■ anticipate changes in regulations in each country 
where the Group operates. 
This policy includes specific targets such as the reuse or 
recycling, internally or externally, of water used in 
industrial processes, and also the challenges of conflicts 
of use in regions of high and very high water stress. 
Saint-Gobain does its utmost to:
■ reduce water withdrawals from the natural 
environment and optimize processes to minimize 
water consumption;
■ reuse “process” water whenever possible;
■ recycle on-site or off-site with appropriate treatments;
■ not harm water quality by reducing and controlling 
discharges into the natural environment and 
preventing accidental pollution;
■ not compete with local populations for access to 
drinking water.
Policy Water Policy

sustainable water management

140 SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 Ë www.saint-gobain.com
The long-term objective is to withdraw as little water as 
possible, especially from water-stressed areas, and to 
aim for zero discharges to avoid generating new impacts 
for other natural environments and/or for other 
stakeholders. 
In the medium term, Saint-Gobain has set itself the 
following objectives:
■ 50% reduction in water withdrawals in absolute value 
between 2017 and 2030;
■ zero liquid water discharge in areas with extremely 
high water risk by 2030.
The associated action plan is based on the 
environmental management framework applied by each 
of the Group’s industrial sites (see section 3.3.4, p. 147), 
the “WCM” program (see section 1.2.7.F.a, p. 67), and the 
action plans of the sites established according to the 
specific risks identified and deployed under the 
responsibility of the countries. 
At Group level, the “Focus Sites” program (see section 
3.7.1.B, p.  206) entails supporting those sites which 
contribute 80% of the Group’s environmental indicator. 
In 2025, 44 sites (42 in 2024) contributed 80% of 
Saint-Gobain’s water discharges and 135 sites (113 in 
2024) 80% of water withdrawals. Each of these focus 
sites has drew up a short-, medium-, and long-term 
action plan to reduce its impact.
To assess the water sensitivity of the location of its sites, 
the Group uses the global “Aqueduct” atlas of the WRI 
organization. This atlas is based not only on qualitative 
and quantitative physical risks (such as water stress or 
flood risk), but also on stakeholder risk (such as access 
to water). This tool enables each industrial site to assess 
its water risk from “low” to “extremely high.” In 2025, 
303  sites (274 in 2024) accounting for approximately 
19% of Saint -Gobain’s water withdrawals and 9% of its 
discharges were located in high-risk or extremely high-
risk areas.
An internal water price mechanism applying according 
to the same model as the internal carbon price was 
implemented in 2024. This internal price is set at €1/m3 
for investments made in low or moderate water stress 
areas and €2/m3 for investments made in high or very 
high water stress areas. 
B – Risks and opportunities
 across the value chain
The material risks and opportunities identified during the 
double materiality analysis concern the risks of water 
pollution linked to the use of chemicals and substances 
of concern on sites and in the value chain, and the use of 
water in areas experiencing water stress. These are 
described in section 3.1.3.B, Environment, p. 106. 
Risks related to accidental releases from industrial sites 
are listed in section 5.1.1, p. 290. 
Regulatory changes related to the use of these products 
and substances could force the Group to accelerate its 
program to replace substances of concern, including the 
risk of having to make additional R&D and investment 
efforts. The costs of raw materials, water treatment, and 
operations during composition substitutions could be 
affected. 
Civil society’s attention to this issue could pose a 
reputational risk for the Group. 
Saint-Gobain’s range of sustainable solutions includes a 
program to replace substances of concern (see section 
1.2.7.A.b, p.  61). The Group’s ability to anticipate 
customer expectations in this area represents an 
opportunity. 
C – Managing water-related risks
a. Control over the quality 
of discharges into water
The impacts of Saint-Gobain industrial sites on water 
quality have three main origins:
■ water contamination following discharges from 
industrial or construction sites;
■ the use of substances of concern in the value chain;
■ the use of plastics in the value chain.
Most of the water discharges are from cooling plants 
where the water does not come into contact with any 
chemicals used in the process.
Since 2024, an action plan to reassess and control water 
pollution risks has been strengthened. The risk exposure 
level of a site is defined by combining the risks inherent 
in the industrial process deployed and the site’s 
geographical location. 
Each industrial Business Unit conducted an analysis of 
the potential risks based on the raw materials inflows in 
compositions, the frequency of contact between water 
and pollutants at each stage of the process, and the 
hazard of the pollutants concerned. 
The risk level associated with the location of a site 
depends on three criteria: 
■ the sensitivity of the natural environment surrounding 
the site:
– proximity to an area of biodiversity protected 
under Natura 2000,
– location in a zone of high or very high water stress 
according to WRI;
■ whether industrial water is discharged via on-site 
treatment facilities, via a wastewater or industrial 
wastewater collection network, or directly into the 
natural environment.
The treatment resources used by the sites are 
monitored. In 2025, industrial water is treated on-site 
before discharge at nearly 70% of high-priority sites 
(69% in 2025 vs. 72% in 2024) and at nearly 50% of 
lower-priority sites. The remainder is treated via external 
facilities.
As a reminder, Saint-Gobain has an environmental 
management system (cf. section 1.2.7.F, p. 67) deployed 
across all industrial sites to identify and manage 
environmental risks.

Lastly, a prioritization factor has been added based on 
the pollutants present, in particular the use of substances 
of concern. Reducing the presence of substances of 
concern is an essential factor in ensuring the quality of 
discharges. Saint-Gobain has implemented a program to 
reduce the presence of hazardous substances on its sites 
and in its production. These substances are identified 
and a program to reduce their presence is initiated 
(cf. section 3.4.2.A.c, p. 156). Concurrently, the innovation 
program for Saint -Gobain’s products and solutions 
(cf.  section 1.2.7.A, p.  60) incorporates the objective of 
eliminating or at least limiting the presence of hazardous 
substances on the sites and controlling potential risks to 
health and the environment during production processes 
and throughout the value chain.
The Group’s contribution to the risks associated with the 
presence of microplastics in water arises mainly from the 
use of plastics in the construction sector. To avoid the 
transformation of plastics into microplastics, the first 
measure is the creation of a recycling route for plastics, 
enabling materials to be collected and recycled. 
In addition, Saint -Gobain has set up an action plan to 
transform the packaging of its products so that this 
packaging can be recycled. An objective of 100% of 
recyclable packaging by the end of 2030 is supported 
by action plans involving buyers, technical teams, to 
adapt industrial equipment where necessary, and 
marketing teams. 
b. Reducing the impact 
on water resources 
Saint-Gobain uses water as a thermal fluid particularly for 
cooling, as a washing fluid, as a raw material for the 
production of mortar and gypsum-based products, and 
to provide Group employees with access to drinking 
water and sanitary facilities. This last use represents a 
marginal share of Saint-Gobain’s water withdrawals. 
For many applications, it is possible to create closed-
loop systems. In this way, water withdrawals are limited 
and correspond to the replacement of water evaporated 
during operations. The proportion of reused water in 
processes reached 85.9% in 2025. Investing in a closed-
loop system is the first step towards reducing water 
consumption and discharges alike.
When water is used as a raw material in a process, 
technical and R&D teams work on optimizing consumption 
and developing processes to reduce water requirements. 
A new pilot project to reduce the water consumption of 
the gypsum industrial process was successfully developed 
in 2025, making it possible to reuse more than 80% of 
water. These process improvements are being 
implemented as a priority in areas where water resources 
are already scarce, particularly in India. 
To address the growing risks associated with access to 
water resources, site continuity plans may incorporate 
this dimension based on their location and the water 
needs of other stakeholders, particularly the drinking 
water needs of local populations and water needs for 
agriculture. This applies in particular to sites in areas 
exposed to water stress.
Specific investments have been directed to priority 
projects in the focus sites (see section 3.7.1.B, p.  206), 
which account for nearly 80% of the Group’s water 
withdrawals and the 303 sites located in zones of high or 
very high water stress. In total, 52 projects (31 in 2024) 
have been identified for 47 focus sites and 5 non-focus 
sites but in areas of high or very high water stress. They 
concern the detection and sealing of leaks or the 
replacement of installations such as washing stations or 
compressors. 
In areas at high or very high risk of water stress, 
rainwater recovery systems can accompany action plans 
to reduce water consumption.

3.3.3 RESOURCES AND CIRCULAR ECONOMY
A – Strategy 
The challenge of the increasing scarcity of natural 
resources facing the world has many causes, all linked to 
human activities, particularly urbanization and 
population growth.
Saint-Gobain’s aim is to promote the recirculation of 
natural resources and manufactured products while 
minimizing waste at every stage of the construction 
value chain: upstream with suppliers, downstream in 
customer operations through to the end user, and within 
the Group’s own operations. 
The supply chain for raw materials (natural resources, 
manufactured materials or products) remains mostly 
local, and includes purchases of over 500 types of 
material. Over 50% of these materials are processed. 
Given this complexity, Saint -Gobain relies on external 
sources to assess the impacts and risks associated with 
the materials it consumes, in particular the “Responsible 
Purchasing” program’s risk mapping tool. Of the 
materials consumed, around 60% are identified as being 
at high or very high risk of becoming scarce, and less 
than 5% are at very high risk. 
A policy on the responsible management of resources 
applies to the entire Group. The main priorities in the 
implementation of this policy are the integration of 
maximum reused, recycled or bio-sourced content into 
its products and the maximum limitation of final waste. 
Policy Circular Economy Policy
Purpose Set strategic guidelines 
for managing and reducing 
the impact of resource use 
throughout the life cycle 
of the Group’s solutions
Scope of application All entities
Under the supervision of Senior Vice President, Human

Saint-Gobain has set targets both on reducing pressure 
on non-renewable raw materials and reducing final 
waste. Access to data to measure the Group’s impact on 
natural resources remains partial. Action plans are being 
implemented to improve performance indicators. 
Saint-Gobain will propose an update of its medium-term 
objectives. 
As regards waste, recovery at Group sites shows that the 
“zero non-recovered waste” objective is attainable. In the 
medium term, the Group has established the target of an 
80% reduction in non-recovered waste between 2017 
and 2030. This makes it possible to work first on 
reducing the overall volume of waste at the sites and 
then on identifying or developing recovery channels. 
Action plans are implemented by each of the country 
platforms according to the portfolio of products and 
solutions on offer, the technical modalities of the 
construction market, the maturity of stakeholders on the 
subject of the circular economy, and local capacities to 
create partnerships. Lastly, waste management 
regulations and public policies encourage the application 
of circular economy principles throughout the 
construction market value chain.
Technical synergies and business expertise are 
fundamental to facilitating the reformulation of product 
compositions and accelerating the substitution of natural 
raw materials for renewable or recycled ones. These 
changes potentially imply changes in industrial 
processes, so the industrial and R&D departments of the 
business lines are at the heart of this approach.
B – Managing risks 
and opportunities
The material risks and opportunities identified during the 
double materiality analysis concerning resources and 
circularity are described in section 3.1.3.B, Environment, 
p. 108.
While the construction sector consumes extracted and/
or non-renewable raw materials, applying circularity 
principles presents opportunities for Saint-Gobain and 
has positive impacts across the entire value chain.
The raw materials used by the construction sector are 
largely extracted and non-renewable. The negative 
impacts concern both the impact on nature due to 
extraction and the reserves of raw materials, which 
increase the risk of resource depletion. 
Reducing waste and treating it along the value chain 
tends to reduce potential negative impacts such as 
pollution and soil contamination from landfilling.
While there are many opportunities for developing 
circularity, they will only materialize through active 
collaboration between all stakeholders in the sector at 
the national or regional level. This is why Saint-Gobain’s 
organization into country platforms and its leadership in 
light and sustainable construction are assets that will 
accelerate the transition to greater circularity.

C – Reducing pressure 
on natural resources
Saint-Gobain has updated the impact assessment on raw 
materials used in the composition of products 
manufactured at its industrial sites. 
The assessment took into account:
■ the environmental impact, including an evaluation of 
resource scarcity;
■ the Group’s dependencies based on the quantities of 
raw materials consumed;
■ the inclusion of lists of critical materials as defined by 
the EU, for materials used by the Group.
For each of the raw materials identified, an operational 
action plan was defined, cutting across the Group’s 
business lines by bringing together purchasing, 
marketing, R&D teams and technical experts.
Action plans aimed at reducing the consumption of the 
most critical raw materials have been rolled out, mainly 
targeting gypsum, sand, soda ash, iron ore, coke, 
cement, asphalt, paper and plastics. 
Critical raw materials were identified based on:
■ annual raw material consumption, identifying the most 
significant in terms of mass;
■ the criticality of the raw material based on recognized 
external sources, in particular the database used for 
responsible purchasing risk mapping. 
Saint-Gobain has two main ways to reduce pressure on 
natural resources in its operations:
■ reducing products’ resource intensity;
■ replacing non-renewable raw materials with bio-
sourced or recycled materials.
a. Reducing natural resource intensity
To reduce the natural resource intensity of its offering, 
Saint-Gobain relies on operational excellence carried out 
in the WCM program (see section 1.2.7.F.a, p.  67). 
Performance in terms of quality and productivity 
constitutes the first step in reducing industrial waste and 
optimizing the use of resources.
Most of the Group’s business lines are working to reduce 
the resource intensity of their products by reducing the 
average weight per product unit without affecting 
technical performance. This is the case, for example, for 
car windshields and plasterboard. Several countries have 
already deployed the BANTAM program, aimed at 
making plasterboard lighter by working on industrial 
processes and product formulations. Some plants have 
been able to reduce the weight of their standard boards 
by more than 20% compared with their initial weight. 
The SLIMWOOL program, rolled out worldwide since 
2018, aims to optimize the weight of glass wool, while 
guaranteeing the product’s thermal performance.
b. Replacing natural resources with 
recycled or renewable materials 
or with by-products
Whether substitution is developed on the basis of 
closed-loop recyclable products, or by changing product 
formulations and adding renewable or recycled materials, 
or by-products from other businesses or markets, the 
quest for maximum substitution of non-recyclable raw 
materials is an element of the WCM industrial 
performance improvement program (see section 1.2.7.F.a, 
p. 67). The aim of this substitution is to maintain or even 
improve the quality and competitiveness of products and 
solutions, while reducing their carbon footprint. Thus, the 
increase in the quantity of cullet (glass from recycling) 
integrated into glass floats is underpinned by the 
creation of a collection channel for windows or glazing 
resulting from deconstruction (see section 3.3.3.D.b, 
p. 146). This enables the traceability of the material and 
quality control, and ensures the economic 
competitiveness essential to the sustainability of the 
circular economy. Similarly, in the United States, gypsum 
recovery channels from renovation or demolition sites 
are developing in an optimized geographical area around 
industrial production sites. 
Other Group products also accept the replacement of 
virgin raw materials by recycled materials from other 
consumption channels, recycling channels from 
industries other than construction. This is the case in the 
production of cast-iron pipes and ceramic grains and 
powders.
The production of glass wool can incorporate recycled 
materials from multiple markets: glass from flat glass 
recycling (window glazing or windscreens), packaging 
glass recycling, and glass wool recycling from 
construction or deconstruction sites. 
These compositional changes, which consist in reducing 
the contribution of extracted virgin materials and 
replacing them with recycled materials from end-of-life 
product recovery circuits, require adaptations to 
industrial sites, particularly in terms of raw material 
storage areas, composition workshops, and even the 
industrial processes themselves. It may also be necessary 
to set up ad hoc sorting and shredding facilities to 
prepare secondary materials.
Each country develops innovations based on its access 
to new sources of recycled or biosourced materials, or 
co-products. Actions concern not only products, but also 
their packaging. Action plans have been deployed to 
reduce packaging overall, increase the proportion of 
recycled or biosourced materials in its composition, and 
ensure that it is recyclable. For example, marketing 
teams and buyers have been working together to 
change packaging materials or their design to encourage 
recycling in existing circuits.

144 SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 Ë www.saint-gobain.com
The quantity of recycled material in products depends 
essentially on the existence, in countries or even 
territories, of efficient and sustainable collection 
networks capable of supplying the sites. Even when 
technical solutions exist to enable virgin raw materials to 
be replaced by recycled or renewable materials, or by 
co-products, increasing the proportion of recycled 
materials in production depends on the availability of 
these alternative materials. Efforts to increase available 
volumes at an acceptable cost and quality are underway 
(see section 3.3.3.D, p.  145), but the creation of supply 
chains will be gradual, country by country.
It is essential to reduce the content of hazardous 
substances in compositions to avoid their being 
disseminated or perpetuated in recycling cycles (see 
section 3.4.2.A.c, p. 156).
D – Optimizing the use 
of natural resources
Optimizing the use of natural resources means limiting 
waste throughout the value chain. This translates into:
■ reducing the waste generated at every stage of the 
life cycle of products and their packaging;
■ recovering waste through recycling channels, thereby 
multiplying the uses to which materials can be put;
■ facilitating reuse, extending the lifespan of products 
and buildings, and anticipating their end-of-life right 
from the design stage.
Saint-Gobain’s long-term ambition is to produce no non-
recovered production waste and to maximize the 
recycled, bio-sourced or co-product content of its 
products and packaging. The Group believes that waste 
should be considered as a strategic resource and that 
secondary materials (from reuse or recycling) or by-
products should be used whenever possible, as a 
substitute for non-renewable virgin resources.
Reducing the consumption of non-renewable primary 
raw materials per functional unit produced and the 
waste generated by industrial processes are the pillars of 
the sustainable resource management policy.
Overall synergies are possible across the businesses for 
each industrial process or non-renewable raw material to 
identify the deposits, material qualities or even best 
technical practices and favorable technical innovations 
that are conductive to optimizing the use of resources. 
Cross-business working groups including the Industrial 
and Technical Departments, purchases, sustainable 
development experts on the collection and processing 
of  recycled materials have been set up to develop 
these synergies.
a. Reducing waste generation 
and maximizing recovery
To achieve its objectives of reducing and recovering the 
waste generated by its industrial and trading operations, 
Saint-Gobain follows the “three Rs” principle: reduce, 
reuse, and recycle. 
The sites strive to reduce the waste generated during 
production operations and seek to reuse production 
residues in their own industrial processes. To that end, 
sites may invest in waste reprocessing units and in 
adapting their industrial processes to encourage the use 
of recycled materials in production and to recover waste 
as much as possible internally or externally. From the 
recovery of paper from plasterboards before the 
reintegration of plaster into the process to manufacture 
new plates to the treatment of waste generated during 
the production of mineral wool for recovery in the 
cement or terracotta industries (tiles and bricks), the 
industrial sites are contributing to the creation of 
recycling channels and promoting waste recovery at 
local level. 
Lastly, inventory management of finished products is 
also optimized to ensure a second life for unsold or non-
marketable products. For example, Saint-Gobain works 
in France with an association of Group retirees, 
“Saint-Gobain Solidarités”, to act as a link between the 
Group’s sites in France and local associations in order to 
facilitate donations of materials, particularly unsold 
stock. This serves to avoid the destruction of certain 
stocks and facilitate their use. 
Beyond their environmental impact and the waste of 
resources represented by industrial waste from sites, 
their recovery in recycling circuits prevents their burial 
and potential environmental consequences such as soil 
pollution or groundwater pollution. 
Saint-Gobain generates a limited amount of hazardous 
waste, 6% in 2025, of which nearly half is recovered. In 
line with the Group’s health policy and in compliance 
with local regulations, the management of hazardous 
waste is subject to special monitoring to ensure the 
health of employees, residents, customers, and users of 
its products and services is protected. 
Saint-Gobain strives to optimize the volume of packaging 
for its products and to ensure that it is recyclable. To this 
end, the Group has set itself the target of having 100% of 
its packaging recyclable by 2030. In 2025, the proportion 
of recyclable packaging reached 91%.

SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 145
b. Creating recycling channels 
for construction materials 
From plasterboards and insulation to glazing and asphalt 
shingles, most of the construction products sold by 
Saint-Gobain are recyclable and can be recycled in the 
Group’s own production processes. 
Saint-Gobain’s experience shows that, while techniques 
for recycling and recovering construction and demolition 
waste do exist, the implementation of sustainable and 
competitive channels integrating waste collection, 
treatment and recycling is highly dependent on the 
region, country or even territory. It requires the support 
of external partners, to educate customers and collect, 
sort and reprocess waste, before turning it into 
secondary raw materials suitable for reintroduction into 
the Group’s processes. 
Lastly, recycling channels will be more efficient and 
competitive if buildings are designed to be more 
modular and incorporate deconstruction from the design 
phase. This will prevent material losses from mixtures of 
materials experienced in current demolitions.
Recovering waste on construction sites 
and during demolition
Whatever the construction products considered, for 
recovery to be effective it is essential that craftsmen sort 
their waste on site during construction, deconstruction 
or renovation operations.
Where present on a country platform, building materials 
trading brands are organizing themselves to take back 
construction site waste from the same types of building 
materials, products and equipment they sell. In France, 
construction site waste collection points for craftsmen 
have been set up close to sales outlets. Various 
partnerships have been set up with specialized 
companies and start-ups such as Tri’n’collect to speed 
up the recovery, sorting and recycling of construction 
site waste.
Saint-Gobain has developed a network in Europe, 
Saint-Gobain Glass Recycling, to facilitate the recycling 
of flat glass from dismantling or processing waste. The 
aim is to qualify local companies capable of collecting 
and dismantling glass products, and which are 
committed to promoting the closed-loop float recycling 
of end-of-life glass. Some 20 partners have already 
joined the network, offering processing and recycling 
services for glass products. In France, the quantities of 
end-of-life glazing from buildings returned to the 
Group’s glass furnaces have more than doubled every 
year over the past three years. Machines have been 
developed by Saint -Gobain in the United Kingdom to 
automatically separate glass from the rest of the 
materials making up a window. These machines are now 
deployed in several European countries.
In 2019, the Group launched its I-LOOP project, 
supported by the European Union through its LIFE 
funding program. The purpose of this project is to 
contribute to the gradual recovery of glass wool waste 
generated on construction, renovation or demolition 
sites, waste currently most often landfilled. The initiative 
aims to offer construction market firms new value chains 
for glass wool recycling in France, Germany and parts of 
Scandinavia, as a cost-effective alternative to landfill.
Ecophon, a producer of acoustic panels and ceiling 
systems, has also developed a recycling and reuse 
service called “SoundCircularity” to collect and recycle 
end-of-life ceilings. This service is available in Sweden, 
Finland and France. The ambition is to extend its 
availability across Europe.
Proven recycling and recovery technologies
Once collected, waste needs to be transformed into a 
new raw material. 
For example, plasterboards recovered from construction 
sites are reprocessed to remove contaminants; the 
processing is completed by shredding and separating 
the paper on both sides of the board. While plaster itself 
can be recycled in a closed loop and under certain 
conditions without any loss of material, the presence of 
paper on both sides of the board has a negative impact 
on the manufacturing process and must therefore be 
eliminated as far as possible. Today, some Saint-Gobain 
plants achieve an average recycled content of 30%, most 
of which comes from construction or demolition 
plaster waste. 
For flat glass, the recycling of window glass, façade glass 
or automotive glass is infinitely possible as long as the 
collected glass elements meet the quality requirements 
of a float furnace, in particular that contaminants of all 
kinds are eliminated. Integration into products is 
therefore mainly dependent on the existence of efficient 
and sustainable collection networks able to ensure 
sorting compliant with the desired quality specifications. 
Glass wool from renovation, building demolition or waste 
generated during construction operations can also be 
recycled for new glass wool production. A new 
technology has been developed by Saint-Gobain and has 
been operational since 2023 at the Chemillé site in 
France. This technology is gradually being rolled out 
across Europe. 
The abrasives business line is also working on the 
development of technologies to recycle grinding wheels 
once they have reached the end of their life, with the aim 
of being able to recover abrasive grains for reuse as a 
replacement for virgin materials. A reprocessing unit 
already exists in Brazil.

146 SAINT-GOBAIN • UNIVERSAL REGISTRATION DOCUMENT 2025 Ë www.saint-gobain.com
The Valoref Group specializes in the treatment and 
recovery of waste from technical ceramics and 
refractories. For example, it recovers bricks during repairs 
or reconstructions of glass furnaces from Saint-Gobain or 
its competitors. The waste collected is primarily recycled 
in the refractory production chain. The other recovery 
circuits are the manufacture of construction materials 
such as mortars or tiles, and other industrial additives.
c. Facilitating reuse and recycling
From the design of products, solutions and services to 
the benefits expected by customers and end users and 
products’ end-of-life management, Saint -Gobain’s 
offering must enable more recycled, renewable materials 
and co-products to be included so as to reduce the 
consumption of virgin raw materials, facilitate the 
recycling or reuse of products at the end of their life 
cycle to successfully meet market needs with a limited 
impact on natural resources, and extend product 
lifespans. The same approach applied to products also 
applies to the packaging that accompanies them. 
Action plans are implemented at Group level and then 
rolled out at national level to improve the recyclability 
and increase the recycled or bio-sourced content of 
packaging used. 
The principle of optimizing natural resources is one of 
the benefits identified as part of the program to develop 
the offering of sustainable, high-performance solutions 
(see section 1.2.7.A, p.  60). This criterion includes both 
limiting the use of exhaustible natural resources and 
integrating recycled or renewable materials or co-
products into product compositions.
While it is difficult to extend the lifespan of construction 
products, it is possible to optimize the use of buildings. 
Thinking about building design and construction 
methods anticipates the possibility of modular buildings 
to make them more flexible and adapt their use during 
their life cycle. For example, Saint -Gobain’s offerings 
include the ability to dismantle and reuse certain 
products, such as lightweight plasterboard partitions. 
For example, the 60,000 square meters of interior 
partitions in the Athletes’ Village buildings were specially 
designed to be dismantled, and the majority of materials 
will be reused, in order to meet the Paris 2024 Games’ 
objectives of being responsible and exemplary in terms 
of natural resource consumption.
3.3.4 CONTROLLING THE IMPACT ON BIODIVERSITY 
AND THE RISKS OF DEFORESTATION
The Group’s impacts on biodiversity are associated with 
the markets it serves, and in particular construction 
markets. New construction generates land take, 
generating a risk of biodiversity loss. These markets 
continue to consume large amounts of extracted raw 
materials, particularly for cement production and 
quarries, modifying the natural environment and 
presenting a significant risk for local ecosystems.
To reduce these pressures, lightweight construction (see 
section 1.2.2.A, p. 43) is an alternative as it limits the use 
of extractive materials. Depending on the context, 
wooden structures can replace heavy concrete, brick or 
cement structures.
In addition, Saint-Gobain sources raw materials likely to 
have an impact on deforestation, including wood for its 
trading activities, wood pulp for paper manufacturing, 
and wood for its packaging (pallets, crates). 
Saint-Gobain reinforced its approach and action plans 
when renewing its commitments to Act4Nature. 
Validated in 2025 by this independent organization, 
these commitments are published on its website and 
that of the Group (Act4Nature).
The commitments are based in particular on the 
implementation of a Forest Policy (see section 3.3.4.B, 
p. 148) and on the increased maturity of the organization, 
which now allows it to more effectively anticipate the 
potential impacts of its activities and supply chain.
A – Biodiversity
Saint-Gobain is committed to protecting biodiversity, in 
particularly at its high-impact sites or in areas with 
remarkable biodiversity. Thanks to the experience 
acquired in the field of extraction activities, the Group 
now has strong internal expertise in the area. It has 
adopted a biodiversity policy aimed at preserving, 
restoring, enhancing and boosting biodiversity and to 
this end is encouraging the involvement of all relevant 
stakeholders.

A mapping study of the Group’s sites assesses their 
sensitivity to ecosystems based on their proximity to 
areas with high biodiversity value (IUCN, Natura 2000, 
RAMSAR). This analysis identified some 100 priority sites, 
mainly quarries, for the implementation of biodiversity 
management plans. 
In 2025, 35% of active quarries had a validated plan 
(28% in 2024).
By the end of 2025, 15 of the Group’s quarries and 
30 active sites (excluding quarries), i.e. 45 sites in total, 
will be located in protected areas. 
For industrial sites, a catalog of best practices in the 
area  of biodiversity was created this year to facilitate 
the  implementation of biodiversity actions at the 
Group’s sites. 
The Group’s quarries are exploited and then restored 
with the aim of preserving the environment in 
compliance with local rules, by reducing visual, sound 
and ecological impacts as much as possible. Of the 108 
(100 in 2024) underground or open quarries operated by 
the Group worldwide, 85 were in operation in 2025, and 
the vast majority are for the production of gypsum 
(more than 50%). A policy on the environment and 
biodiversity at all Saint-Gobain’s quarries and mines was 
published in 2019, capitalizing on the experience 
acquired over many years in gypsum.

B – Combating deforestation
To manage deforestation risks, Saint -Gobain has 
implemented a Forest Policy applicable to all Group 
entities and is committed to non-deforestation. This 
policy is based on the principles recommended by 
recognized international institutions in this area. 
This general policy is supplemented by two specific 
policies:
■ a timber purchasing policy in place since the early 
2000s and updated in 2025;
■ a paper and wood pulp purchasing policy published 
in 2025.

commitment” in October 2025. The brochure specifies 
that the Group purchases most of its timber in Europe 
(93% in 2024, and 95% in 2025).
The actions taken to control the risks associated with 
timber purchases are described in section 3.4.6.C, p. 177. 
With regard to the use of paper, suppliers have for many 
years developed paper recycling routes in the main 
countries where the Group operates, increasing the 
recycled materials use rate to nearly 100%. 
For some technical paper purchases, where it is more 
difficult to integrate recycled material, Saint -Gobain 
adopts a reasonable diligence approach and relies on 
recognized certifications to verify the responsible 
management of forests.

B – Strategy
The Principles of Conduct and Action (section 1.2.7.E.a, 
p. 64) are the Group’s benchmark for business conduct, 
in particular the four Principles of Action that govern the 
decision-making of all managers and employees in the 
performance of their duties. The five Principles of 
Conduct are the fundamental values that unite all 
employees. 
This Saint-Gobain code of ethics is underpinned by the 
applicable conventions of the International Labor 
Organization (ILO), the International Bill of Human 
Rights, the Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises of the 
Organization for Economic Co-operation and 
Development (OECD), and the OECD Anti-Bribery 
Convention. 
The implementation of the Principles of Conduct and 
Action takes the form of specific commitments and 
policies applicable to all entities and employees in their 
work for Saint-Gobain, including dialog with stakeholders. 
In particular, the signing of the supplier policy by the 
partners shows their commitment to the Group’s values 
and their desire to develop medium- and long-term 
partnerships. Suppliers and subcontractors commit not 
only to ethical business practices but also to respect for 
their employees’ rights, workplace health and safety 
compliance, and respect for individuals. 
Whether industrial sites, logistics platforms or builders’ 
merchants, Saint-Gobain’s operations (see value chain 
diagram, section 1.2.5, p. 53) directly or indirectly impact 
the lives of individuals and communities. 
In particular, industrial sites, and the sites of Group 
customers or suppliers, present exposure to specific risks 
for individuals and communities owing to the raw 
materials used and stored, the industrial processes 
followed, or the circulation of goods, raw materials or 
finished products. Risk prevention and accident 
monitoring measures are deployed wherever the Group 
operates (see section 1.2.7.F.a, p. 67).
3.4.2 CREATE A HEALTHY, SAFE AND ENGAGING 
WORK ENVIRONMENT
Saint-Gobain’s Human Resources (HR) policy ensures the 
provision of an environment that is conducive to the 
employee’s professional and personal growth and 
balances job-related performance with their well-being. 
This policy requires the compulsory buy-in of all 
employees for the Group’s values as expressed in its 
code of ethics, the Principles of Conduct and Action. 
Saint-Gobain’s Human Resources policy must allow 
for  the rapid adaptation of the organization and, in 
particular, careful management of changes in skills 
requirements, support for employees in the face of 
major transformations, as well as attraction and retention 
of talent.
To do so, it incorporates two dimensions:
■ global coordination tasked with defining a common 
framework for all Group employees, incorporating 
ethical values, respect for human rights, the 
deployment of managerial principles based on trust, 
empowerment and collaboration, and the offering 
of training programs to better handle major cultural 
and market transformations, the establishment of 
ambitious and demanding health and safety 
objectives, social protection, diversity or any other 
subject that brings about decent working 
conditions for all;
■ local implementation, by the HR teams in charge of 
social dialog, wage policy, local adaptation and 
implementation of action plans serving to achieve 
Saint-Gobain’s objectives following a philosophy of 
subsidiarity and close proximity.
The new organization structure implemented in 
July  2025 further strengthens this balance between 
the global and local dimensions. 
Each country implements Saint- Gobain’s policies and 
major commitments (health, safety, diversity, etc.) by 
adapting the action plans, stages of attainment and 
tools to specific factors in the country (regulatory, 
cultural, etc.), without compromising on the expected 
performance level or the Group’s values. HR policies 
are disseminated by the global HR network. The local 
teams have guides to support their deployment, and 
special training sessions are organized by the HR 
Academy. Practical guides and training provided by 
the global support teams are available for the 
following topics in particular: social dialog, diversity, 
remuneration and benefits, talent management, 
recruitment and integration, and mobility.
The Human Resources Committee meets every month 
under the presidency of the Senior Vice President, 
Human Resources and Corporate Social Responsibility. It 
brings together the directors of the HR support 
functions, in particular the Director of Social Affairs and 
the Director of Group Talent and Executive Career 
Management, and the HR directors of the various 
regions. These meetings ensure the regular monitoring of 
local and global action plans and the analysis of key 
HR indicators.
In addition, when companies are acquired, coordination 
takes place in order to align the HR policies of the new 
entities with the Group’s principles. Newly integrated 
entities are monitored centrally to ensure that the 
policies applied correspond to those disseminated by 
the Group and applied within the network.
